metadata.title: Business Broker vs M&A Advisor vs Investment Banker: Which Advisor Do You Actually Need?
metadata.author: Exit On Your Terms
metadata.shortDescription:
Choosing between a business broker, an M&A advisor, or an investment banker to sell your company comes down to deal size, buyer access, fees, and licensing.

Not sure which one fits your business? Use the free exit planning tools at https://exitonyourterms.com/tools.

What's the difference between a business broker, an M&A advisor, and an investment banker? Business brokers typically sell smaller Main Street companies (owner earnings usually under $1 million) in asset sales, marketing them through blind ads and buyer databases. M&A advisors handle more complex sales, often $1–5 million+ in EBITDA, going to private equity groups, strategic buyers, and wealthy individuals or families. Investment banks generally start around $10–20 million in EBITDA and up. Hiring the wrong one for your size can cost you upfront fees and the right buyers.

In this video you'll learn:
• What does a business broker do, and which businesses do they sell?
• When does it make sense to hire an M&A advisor?
• Why a structured auction process can backfire for smaller companies
• How much brokers, M&A advisors, and investment bankers charge
• How each type of intermediary is licensed (real estate vs FINRA/SEC)
• Why access to the right buyer pool matters more than prestige

FAQ
Q: Do I need an investment banker to sell my small business?
A: Usually not. Investment banks typically work on much larger deals, and their fees and buyer networks aren't built for small companies.

Q: How are business brokers paid?
A: Mostly at closing, as a percentage of the sale price that often steps down as the price rises (for example, 10% of the first million, 8% of the second, 6% of the third).

Q: Do M&A advisors charge upfront fees?
A: Many do, such as a retainer, valuation, or market assessment fee (often $5,000–$15,000), and sometimes a monthly work fee credited back at closing.

Michael Wildeveld of Exit On Your Terms draws on 24 years of sell-side M&A experience to help business owners plan their exit. This video is for owners comparing sell-side intermediaries before a business sale, whether a Main Street business or a lower middle market company sold to private equity, strategic, or family office buyers.

This video is educational and not financial or legal advice.

metadata.title: M&A Advisor vs Business Broker: Which One Should You Use to Sell Your Business?
metadata.author: The Digital Merchant
metadata.shortDescription:
f you're planning to sell a business, I break down the real differences between an M&A Advisor vs Business Broker and explain how deal size changes everything from fees and due diligence to buyer networks and sale structure. I compare local business brokers, online business brokerages, and institutional M&A firms while covering platforms like Quiet Light, Empire Flippers, Website Closers, Houlihan Lokey, and Lincoln International.

I also explain:
* Why business brokers usually handle smaller local and online business sales
* How M&A advisors manage complex 7, 8, and 9-figure transactions
* The difference between broker commissions and M&A advisory fee structures
* What confidential information memorandums and sell-side processes look like
* Which platforms fit six-figure, seven-figure, and enterprise-level exits

I share where Quiet Light fits for online businesses, why Empire Flippers works for smaller deals, when Website Closers makes sense for large online exits, and how firms like Houlihan Lokey and Lincoln International operate in high-value M&A transactions.

Read our complete write-up here: https://thedigitalmerchant.com/ma-advisor-vs-business-broker/

#MAAdvisorVsBusinessBroker #BusinessBroker #MAAdvisor #SellABusiness #BusinessAcquisition #BusinessSale #EmpireFlippers #QuietLight #WebsiteClosers #MergersAndAcquisitions

metadata.title: What does “Market” actually mean? | Main Street Deals
metadata.author: SMB Law Group LLP
metadata.shortDescription:
Eric Pacifici and Kevin Henderson tackle one of the most contentious issues in deal negotiations on Main Street Deals: determining what terms are actually "market" in lower middle market M&A. They break down how market standards vary dramatically based on deal size, with escrows being standard in mid-market transactions but nearly nonexistent on Main Street. The discussion covers how buyer type, financing structure, industry, and negotiating leverage all influence what qualifies as market practice, and why even experienced attorneys from different markets can have completely opposing views on the same deal points.

They discuss:
- Why the ABA Private Target M&A Deal Points Study is considered the gold standard for market data despite its membership requirements
- How inexperienced lawyers misuse deal point studies by citing statistics without understanding the underlying rationale
- The critical role of deal diplomacy in challenging opposing counsel's market positions without destroying the transaction
- Why clients ultimately live with post-closing risk regardless of what market studies suggest

This episode gives buyers, sellers, and their advisors a practical framework for navigating market standard disputes in small business acquisitions.

Topics:
00:00 - Intro
05:00 - What does market actually mean in M&A
06:08 - Why market varies by deal context
06:45 - Escrows in middle market versus Main Street
12:09 - Deal point studies and market research
12:18 - The ABA private M&A deal point study
16:00 - Using deal point studies in negotiations
18:12 - Client decision-making versus lawyer advice
21:00 - The lawyer's role beyond form documents
24:03 - Identifying experienced M&A counsel
26:48 - Navigating market disputes between lawyers
27:03 - Deal diplomacy and sidebar conversations
28:54 - When inexperienced lawyers misuse market data
30:24 - Understanding the forest from the trees
36:22 - Volume and expertise in M&A practice
38:49 - Closing thoughts
______________________________________________________

Learn more: https://smblaw.group/

Financial advisors, this 2019 episode explains the three specialists who help sell a business: the business broker, the M&A advisor, and the investment banker. I cover the difference between them and how to use your team to pick the right one based on the size of the business.

Owners my RIA served often didn't know which of these three to call when they planned an exit.

Owners often don't know who to call when it's time to sell. Knowing these players and having good relationships with them makes you very valuable to owner clients.

- The Business Broker, M& A Advisor, Investment Banker
- Three specialist players for your team
- The Business Broker
- The Mergers & Acquisitions Advisor
- The difference between an M&A Advisor and Business Broker
- Investment Banker
- Which player do you need?
- Use your team to pick the right player

LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/justingoodbread/

metadata.title: How Much Is My Business Really Worth? (How Buyers, Lenders & Brokers Value Small Businesses)
metadata.author: Deal Street - Small to Lower Middle Market M&A
metadata.shortDescription:
DESCRIPTION
What is your business really worth? Most owners already have a number in mind, and it's often too high or too low. Either way, it can cost you hundreds of thousands of dollars.

In this video, M&A advisor and business broker Shep Campbell breaks down how small businesses actually get valued: what the business earns (SDE or EBITDA), the multiple the market will pay, and the risks that move that multiple. You'll also hear the mistakes owners make most often and why the bank gets a vote on your price.

Want a professional opinion of what your business is worth? Visit https://dealstreetdigest.com to work with me directly.

metadata.title: Understanding Aircraft Brokerage: Standards, Risk, and Trust
metadata.author: Own The Jet
metadata.shortDescription:
Anyone can sell a private jet.

In this episode of Own The Jet, Phil Jordan, Chairman of the Global Aircraft Dealers Association (GLADA), breaks down what that means in practice, and why it creates real risk in high-value aircraft transactions.

With no licensing requirement in aircraft brokerage, the gap between experienced professionals and opportunistic sellers is wider than most buyers realize. Phil shares how deals actually happen behind the scenes, where transactions tend to break down, and what separates disciplined operators from the rest.

We also discuss how GLADA is working to bring structure, training, and accountability to the industry, and what buyers should look for when choosing who to trust in a multi-million dollar deal.

For anyone considering buying or selling an aircraft, this is a clear, experience-driven look at how to navigate the market the right way.

To learn more, visit https://www.glada.aero/

Brought to you by: https://www.aspenaerogroup.com

Produced by: https://www.savagemedia.com

#privatejet #aviation #businessaviation #ownthejet #podcast

metadata.title: How To Become A Yacht Broker – My favorite work ever!
metadata.author: Gerry Mendria
metadata.shortDescription:
http://www.workwithgerry.com - How To Become A Yacht Broker  

Don’t stop at how to become a yacht broker … become the best yacht broker!

In all sales, as in life … integrity is the most important ingredient.

I had just returned home from crossing the Pacific Ocean on my 30’ sloop, was back, I’d boated most of my life and knew and loved boats! 

I started a yacht brokerage office for a larger company.  They thought I’d lost my mind when I negotiated my wages … I wanted no base salary, but a larger % of the commissions.

  They were thrilled – and so was I.  

My entire focus was always on being honest and helpful to everyone, even my competition, for the benefit of the customers.
 
This served me really well in the end.  Soon customers were knocking on my door.

In 6 months, rather than 2 years projected … our brokerage was profitable. 

 I had fun … but, there was a huge downside!!!!!

Every single day of the summer, even weekends….I worked.  I didn’t get to spend time with my wife and friends.

  Not good!  And, no time for boating.

Recently, I took that same passion and those principles to a business where I can help a lot of people….got my time back. 

I am having a great time doing it … Boating anyone?

If you’re looking for the best of both worlds….click on http://www.workwithgerry.com. 

 I’ll bet anything you’ll get as excited about this as I did.

metadata.title: HOW DO I GET STARTED AS A YACHT BROKER
metadata.author: Yacht Broker Masterclass
metadata.shortDescription:
www.yachtbrokermasterclass.com

Some recipients of the Yacht Broker Master Class Newsletter already work for brokerage companies, but most do not and wonder how they can get in to the yachting industry. This week I want to give you some advice based on a reality of this business. 
If you want to be successful, you really need to live in a place where there are yachts and yacht owners. If you live far from the ocean and seriously want to be a part of this amazing world, the first thing you need to do is find work in Fort Lauderdale, Palma, Antibes, any one of hundreds of locations where yachts can be found. You may not immediately find work with a yacht brokerage company, but it is very likely that you will find work with a business that is associated with yachting.
This will give you an opportunity to build up your contacts and connections, to meet yacht Captains and yacht managers, and above all to network with folk who one day will become valuable sources of information and leads. As you continue to develop these connections there is no doubt that you will learn of buyers and sellers who need the services of a yacht broker. It may not happen immediately, but it will most certainly happen eventually if you are patient, and tenacious, and keep your eyes and ears open. 
For those of you reading this who already live in such a location, I highly recommend that you find work withing the yachting industry as a first step in becoming a broker. Be strategic in your thinking, look for opportunities, learn the names and types of yachts that you are providing a service for, start to build your reputation as soon as you can.
And of course, lay the basis of becoming a future yacht broker by enrolling in the Yacht Broker Master Class!

Ever wondered how a yacht broker can realistically earn €1,000,000 in commissions?
In this video I break down the mindset, math and method behind the so-called “million-dollar myth” in yacht sales.

We’ll talk about:
 • Why the hardest part isn’t the money, but your mindset
 • How a broker can earn €1,000,000 in commissions with a 5% fee
 • Realistic examples: 2 × €10M yachts, 4 × €5M, 10 × €2M, 20 × €1M
 • Why yacht sales is not a closed club for the rich only
 • The hard work behind luxury commissions (calls, viewings, surveys, negotiations)
 • A clear, professional path to your first million in commissions

This is not a “get rich quick” video.
It’s a realistic look at what it takes to succeed in yacht brokerage – and why your first million is possible if you are ready to do the work.

I also share how I’ve structured my experience into my program The Yacht Closer – a step-by-step system for people who want to enter or scale in the yacht sales industry.

metadata.title: How Private Jet Brokers Actually Make Money | Hidden Commissions Explained
metadata.author: MarginCallMedia
metadata.shortDescription:
Private jet quotes usually show one big number—concealing how much the broker is actually taking off the top.

In this video, we break down how private aviation brokers make money, the difference between operator commissions and hidden markups, and how to make sure you're getting a fair rate.




#PrivateJets #PrivateAviation #CharterBroker #AviationFinance #HiddenFees #losangeles

segments.text: You request a private flight from Dubai
to London and a broker sends you a sleek
professional quote. The bottom line, a
Then you check with a second broker.
They offer you the exact same aircraft
departing on the exact same day, but
their price is $85,000.
Looking at this invoice diagram, that
$15,000 difference isn't covering extra
jet fuel, higher landing fees, or better
crew salaries.
The bundled number is an illusion.
You're actually looking at the hidden
margin, an unregulated commission
secretly baked into the quote before it
reaches your inbox.
Accepting a bundled price without
knowing the broker's cut creates a
massive structural conflict of interest.
It drains cash from the client and as we
will see, it actively compromises flight
safety. To understand why this happens,
we have to look at exactly how private
aviation brokers make their money.
The industry splits into two very
distinct camps, aircraft sales and
aircraft charter.
Aircraft sales brokers operate a lot
like high-end agents. When a client buys
a $20 million jet, the broker earns a
predictable commission paid at closing.
It is a low frequency, high value
transaction.
This data visualization shows the stark
difference in compensation.
While a $20 million sale yields a tiny
sliver of commission, charter brokers
arrange individual lower value flights
where their cut swings wildly, taking up
anywhere from 5 to 30% of the total cost
per trip.
Because charter brokers rely on high
percentages taken from lower value
frequent transactions, their primary
financial incentive is to maximize their
margin on every single flight they book.
So, how exactly do they extract that
margin from a client? There are three
specific financial models charter
brokers use.
The first is the operator cut. In this
setup, the client pays the retail price
and the aircraft operator quietly kicks
back a set percentage to the broker out
of their own wholesale profit.
The second is the transparent fee.
Here, the broker shows the client the
exact wholesale cost of the flight plus
a fixed, clearly defined advisory fee.
Both numbers appear as separate line
items on the bill.
This flowchart maps out the third and
most prevalent method, the undisclosed
markup, known in the industry as the
spread.
The broker buys the flight at a
wholesale baseline and resells it to you
at whatever retail ceiling the market
will tolerate.
Because the spread is the dominant
compensation model in charter aviation,
the vast majority of private flyers end
up paying a blind premium that they can
neither verify nor negotiate.
This creates a direct behavioral
consequence.
If a broker's income relies entirely on
the size of the markup, they are
financially driven to recommend
operators who offer the widest margins
rather than the operators who provide
the best aircraft for your specific
route.
This network node diagram traces a
practice called sub-brokering, where a
flight request bounces through multiple
middlemen. Each layer quietly tax on
their own margin.
To protect the spread, brokers
aggressively squeeze the operator's
wholesale price, forcing them to find
immediate cost savings.
But in the real world, finding cost
savings on a private jet means cutting
deeply into the operational budget. It
translates to operators reducing crew
rest periods, hiring less experienced
pilots, or delaying crucial maintenance
scheduling.
An undisclosed markup is a structural
hazard. It takes the broker's profit
margin and pits it directly against the
client's physical safety.
Take a recent case study involving the
firm X1 Jets.
When a group of 12 clients requested a
private flight from London to Ireland,
the firm checked the commercial
schedules and realized the group could
save 97%
of the cost by flying on a standard
airline.
X1 Jets did the right thing and
recommended the commercial flight to
their clients,
but that decision highlighted severe
paradox.
Under the standard commission model,
giving the client the most efficient,
cost-effective travel advice earned the
broker exactly zero dollars.
This reveals the core flaw in how the
traditional industry is structured.
Because brokers are paid strictly to put
passengers on private jets, the system
actively punishes objective client-first
travel advice.
As long as a broker's revenue depends
entirely on a client boarding a private
jet, they can never truly act as an
independent advisor.
Recognizing this flaw is actively
fracturing the private aviation
industry. It has paved the way for
fee-only consultancy models that
separate the advice from the asset.
In a consultancy model, clients pay a
flat membership or coordination fee. In
return, the operator's exact wholesale
price is passed directly to the client
with absolutely zero markup.
This means there is one highly specific
question every client must ask before
putting pen to paper on a charter
agreement.
What is the operator being paid for this
flight, and what are you being paid?
If a broker deflects that question,
talks about all-inclusive pricing, or
refuses to provide two distinct numbers,
it is the ultimate proof that you are
paying an undisclosed markup.
Securing a transparent contract
eliminates the hidden financial
incentives that lead to compromised
flights.
When you know exactly how a broker makes
their money, you can verify whether they
are working for your benefit or simply
protecting their spread.

✈️ Book a 1-on-1 call with me: https://www.everyexpert.com/alexbengoechea
Free 30-min intro calls available. Paid sessions for aircraft buyers, aspiring brokers, and pilots chasing a career in aviation.

Want to become an aircraft broker but don’t know where to start? In this video, I walk you through the exact steps to launch your own aircraft brokerage business — from legal setup to finding clients and closing deals. Whether you're passionate about aviation or looking for a new business opportunity, this step-by-step breakdown will give you the clarity and roadmap you need to get started.

📘 Download my eBook
Want a written copy of the steps I cover in this video? Grab the free eBook here:

My Aircraft Broker Course shows you everything you need to launch and grow your aircraft brokerage — in detail. It includes:
✅ Business setup guidance
✅ Client acquisition strategies
✅ Learn how the sales process works
✅ Templates for all the contracts and agreements used in real transactions
✅ And much more
👉 Enroll here: https://www.aircraftbrokeracademy.com/the-course

Some states require aircraft brokers to secure a surety bond as part of licensing. If that applies to you, you can get one from:

Trade Base Hub | NCNDA Professional Protection

In this video, Trade Base Hub explains why an NCNDA — Non-Circumvention and Non-Disclosure Agreement — is essential before parties exchange sensitive information, disclose contacts, or progress serious commercial transactions.

An NCNDA helps protect confidential information, business introductions, broker relationships, transaction pathways, and defined commercial opportunities. It also reduces the risk of circumvention, unauthorised disclosure, confusion, and undocumented deal activity.

Trade Base Hub supports principals, brokers, consultants, and intermediaries with structured document services, including NCNDA drafting and review, CIS/KYC preparation, IMFPA and fee protection, Proof of Funds review, Proof of Product review, deal summaries, broker genealogy disclosure, private deal room setup, and dispute notice support.

Trade Base Hub does not act as a bank, law firm, broker-dealer, investment adviser, escrow agent, or regulated financial intermediary. Our focus is document preparation, transaction organisation, commercial process support, and deal-readiness.

Serious transactions require serious documentation.

Visit Trade Base Hub:
https://whop.com/trade-base-hub-b0aa

#TradeBaseHub #NCNDA #BrokerProtection #DocumentServices #FeeProtection #TransactionReadiness

This series explains what N C N D A's are, when they work, why many [music] fail, and how professionals use them properly across jurisdictions. An N C N D A is a contractual protection tool. It governs how information is shared and prevents parties from bypassing introductions or misusing confidential material. It applies equally in domestic transactions [music] and cross-border engagements. For an N C N D A to be enforceable, the parties must be clearly identified. Each party should complete a client information sheet or know your client process and provide valid government-issued photo identification. Courts do not enforce agreements where the parties cannot be clearly identified. One of the most common reasons N C N [music] D A's fail is vague scope. Non-descriptive opportunities and generic language [music] are rarely enforceable. N C N D A's should define a specific opportunity or clearly list scopes [music] through a formal annexure that is updated and executed by all parties. Not all information qualifies as confidential. For protection to apply, >> [music] >> the information must be substantive and unique. Publicly available information or information that can reasonably be obtained elsewhere is not protected under an N C N D A. N C N D A's are effective for protecting introductions, proprietary deal structures, and sensitive commercial exchanges. They are not a replacement for commercial or compensation agreements. N C N D A's are protective instruments, not commercial agreements. They do not define payment, commissions, [music] or services. Using an N C N D A as a substitute for these agreements is a common and costly mistake. [music] An N C N D A must be executed before any protected information is shared. It must be signed by authorized parties and stored [music] with proper records. Poor execution undermines enforceability. Properly structured NCNDAs are enforceable both domestically and internationally. Courts focus on clarity, identification, scope, and substance, not geography. Poor drafting [music] fails everywhere. Good drafting holds up. Professional transactions rely on process, [music] not hope. Trade base hub supports NCNDA templates, drafting, execution workflows, and CS and KYC processes, [music] helping professionals structure transactions correctly from the start. Define clearly. Document properly. Protect professionally.

NCNDA Explained: How to Protect Your Commission in International Commodity Trading (2026 Guide) | IXH TRADING


A broker introduces a supplier to a buyer… and gets cut out of the deal. The NCNDA (Non-Circumvention & Non-Disclosure Agreement) is built to prevent exactly that.

In this video, IXH TRADING explains:
00:00 Introduction
00:37 What is an NCNDA?
01:22 Where NCNDAs are used
01:55 7 key clauses

06:12 ICC arbitration in numbers (2025)
07:02 Case scenario
07:42 Due-diligence checklist
08:34 Quick Q&A
09:27 7 golden rules

metadata.title: Does A Non Disclosure Agreement Need To Be Notarized?
metadata.author: County Portal Law
metadata.shortDescription:
Does A Non Disclosure Agreement Need To Be Notarized?

While a Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA) is a legally binding contract, notarization is generally not a mandatory legal requirement for an NDA to be enforceable in most jurisdictions. The validity of an NDA stems from the agreement of the parties involved and their understanding and acceptance of its terms, typically demonstrated through their signatures. However, notarization can offer significant benefits by providing an additional layer of authentication, serving as proof that the signatures on the document are indeed those of the individuals who signed it and that they appeared before the notary public. This can be particularly valuable in disputes, as it can deter claims of forgery or duress, making the NDA more robust and easier to enforce in court. Therefore, while not strictly necessary, notarizing an NDA is a highly recommended practice for enhanced security and evidentiary support.

metadata.title: Understanding NCND Agreements  Protecting Intermediaries in Business Deals
metadata.author: UpCounsel
metadata.shortDescription: Learn how an NCND agreement protects intermediaries in trade deals, prevents circumvention, and ensures confidentiality between unfamiliar business parties.

segments.text: NCND agreements are crucial tools for
protecting intermediaries in business
transactions.
When a broker or middleman [music]
connects buyers and sellers who don't
know each other, these agreements ensure
they don't get cut out of the deal after
making the introduction.
An NCND, which stands for
non-ircumvention and non-disclosure
agreement, serves two essential
purposes.
It prevents parties from bypassing
[music]
the intermediary who brought them
together and it ensures that
confidential business information
remains secure. These agreements are
particularly common in international
trade [music] where multiple brokers may
be involved in a single transaction.
The structure of an NCND agreement
typically includes two distinct parts.
Part A contains special conditions
unique to the specific agreement and
must be completed by each party
involved. Part B includes standard
clauses that follow the [music]
International Chamber of Commerce
guidelines for NCND agreements.
Both sections are necessary to create a
valid and [music] enforcable agreement.
Intermediary services can range widely
in scope. At the most basic level, an
intermediary might simply share
information or provide introductions
between parties. In more involved
arrangements, they might facilitate
direct contact [music] between the
counterpart and third parties. Some
intermediaries take on even more active
[music] roles by assisting with contract
negotiations or providing support
throughout the performance of the
contract. [music]
The flexibility of intermediary roles
allows for customization [music]
based on the specific needs of the
transaction.
An intermediary might serve in a passive
capacity by sharing non-conidential
market opportunities or they might take
on an active role by facilitating
introductions and remaining involved
throughout the deal life cycle. Some
even monitor contract performance to
ensure compliance and assist with
dispute resolution.
[music] Customer protection is another
critical element of NCND agreements.
This determines whether an intermediary
has [music] exclusivity in promoting a
business opportunity. While the standard
practice is not to grant general
exclusivity, intermediaries are often
given exclusive rights when promoting
specific deals with particular third
parties. This protection gives the
intermediary certain rights regarding
future business with [music] that third
party. Duration and territorial
limitations must be clearly defined in
customer protection clauses.
Most NCND agreements last for
approximately 2 years, though this can
vary. Geographic scope [music] is
equally important, restricting
protection to specific markets or
territories where the intermediary
operates. Without clear boundaries,
these protections become difficult to
enforce. Non-compete provisions address
whether an intermediary can work with
competitors of the other party. The
agreement should explicitly state if
this is prohibited and what measures the
intermediary must take to avoid
conflicts.
Typically, an NCND offers two
alternatives. Either the intermediary
agrees not to compete [music] or they
remain free to work with competitors.
The default position, unless otherwise
specified, [music] is that
intermediaries cannot act for
competitors unless they have exclusive
rights to a certain type of business.
For an NCND to be legally enforcable, it
should include specific language on
dispute resolution, applicable law, and
jurisdiction.
These provisions create a predetermined
legal pathway for resolving
disagreements.
A jurisdiction clause specifies which
country's laws govern the agreement,
[music] while arbitration or mediation
clauses outline the preferred method for
resolving disputes. A severability
clause [music] ensures that if one part
of the agreement is found uninforcable,
the remainder stays intact.
Confidentiality forms the cornerstone of
any NCND agreement.
parties agree not to disclose sensitive
information shared during their
relationship, including business models,
[music] pricing strategies, customer
lists, trade secrets, and draft
contracts.
Violations [music] can result in
reputational damage, financial loss, or
legal action, including penalty clauses
for [music] breaches, reinforces the
seriousness of this obligation.
NCND agreements provide essential
protection for intermediaries [music] in
business transactions
by clearly defining roles,
responsibilities, exclusivity, and
confidentiality requirements. These
agreements [music] help ensure fair
treatment for all parties involved.
When [music] properly drafted with
specific terms regarding duration,
territorial limitations, and dispute
resolution mechanisms, NCNDs create a
secure framework for business
introductions and negotiations across
borders.

metadata.shortDescription:
Nonresident broker-dealers is a niche but testable topic inside the Series 24 supervision exam, falling under broker-dealer books and records. In this 7-minute explainer we walk through the U.S.-copy mandate, the trap between foreign firms and U.S. firms with foreign branches, the 14-day production clock, and why the rule exists, so you recognize every SEC demand-scenario on exam day.

By the end of this video you'll be able to confidently answer Series 24 questions about:

• The exact definition of a nonresident broker-dealer: a foreign firm with no permanent U.S. place of business or one whose principal records are maintained outside the U.S., whether registered or applying with the SEC
• The critical distinction between a nonresident broker-dealer covered by the rule and a U.S.-resident firm with merely a foreign branch, which is not covered
• The four components of the U.S.-based copies requirement: where (inside the U.S.), what (true, correct, complete, and current copies of all SEC-required records), notice (written notice to the SEC of the U.S. address), and status (records must be current, not stale duplicates)
• The written undertaking: a legally binding promise to produce records at the firm's own expense upon SEC written demand
• The 14-day production window starting from written demand forwarded by registered mail, not from when the firm opens or sees the demand
• Where production must be delivered: the SEC's principal office in Washington, D.C. or any designated Regional Office
• The three policy reasons for the rule: establishing U.S. jurisdictional reach, preventing international procedural delay, and placing production costs on the firm

metadata.title: The SEC's Authority and What an SRO Is | Six Minutes: SIE, Part 2
metadata.author: Six Minutes
metadata.shortDescription:
Six Minutes: SIE, Part 2: The SEC's Authority and What an SRO Is: One decision tree for issuers, broker-dealers, and advisers; then What an SRO Is

Build a three-question decision tree that places any firm or person under the right SEC law: issuers under the Securities Act of 1933, broker-dealers under the Exchange Act of 1934, and advisers under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940. Work an invented three-firm IPO scenario down the tree and check it by matching each law's year to its subject. Then: Defines self-regulatory organizations: private groups the SEC authorizes to write rules, examine, and discipline their own members. Stresses the limits of SRO authority and the oversight chain from firm to SRO to SEC.

Chapters
0:00 Introduction
0:26 The decision tree
1:07 Three branches
2:04 Edge cases
2:45 Worked example
3:52 Trap
4:11 Recap
4:31 What an SRO Is
4:44 The idea
5:41 Two layers of oversight
6:14 Worked example
7:24 The trap
7:58 Recap
8:19 Thanks for watching

Practice problems
1. Northgate Capital is paid to manage client portfolios of stocks and bonds. Which law governs its registration with the SEC? Answer: the Investment Advisers Act of 1940, because Northgate advises on securities for pay.
2. Delta Metals registers a new bond offering for the public, and Ridgeline Securities sells it to customers. Match each firm to its law. Answer: Delta is an issuer under the Securities Act of 1933; Ridgeline is a broker-dealer under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934.
3. An SRO wants to punish a member firm that violated its rules. Which action is within its authority? (A) Revoke the firm's registration with the SEC, (B) Impose a fine on the firm, (C) Bring criminal charges against the firm's CEO, (D) Regulate a non-member broker-dealer. Answer: B — SROs discipline their own members with fines and suspensions; criminal power belongs to the government, SEC registration is not revoked by an SRO, and SRO authority covers members only.
4. True or false: because an SRO is self-regulatory, it does not answer to any government agency. Answer: False — self-regulatory means the industry regulates its own members under SEC supervision; every SRO answers to the SEC.

In this lesson we explore registration and licensing requirements within the U.S. securities industry, an essential topic tested on the SIE exam.

Financial professionals must meet specific regulatory requirements before they are allowed to sell securities or provide investment advice. Understanding these rules helps ensure that only qualified professionals operate in financial markets.

In this lesson you will learn:

• Why registration requirements exist
• Licensing rules for securities professionals
• The role of broker-dealers
• Registration of associated persons
• Qualification examinations in the securities industry
• Continuing education requirements
• Regulatory oversight of financial professionals

Regulatory supervision is primarily conducted by the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission and industry self-regulation is overseen by the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority.

These regulatory frameworks ensure that professionals working in financial markets meet competency standards and operate within established rules designed to protect investors.

metadata.author: ALC Lawcast: Finance in Focus

segments.text: I am attorney Laura Anthony founding partner of Legal & Compliance, a full service corporate,
securities, and business transactions law firm.
Today is the continuation in a LawCast series talking about the federal and Florida M&A
broker exemption.
On January 31, 2014, the SEC Division of Trading and Markets issued a no-action letter in favor
of entities effecting securities transactions in connection with the sale of equity control
of private operating businesses called an M&A broker.
The SEC stated that it would not require broker-dealer registration for M&A brokers arranging for
the sale of privately held businesses.
The SEC M&A Broker no action letter specifically excludes transactions involving an Exchange
Act reporting public company.
In addition, the SEC set forth the following limitations and restrictions.
M&A brokers cannot bind third parties to a transaction.
M&A brokers cannot directly or indirectly provide financing for M&A transactions.
M&A brokers cannot have custody, control or possession of or otherwise handle funds or
securities issued or exchanged in connection with an M&A transaction.
No M&A transaction can involve a public offering.
Any offering or sale of securities must be conducted in compliance with an applicable
exemption from registration.
No party to any M&A transaction may be a shell company.
To the extent that M&A brokers represent both buyers and sellers, they must provide clear
written representations as to whom they are representing and must obtain written consent
from both parties for joint representation.
If the M&A transaction involves a buyer group, the M&A broker may not be involved in forming
the group; The buyer or group of buyers must control and actively operate the company or
business and cannot be passive buyers.
The buyers will be considered to have control if it has the power, directly or indirectly,
to direct management or policies of the company, whether through ownership of securities, by
contract or otherwise.
The necessary control will be presumed if, upon completion of the transaction, the buyer
or group of buyers has the right to vote 25% or more of the securities, has the power to
sell or direct the sale of 25% or more of the securities, or in the case of a limited
partnership or LLC, has the right to receive upon dissolution or has contributed 25% or
more of the capital.
Any securities received by the buyer or M&A broker in the transaction will be restricted
within the meaning of Rule 144; and the M&A broker, and if an entity, each officer director
or employee of the M&A broker: has not been barred from association with a broker-dealer
by the SEC or any state or any self-regulatory organization; and is not suspended from association
with a broker-dealer.
I am securities attorney Laura Anthony, founding partner of Legal & Compliance, and producer
of LawCast.
Should you have any questions about today’s topic, please visit SecuritiesLawBlog.com
and LawCast.com, or contact me directly.
Inquiries of a technical nature are always encouraged.

metadata.title: Laura Anthony Attorney; M&A Broker Exemption
metadata.author: ALC Lawcast: Finance in Focus
metadata.shortDescription: Laura Anthony Attorney M&A Broker Exemption- Following the SEC’s lead, effective July 1,  2016, Florida passed a statutory exemption from the broker-dealer registration requirements for entities effecting securities transactions in connection with the sale of equity control of private operating businesses (“M&A Broker”).

segments.text: I am attorney Laura Anthony founding partner of Legal & Compliance, a full service corporate,
securities, and business transactions law firm.
Today is the continuation in a LawCast series talking about the federal and Florida M&A
broker exemption.
Following the SEC’s lead, effective July 1, 2016, Florida passed a statutory exemption
from the broker-dealer registration requirements for entities effecting securities transactions
in connection with the sale of equity control of private operating businesses, called an
M&A broker.
New Section 517.061(22) provides an exemption from the securities registration requirements
for: the offer or sale of securities, solely in connection with the transfer of ownership
of an eligible privately held company, through a merger and acquisition broker in accordance
with section 517.12(22).
New section 517.12(22) in turn details the merger and acquisition broker registration
exemption.
Like the SEC no action letter, the Florida broker registration exemption pertains to
persons and entities effecting securities transactions in connection with the sale of
equity control of private operating businesses.
Florida statutes define an M&A broker as one that is: “engaged in the business of effecting
securities transactions solely in connection with the transfer of ownership of an eligible
privately held company, regardless of whether that broker acts on behalf of a seller or
buyer, through the purchase, sale, exchange, issuance, repurchase, or redemption of, or
a business combination involving, securities or assets of the eligible privately held company.”
Subject to certain restrictions, the Florida rule exempts the registration of an M&A broker
that conducts transactions under chapter 517.061.
That is, a person that falls within the definition of an M&A broker and who completes transactions
involving the offer or sale of securities, solely in connection with the transfer of
ownership of an eligible privately held company can collect fees, including success fees and
commissions, and does not have to hold a securities broker-dealer license to do so.
The Florida statute is more restrictive than the SEC in its definition of a privately held
company and in particular, the statute defines an “eligible privately held company” as
one that does not have any class of securities registered, or required to be registered with
the SEC under the Exchange Act, or which files, or is required to file, periodic information,
documents, or reports under Section 15(d) of the Exchange Act; and, two, in the fiscal
year immediately preceding the fiscal year during which the M&A broker begins to provide
services for the securities transaction, the company has EBITDA of less than $25 million
or gross revenue of $250 million with a provision for future adjustments for inflation.
In the next LawCast in this series, I will detail the restrictions and particular obligations
required to rely on the Florida statute.
I am securities attorney Laura Anthony, founding partner of Legal & Compliance, and producer
of LawCast.
Should you have any questions about today’s topic, please visit SecuritiesLawBlog.com
and LawCast.com, or contact me directly.
Inquiries of a technical nature are always encouraged.

metadata.title: Florida Broker-Dealer Registration Exemption For M&A Brokers
metadata.author: ALC Lawcast: Finance in Focus
metadata.shortDescription: Florida Broker-Dealer Registration Exemption For M&A Brokers- Following the SEC’s lead, effective July 1, 2016, Florida passed a statutory exemption from the broker-dealer registration requirements for entities effecting securities transactions in connection with the sale of equity control of private operating businesses (“M&A Broker”).
keywords: Florida Broker-Dealer Registration Exemption For M&A Brokers

segments.text: I am attorney Laura Anthony founding partner of Legal & Compliance, a full service corporate,
securities, and business transactions law firm.
Today is the first in a LawCast series talking about the Florida and federal M&A broker exemption.
Following the SEC’s lead, effective July 1, 2016, Florida passed a statutory exemption
from the broker-dealer registration requirements for entities effecting securities transactions
in connection with the sale of equity control of private operating businesses, called an
M&A broker.
Interestingly, the new Florida statute, together with the SEC M&A Broker exemption, may have
paved the way for Florida residents to act as an M&A broker in a reverse or forward merger
involving OTCQX traded public companies without broker-dealer registration.
Florida has historically had stringent broker-dealer registration requirements in connection with
the offer and sale of securities.
Moreover, Florida does not always mirror the federal registration requirements or exemptions.
For example, Florida is one of five states that does not have an issuer’s exemption
from the broker-dealer registration requirements for public offerings.
However, in a move helpful to merger and acquisition transactions or M&A transactions in the state,
Florida has now passed an M&A broker-dealer exemption and concurrent securities registration
exemption for M&A transactions.
As I will talk about, the Florida exemption is similar but not identical to the federal
exemption.
The SEC exemption specifically limited itself to the federal broker-dealer registration
requirements, and not state law.
The sale of securities in Florida is regulated by the Florida Office of Financial Regulation,
Division of Securities and is generally found in the Florida Securities and Investor Protection
Act in Chapter 517 of the Florida Statutes and corresponding rules adopted under the
Florida Administrative Code.
Any offer or sale of securities in Florida, which offer or sale is not pre-empted by federal
law, must either be registered or exempted from registration in accordance with the state
securities laws.
The Florida registration exemptions can be found in Florida Statutes section 517.061.
All sales of securities in Florida must be made by a properly registered broker-dealer
or by someone utilizing an exemption provided by Chapter 517.12, of the Florida Statutes.
The new M&A offer and sale exemption has been codified by adding a new securities registration
exemption to Section 517.061 and a new broker-dealer registration exemption to Section 517.12.
From a very high level, the new Florida statute provides an exemption from the broker-dealer
registration requirements for brokers that effect M&A transactions with a privately held
company that does not involve a public offering of securities and where the company is not
a shell company.
In the next LawCast in this series, I will drill down on the specific Florida statutory
requirements and provide a comparison to the federal guidance.
I am securities attorney Laura Anthony, founding partner of Legal & Compliance, and producer
of LawCast.

and LawCast.com, or contact me directly.

metadata.author: CertFuel
metadata.shortDescription:
The definition of a broker-dealer is one of the highest-frequency testing grounds on the Series 63, sitting inside the broker-dealer regulation unit that can represent roughly 15-20% of the exam. In this 10-minute session we work through the statutory definition, the broker-dealer capacity distinction, every excluded entity, the two no-office routes, and the Canadian broker-dealer limited registration framework, so you spot every trap NASAA sets around the term.

By the end of this video you'll be able to confidently answer Series 63 questions about:

• The statutory definition of broker-dealer under the Uniform Securities Act (USA): any person engaged in the business of effecting transactions in securities for the account of others or for its own account
• Why broker capacity (agent, commission) and dealer capacity (principal, markup or markdown) can never coexist on the same trade, even though a firm registers as both
• The four categories of excluded entities: agents, issuers, banks/savings institutions/trust companies, and certain persons with no place of business in the state
• Why bank holding companies are not excluded from the broker-dealer definition even though banks are, and why "excluded" is stronger than "exempt"
• Route A (institutional-only transactions with no in-state office) versus Route B (existing non-resident customers with no in-state office) for no-office exclusions
• Why there is no dollar threshold for pension trusts under the broker-dealer exclusion, unlike the investment adviser exemption
• The three requirements for Canadian broker-dealer limited registration: good standing in Canada, no US office, membership in a Canadian self-regulatory organization (SRO)
• The 30-day effective date and December 1 renewal deadline for Canadian limited registration, and the two permitted client types

metadata.title: Broker-Dealer Regulation: Rapid Fire - Series 66 Exam Prep
metadata.author: CertFuel
metadata.shortDescription:
Broker-dealer regulation sits inside the laws, regulations, and ethics section of the Series 66 exam outline (approximately 30% of the test, or roughly 30 questions). In this 10-minute rapid-fire session we lock down the broker-versus-dealer distinction, underwriting risk transfer, dual registration traps, record retention numbers, and supervision rules that exam writers bait with nearly identical wrong answers.

By the end of this video you'll be able to confidently answer Series 66 questions about:

• Whether a firm is acting as a broker (agent, commission) or dealer (principal, markup or markdown) on a given trade, and why the label is capacity-based, not permanent
• Which entities are excluded from the broker-dealer definition under the Uniform Securities Act (USA), and why banks have a blanket state exclusion but only activity-specific federal exceptions
• How firm commitment underwriting shifts unsold-share risk to the underwriter, while best efforts leaves that risk with the issuer
• What makes a market maker different from an ordinary dealer: the two-sided market requirement, continuous basis, and spread-based profit
• The dual registration requirement for broker-dealers at the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), self-regulatory organization (SRO), and state level, plus the two fragile no-place-of-business exceptions and what breaks them
• The books-and-records creation rule versus the retention rule, and the specific look-back and retention periods: 10 years for disciplinary disclosure, 6 years for primary financial and transactional records, 3 years for communications and superseded procedures
• Why tiered branch inspections require annual reviews for offices of supervisory jurisdiction (OSJs) and non-supervisory branches every three years, and how strict liability applies to firms with inadequate supervisory procedures

2:02 Who is excluded from the broker-dealer definition
2:52 Firm commitment versus best efforts underwriting
3:48 Market makers and associated persons
4:42 Dual registration and the two fragile exceptions

Each Series 66 explainer covers one section of NASAA's Uniform Combined State Law Examination. metadata.title: Exclusions from the Broker-Dealer Definition - Series 63 Exam Prep
metadata.author: CertFuel
metadata.shortDescription:
Exclusions from the broker-dealer definition sit inside the 30% regulations-of-broker-dealers section of the Series 63 (roughly 9-10 questions for the unit). In this 8-minute explainer we walk through the five categorical exclusions, the no-place-of-business exclusion with its two conditions, and the federal-versus-state registration boundary so you stop mixing up exclusions with exemptions on test day.

By the end of this video you'll be able to confidently answer Series 63 questions about:

• Why agents, issuers, banks, savings institutions, and trust companies fall outside the broker-dealer (BD) definition entirely, and why bank holding companies do not
• The distinction between an exclusion (never a BD) and an exemption (a BD relieved from registering), and why the Uniform Securities Act (USA) uses exclusions for this topic
• Why excluded persons remain fully subject to the antifraud provisions despite never needing BD registration
• The two-step formula for the no-place-of-business exclusion: zero in-state office plus either exclusively institutional transactions or an existing customer whose residence is outside that state
• Why the word "exclusively" in Condition A means literally one retail resident client destroys the exclusion, and why pension trusts under Condition A have no minimum asset size
• How the Snowbird Rule works under Condition B: residence outside the no-office state is the test, not vacation length
• Why the BD de minimis exemption is zero (not the investment adviser's five), and why federal Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) registration never substitutes for state registration

▶️ CHAPTERS
0:00 Antifraud provisions apply to everyone, even excluded persons
1:23 Exclusion versus exemption: the most tested distinction
2:04 The five categorical exclusions and the bank holding company trap
3:13 No-place-of-business exclusion: the two-step formula
3:55 Condition A: institutional-only and the exclusively trap
4:45 Condition B: the Snowbird Rule for existing non-resident customers
5:15 BD de minimis is zero, not five: the adviser rule never applies
6:06 Federal SEC registration never replaces state registration
7:21 Rapid-fire exam recap: the physical office kills the exclusion

Each Series 63 explainer covers one section of NASAA's Uniform Securities Agent State Law Examination. The full Series 63 has 60 scored questions and runs 75 minutes at Prometric, focusing on state-securities-law content including registration, regulation, and client communication. CertFuel breaks the exam into short units so you can study in 20-50 question blocks and track your readiness to the 75% confidence threshold.

from the broker-dealer registration requirements for entities effecting securities transactions
in connection with the sale of equity control of private operating businesses, called an
M&A broker.
Like the federal rule, the Florida M&A broker exemption sets forth certain limitations and
restrictions related to the ability to use the exemption.
In particular: M&A brokers cannot have custody, control or possession of, or otherwise handle
funds or securities issued, or exchanged in connection with an M&A transaction.
M&A brokers cannot engage in any public offering of securities which is registered or required
to be registered under the federal or state securities laws, or in a transaction that
will result in the company being required to file reports under the Securities Exchange
Act; no party to the transaction can be a public shell company as defined by the Florida
statute.
The M&A broker cannot be subject to certain bad actor disqualifications.
In particular, they cannot be barred from association with a broker-dealer by the SEC,
any state or any self-regulatory organization; be suspended from association with a broker-dealer;
be subject to any federal order censuring or placing limitations on the person related
to acting as or being associated with a broker or dealer; be subject to the disqualifications
under either Rule 506 or Regulation A; or be subject to any final order of a state securities
commission or agency barring association or activity with any bank, savings or loan or
credit union.
Prior to completion of the transaction, the M&A broker must obtain written assurances
from the control persons with the largest percentage ownership of both the buyer and
seller that after the transaction is complete the buyer, acting alone or with others, will
be a control person of the acquired company or of the business conducted with the assets
of the acquired company; and prior to completion of the transaction, the M&A broker must obtain
written assurances from the control persons with the largest percentage ownership of both
the buyer and seller that if the transaction involves the offer of securities in exchange
for securities or assets, the person receiving securities will receive certain disclosures,
including the most recent year-end financial statements of the issuer of the securities,
prepared by the issuer in the normal course of business.
These financial statements need not be audited or reviewed, though if an auditor review is
available, it must be provided; the person must also receive a balance sheet dated not
more than 120 days before the date of the offer of exchange of securities; and finally,
information pertaining to the management, business, results of operations, and material
loss contingencies.
The Florida statute defines a control person as an individual or entity that possesses
the power, directly or indirectly, to direct the management or policies of a company through
ownership of securities, by contract, or otherwise.
A person is presumed to be a control person of a company if, with respect to a particular
company, that person Is a director, a general partner, a member, or a manager of a limited
liability company, or is an officer who exercises executive responsibility or has a similar
status or function; has the power to vote 20 percent or more of a class of voting securities
or has the power to sell or direct the sale of 20 percent or more of a class of voting
securities; or In the case of a partnership or limited liability company, may receive
upon dissolution, or has contributed, 20 percent or more of the capital.
I am securities attorney Laura Anthony, founding partner of Legal & Compliance, and producer
of LawCast.

and LawCast.com, or contact me directly.
Inquiries of a technical nature are always encouraged.

segments.text: I am attorney Laura Anthony founding partner of Legal & Compliance, a full service corporate,
securities, and business transactions law firm.
Today is the continuation in a LawCast series talking about the federal and Florida M&A
broker exemption.
Following the SEC’s lead, effective July 1, 2016, Florida passed a statutory exemption
from the broker-dealer registration requirements for individuals and entities affecting securities
transactions in connection with the sale of equity control of private operating businesses,
called an M&A Broker.
In this LawCast series I have gone through the specifics of the new Florida exemption.
In this and the next LawCast in the series I will discuss the federal exemption.
On January 31, 2014, the SEC division of Trading and Markets issued a no-action letter in favor
of entities affecting securities transactions in connection with the sale of equity control
of private operating businesses.
The SEC stated that it would not require broker dealer registration for M&A brokers arranging
for the sale of privately held businesses in accordance with the facts and circumstances
set forth in the no action letter.
The no action letter does not cover the facilitation of sales, mergers or acquisitions, or acquisitions
of publicly reporting, operating, or shell companies, which activities still require
broker dealer registration.
The SEC defined M&A broker as a person engaged in the business of affecting securities transactions
solely in connection with the transfer of ownership and control of a privately held
company through the purchase, sale, exchange, issuance, repurchase, redemption of, or a
business combination involving securities or assets of the company to a buyer that will
have that will actively operate the company or the business conducted with the assets
of the company.
The buyer would not have to be involved in daily operations, but could actively operate
the company through the power to elect executive officers, and approve the annual budget, or
by service as an executive.
The SEC defined privately held company as a company that does not have any class of
securities registered or required to be registered with the SEC under Section 12 of the Exchange
Act or with respect to which the company files, or is required to file periodic information
documents and reports under Section 15D of the Exchange Act.
The SEC specifically states, that the no action letter does not cover shell companies.
The SEC no action letter provides an exemption for M&A brokers that facilitates mergers,
acquisitions, business sales and business combinations between sellers or buyers have
privately held companies.
M&A Brokers may advertise the sale of businesses, including descriptions of the business location
and price range.
In the next and last LawCast in this series, I will go through the limitations to the federal
M&A broker exemption.

metadata.title: Definition of an Agent of a Broker-Dealer - Series 63 Exam Prep
metadata.author: CertFuel
metadata.shortDescription:
The legal definition of "agent" under the Uniform Securities Act is narrower than everyday usage, and the exam tests its edges heavily; this topic sits inside the regulations of agents of broker-dealers section, which comprises roughly 30% of the Series 63 outline (about 15 questions). In this 8-minute explainer we walk through the three required elements, why titles do not matter, what counts as effecting or attempting to effect transactions, and the broker-dealer registration shortcut that does not apply to issuers.

By the end of this video you'll be able to confidently answer Series 63 questions about:

• Why an agent must always be an individual natural person, never a firm, corporation, or entity
• The three simultaneous elements required for agent status: individual, represents a broker-dealer or issuer, and effects or attempts to effect securities transactions
• Why a partner, officer, or director is an agent only if they actually do agent work, and why title alone does not qualify them
• What activities trigger agent status: soliciting, recommending, taking or transmitting orders, executing trades, and attempting any of the above
• Why attempting to effect a transaction is sufficient, even if no sale is ever completed
• Which activities do not trigger agent status: bookkeeping, clerical, administrative work, back-office settlement, information technology, and marketing
• The automatic registration shortcut for a broker-dealer's partners, officers, and directors who qualify as agents, and why this shortcut never applies to an issuer's personnel

📚 Free written study guide, flashcards, and adaptive practice quizzes for this section (no signup wall to read):
https://app.certfuel.com/series63/learn/regulations-of-agents-of-broker-dealers/definition-of-an-agent-of-a-broker-dealer/definition-of-an-agent?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=series63-explainers&utm_content=definition-of-an-agent-description

🎯 Try CertFuel free for the full Series 63 adaptive study experience:
https://www.certfuel.com/series-63/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=series63-explainers&utm_content=definition-of-an-agent-signup

▶️ CHAPTERS
0:00 The natural person requirement: no firms, no dogs
1:38 The three must-have elements for agent status
2:19 Function over title: why vice presidents may not be agents
3:55 Effecting or attempting to effect: what triggers and what does not
5:22 The broker-dealer automatic registration shortcut
6:19 Final exam trap review: five core rules
7:16 Dealer vs. agent: the identity shift to ponder

About this series:
Each Series 63 explainer covers one section of NASAA's Uniform Securities Agent State Law Examination. The full Series 63 has 60 scored questions and runs 75 minutes at Prometric, focused exclusively on state securities laws and the ethical obligations of persons effecting transactions in securities. CertFuel breaks the exam into short units so you can study in 20-50 question blocks and track your readiness to the 75% confidence threshold.

metadata.title: Considerations for Broker-Dealers under Rule 15a-6
metadata.author: Mayer Brown
metadata.shortDescription:
https://www.mayerbrown.com/en/capabilities/practices/financial-services-regulatory--enforcement/broker-dealer-regulation-compliance?tab=overview

During this webcast, we will cover issues pertaining to Rule 15a-6 under the U.S. Securities Exchange Act of 1934, which provides foreign broker-dealers with exemptions from U.S. broker-dealer registration.

Among other topics, we will discuss:

The origin and meaning of Rule 15a-6;
Implications of Rule 15a-6 for foreign investment growth;
Proposed amendments and additional matters raised in SEC comment letters; and
Recent market trends and their impact on regulatory developments.

metadata.title: Buy-Side M&A 101: Should You Do an Acquisition? | Buy-Side Masterclass Moment
metadata.author: POTOMAC M&A
metadata.shortDescription:
Not every acquisition is a good idea. In fact, most aren’t.  
In this Buy-Side Masterclass Moment, Paul Giannamore explains why acquisitions must serve strategy—not ego—and how to avoid ending up in Jennifer’s position: doubling revenue on paper but creating a cultural and operational dumpster fire.  

You’ll learn:
🔹 Why acquisitions are tactics, not strategy  
🔹 The two levers of value: increasing cash flow & reducing risk  
🔹 How customer concentration, technology obsolescence & culture impact value  
🔹 Why organic growth usually beats acquisitive growth  
🔹 How to avoid “solution in search of a problem” deals  

This is the foundation of the Buy-Side Masterclass series—before you think about valuations, LOIs, or negotiation, you must ask: Should we even do a deal at all?  

**Connect with Paul Giannamore**  
LinkedIn ▸ https://www.linkedin.com/in/paulgiannamore  
Instagram ▸ https://www.instagram.com/pgiannamore  

📌 **Watch the Full Buy-Side Masterclass:** 
https://youtu.be/RLr8PdCZ6U0

📌 **Subscribe for Weekly M&A Insights:** https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCcIwu1ye9EHnYHSml9tu_4Q?sub_confirmation=1  

📌 Subscribe to receive Buy-Side M&A materials when they become available:
https://the-potomac-company.kit.com/271b2e3f88


🌐 More resources ▸ https://www.potomaccompany.com/  

🎬 *Directed, produced & filmed by Dylan Seals, Verbell Ltd.*

00:00 – Why Acquisitions Are Tactics, Not Strategy  
01:30 – The Two Levers: Cash Flow & Risk  
03:00 – Customer Concentration & Risk Profiles  
04:00 – Tech Obsolescence & Competitive Risk  
05:00 – Jennifer’s Case Study: The Wrong Deal  
07:00 – Culture Clashes & Failed Integrations  
09:00 – Opportunity Cost: Organic vs. Acquisitive Growth  
10:30 – The Dangers of Excitement-Driven Deals  
12:30 – Lessons Learned: Strategy Before Acquisition  


#mergersandacquisitions #buyside #dealstrategy #businessgrowth #middlemarket #businesssale #MAMasterclass #paulgiannamore #potomactv #exitstrategy #privateequity #businessvaluation

Business Broker Insider: Buy Side & Sell Side Secrets #TrentLee

Business Broker Insider: Buy Side & Sell Side Secrets

The biggest wealth opportunities over the next 10 years may come from buying existing businesses — not starting from scratch. But the people winning are the ones buying responsibly, understanding the industry, and building systems that create long-term cash flow and ownership.

In this episode, I sit down with Trent Lee — one of the top business brokers in the country with 600+ business sales completed — to talk about the REAL truth behind buying businesses, SBA loans, and “passive income” acquisitions.

We cover:

Why most business buyers fail
The danger of “no money down” deals
What banks are tightening up on right now
Why your experience matters more than your buy box
How owners accidentally destroy their valuation
What actually makes a business sellable
The biggest opportunities in small business acquisitions over the next 10 years

If you're looking at buying a business, using SBA financing, or building wealth through acquisitions, this episode is packed with practical insights most people online never talk about.

Connect with Trent Lee:

Website: https://www.sellbusinessinlasvegas.com
LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/trentlee
YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/@TrentLeeBizBroker

Subscribe for more interviews on business buying, SBA lending, entrepreneurship, and wealth building.

👉 Not sure which business model fits you? Take the free Business Ownership Assessment: https://businessownershipblueprint.com
📞 Need financing or have questions about buying or owning a business? Book a call: https://bookwithbeau.com

If you are interested in an investment banking job, you often find people talking about the buy-side versus the sell-side. You may not have asked that question yet, but perhaps you have heard exchanges about the buy-side and the sell-side M&A. So, how do these two actually differ?

In terms of M&A, Sell-side M&A, means working with the sellers who are trying to find a counterparty for the sale of a client’s business.

On the other hand, the buy-side means working with the buyers and finding opportunities for them to acquire other businesses.

metadata.title: Sell Side M&A - After The Sale: Reflecting on the M&A Transaction Process
metadata.author: Carter Morse & Goodrich
metadata.shortDescription:
In this video, we sit down with Jeff Garber, CEO of Resident Essentials, to discuss life after the M&A transaction. 

Jeff shares his insights and experiences, including what his criteria was for choosing his ultimate partner (other than purchase price), recommendations he would give to someone considering selling their business and more.

Whether you're a buyer or seller, this interview provides valuable insights to help you navigate the complex world of M&A and maximize the value of your transaction. 

About Carter Morse & Goodrich
‍
Located in Southport, Connecticut, Carter Morse & Goodrich is a boutique M&A advisory firm that specializes in representing founder-led and family-held businesses valued between $25 million and $250 million. While CMG provides a full range of investment banking services, our primary focus is representing owners who are pursuing their once-in-a-lifetime M&A transactions. CMG specializes in advising leading companies in niche markets to plan, prepare, execute, and close successful transactions that maximize shareholder value. CMG fully understands and appreciates the unique dynamics of closely-held businesses and the importance of owner legacies. For 35 years, the combination of our hands-on approach, senior banker attention, strategic guidance, seamless transaction execution and extensive network of domestic and international resources has enabled us to become a trusted advisor to hundreds of business owners.
‍
CMG's Broker/Dealer affiliate, Carter Capital Corporation, is a FINRA member firm registered with the SEC and SIPC.

metadata.author: The Digital Merchant
metadata.shortDescription:
Hey everyone, Francis Walshe here! In today’s video, we’ll be diving deep into some of the best alternatives to FE International for mergers and acquisitions (M&A). FE International is a big name in the industry, particularly for mid-to-large cap online businesses looking for an exit. But is it the best option for you? Let’s explore some other platforms that offer different services, ranging from buyer-seller platforms to full-service M&A brokerage firms.

In this video, I’ll cover:
* What does an M&A advisor do? Learn the crucial role these experts play in helping you sell your business and find the right buyer.
* The pros and cons of FE International: I'll talk about their success rate, lack of upfront pricing, and restricted buyer access.

Alternatives to FE International:

* QuietLight – A transparent, entrepreneur-driven platform that specializes in high-value business sales.
* Flippa – A more budget-friendly and DIY option for smaller businesses.
* Acquire.com – Best for SaaS startups, with a focus on specialization.
* Onfolio – A unique acquirer of businesses, focusing on larger companies with annual profits of $500K+.
* Empire Flippers – A well-respected platform, but I’ll share why I prefer Quiet Light over Empire Flippers for mid-market companies.
* BusinessesForSale.com – Great for brick-and-mortar businesses looking to sell.

I’ll also discuss how the level of service and pricing can vary between these firms and help you determine which is best for your business based on size, industry, and your specific needs.

Is FE International the right choice for you?
I’m going to give you my honest opinion on whether it’s worth considering, and if not, why I believe platforms like Quiet Light or Flippa might be better fits for different types of sellers.

🔑 Key Takeaways:

* Learn about the success rates, fees, and buyer access when comparing these M&A platforms.
* Get an inside look at Quiet Light’s transparent pricing and the realistic approach they take to selling businesses.
* Discover how Flippa is a great option for DIY sellers or smaller businesses.
* Understand which platforms specialize in which sectors (SaaS, brick-and-mortar, etc.).

If you’re considering selling your business or just exploring your options, this video will help you make an informed decision!

📌 Don’t forget to LIKE, COMMENT, and SUBSCRIBE for more business, tech, and M&A insights from TheDigitalMerchant.com. Let me know which platform you’re thinking about using or if you have any questions!

metadata.title: Quiet Light Brokerage Review: Specialized Online Business Brokers Explained
metadata.author: The Digital Merchant
metadata.shortDescription:
In this video, I share my experience reviewing Quiet Light Brokerage after working with many brokers over the years. I explain why I prefer specialized brokers, especially when focusing on online businesses, and what makes this firm stand out.

I walk through their user-friendly website, their strong emphasis on confidentiality, and how every advisor has real operator experience—having bought, sold, or built businesses themselves. I also break down their process, from vetting buyers to preparing financials, and why their structured approach works best for businesses in the $250K–$5M range.

I cover key points about their services:
* No upfront fees, retainers, or listing costs—just standard commission structures.
* A highly vetted pool of buyers, including individuals, equity groups, and experienced operators.
* A strict, confidentiality-driven process with NDAs and proof of funds.
* A focus on preparation and quality, emphasizing that selling is a process—not a quick transaction.

I also explain when this brokerage may not be the right fit, such as for very small businesses, rushed sales, or unpolished financials.

If you’re serious about buying or selling an online business and want a specialized, process-driven brokerage, this review will help you decide.

Read the complete write-up here: https://thedigitalmerchant.com/quiet-light-brokerage/

#BusinessBroker #OnlineBusiness #Entrepreneurship #BusinessSale #QuietLight #MergersAndAcquisitions #StartupExit

metadata.title: Why I Immediately Reject Most "Full Price" Offers
metadata.author: Quiet Light Brokerage
metadata.shortDescription:
Not all full-price offers are created equal. In this video, Quiet Light broker Brad Wayland explains why he pushes back hard on 100% seller-financed LOIs, what the real transfer of risk looks like in an online business sale, and why the buyers sending these offers are usually following bad advice from social media influencers. He also makes the case for why cash buyers at a lower price point are often in a far stronger position than people realize. If you're buying or selling, this will change how you think about deal structure.

Curious about buying or selling? Explore your options...

Get a free, no-pressure business valuation ➡️ https://quietlight.com/sell
Meet our expert advisors ➡️ https://quietlight.com/team

metadata.title: 3 Big Levers to Maximize SaaS Business Valuation with David Newell
metadata.author: Quiet Light Brokerage
metadata.shortDescription:
Quiet Light advisor and SaaS expert David Newell shares the three most important things you need to successfully scale your SaaS business and prepare to sell it for the most money, best deal terms, and highest number of offers. 

SaaS businesses receive the highest multiples in the online industry, so if you're a found of a software, plugin, or app you want to check out this webinar to learn how you're probably leaving money on the table when it's time to sell.

You're going to learn:
-Metrics like MRR, ARR, and acquisition that drive value
-The importance of reducing risk
-Tips on eliminating scaling restraints
-How does SDE differ from EBITDA
-Strategies for reducing churn
-The growth strategies to avoid because they destroy your value

Sponsor for this webinar

https://www.quietlight.com

This episode is brought to you by Quiet Light, a brokerage firm that wants to help you successfully sell your online business.  

There is no wrong reason for selling your business. However, there is a right time and a right way. The team of leading entrepreneurs at Quiet Light wants to help you discover the right time and strategy for selling your business. By providing trustworthy advice, effective strategies, and honest valuations, your Quiet Light advisor isn’t your every-day broker—they’re your partner and friend through every phase of the exit planning process.

If you’re new to the prospect of buying and selling, Quiet Light is here to support you. Their plethora of top-notch resources will provide everything you need to know about when and how to buy or sell an online business. Quiet Light offers high-quality videos, articles, podcasts, and guides to help you make the best decision for your online business.

Not sure what your business is really worth? No worries. Quiet Light offers a free valuation and marketplace-ready assessment on their website. That’s right—this quick, easy, and free valuation has no strings attached. Knowing the true value of your business has never been easier!

What are you waiting for? Quiet Light is offering the best experience, strategies, and advice to make your exit successful. To learn more, go to quietlight.com, email inquiries@quietlight.com, or call 800.746.5034 today.
