segments.text: Hey everyone, welcome back to the
channel. Today we're diving into a topic
that's key for property owners,
investors, and anyone dealing with
telecom leases. Telecommunications
easements. What are they? How do they
work? And why do they matter? Let's
break it all down so you can make
informed decisions. A telecommunications
easement is an exclusive used area
designated for telecom equipment. This
includes everything from the cell tower
to the equipment pad, shelter, and even
electrical connections. It's essentially
a way to define and protect the space
used for telecommunications purposes.
When it comes to cell tower easements,
there are three main types: specific
easements, general easements, and
expanded easements. Each has unique
benefits and limitations depending on
your goals. Let's break them down.
First, specific easements. These focus
on the exact footprint of the leased
area. The square feet matches the lease
terms and no extra space is added. While
simple, specific easements are the least
preferred option because they don't
allow for additional tenants, meaning no
potential revenue growth for landlords
or tower investors. Next, general
easements. These are popular for rooftop
antenna sites and give exclusive rights
to the entire rooftop. The big perk
here, room for new tenants. Site owners
typically get the highest valuation and
may even receive a 50/50 revenue share
for additional tenants outside the
original lease area. Finally, expanded
easements. These include the current
leased area plus additional space, often
around 500 square ft. This extra space
creates opportunities for new tenants
while maintaining a defined easement
footprint. Like general easements,
expanded easements can include a revenue
sharing agreement. Now, let's talk about
how long these easements last. There are
two main time frames, perpetual
easements and fixedterm easements.
Here's how they compare. Perpetual
easements are the most common. They last
for 99 years or more and provide
excellent tax advantages. For example,
they qualify as real estate sales under
IRS 1031 exchange rules, allowing
property owners to defer taxes by
reinvesting in like kind of real estate.
It's a great way to maximize financial
benefits while ensuring long-term
stability for the property. Fixedterm
easements, on the other hand, have a set
duration, often tied to the current
lease term. Once the term ends, the
easement reverts to the original owner
or their heirs. While this provides
flexibility for recapturing future
revenue, fixedterm easements typically
don't qualify for 1031 exchanges and may
result in capital gains taxes. Finally,
if you're considering selling your lease
through an assignment or easement, it's

metadata.title: Data Center Site Selection: How to Choose Land (Power, Water, Fiber, Zoning)
metadata.author: Data Center Build Academy
metadata.shortDescription:
Before a data center can be built, the site has to be right. This lesson explains how professionals evaluate land for a data center campus: utility power availability and timelines, water, fiber routes, zoning and permitting, flood risk, and the site development work that follows.

Part of the free course Data Center Construction Management: Beginner to Advanced.
Course section: Section 1: Development and Pre-Construction

Chapters
0:00 Introduction
0:47 Factor 1: Power
1:45 Technology Spotlight: When the grid can't keep up
2:57 Factor 2: Fiber
3:11 Factor 3: Water
3:27 Factor 4: The land
3:59 Factor 4: The surroundings
5:22 Stage 1: Due diligence
5:35 Technology Spotlight: Surveying a site in days, not months
6:08 Stage 2: Entitlements and agreements
6:34 Key Takeaways

About this channel: practical training for data center construction managers, engineers and project teams, from site selection to commissioning. New lessons every Tuesday and Friday.

Narration uses the presenter's own cloned voice. Some scenes are AI-generated illustrations; real photos are credited below where used. No equipment manufacturer is shown or endorsed.

#DataCenter #DataCenterConstruction #MissionCritical

— About this video —
General education only, not engineering, legal, financial or safety advice. Follow your contract, local codes and qualified professionals. Some visuals are AI-generated or AI-edited, and the narration is an AI-generated voice. Companies and products shown are not affiliated with this channel and don't endorse it.

segments.text: Imagine your company buys two hundred acres for a new data center campus.
Great location.
Flat land.
Fair price.
Then you call the utility, and they tell you the power you need won't be available
for six years.
That scenario is real, and it's happening across the industry right now.
In this video, you'll learn how professionals select land for a data center, so you
never end up owning the wrong site.
And stay to the end, because I'll walk you through three real-world style site
options, and show you exactly which one an experienced team would buy, and why.
Choosing land for a data center is nothing like choosing land for an office or a
warehouse.
For a data center, the most important thing about a site isn't the view, or even the
price.
It's what's under it, around it, and connected to it.
Professionals score every site against the same checklist.
Let's go through it, one factor at a time.
Factor number one, and it's not close.
Power.
A large campus can need hundreds of megawatts.
That's the demand of a small city.
So the very first call isn't to a real estate broker.
It's to the utility.
And there's only one question that matters.
How many megawatts can you deliver to this site, and when?
In many markets today, the answer is measured in years.
New transmission lines and substations can take three to seven years to permit and
build.
That's why experienced developers look for land close to existing high-voltage lines
and substations with spare capacity.
And it isn't just how much power.
It's how reliable.
Owners want at least two independent utility feeds, ideally from two different
substations, so one failure can never take the whole campus down.
Before buying, experienced teams ask the utility for a will-serve letter or a
capacity study.
It confirms how much power is available, from which substation, and by what date.
In busy markets, owners even pay deposits to hold their place in the utility's
connection queue, because that line can be years long.
So what happens when the grid simply can't deliver power fast enough?
This is where some of the most exciting technology in our industry comes in.
Some developers now build their own power on site.
Natural gas turbines or engines can provide what's called bridge power, running the
campus until the utility connection is ready.
Fuel cells generate electricity quietly, through a chemical reaction instead of
combustion.
And huge battery systems, the size of shipping containers, store energy and help
balance the grid.
And A I is making the problem bigger.
Servers built for artificial intelligence draw far more power than traditional
servers, so a single A I campus can need as much electricity as several older data
centers combined.
And the biggest change of all is nuclear.
In the last few years, major cloud and A I companies have announced agreements to
buy power from existing nuclear plants, including restarting a plant that had been
shut down, and to support a new generation of small modular reactors.
These are compact reactors, built partly in a factory, that could one day sit right
next to a data center campus.
For a construction manager, this changes the job.
On-site power plants mean more equipment, more permits, and more trades on your
site.
So the power strategy has to be part of the plan from day one.
Factor two.
Fiber.
A data center without connectivity is just an expensive warehouse.
Good sites have several fiber carriers available, arriving by physically separate
routes.
Why separate?
Because one backhoe cutting one cable shouldn't be able to isolate your entire
building.
Factor three.
Water.
Many cooling systems use water, and some use a lot of it.
Even a site designed for very low water use still needs a reliable supply for fire
protection and people, and a plan for wastewater.
In dry regions, water can become the issue that stops the project, so check it
early.
Factor four.
The land itself.
Is it big enough for the whole campus and future phases?
Is the zoning right, or will it need to be rezoned?
Is it out of the flood plain?
What's the risk of earthquakes, tornadoes, or hurricanes?
And what's under the ground?
Rock, poor soil, wetlands, or contamination can all add months and millions.
And remember, a data center campus needs far more land than its buildings.
Substations, generator yards, cooling equipment, parking, security setbacks, and
stormwater ponds all take space.
That's why large campuses often cover hundreds of acres.
Look at the surroundings too.
Roads that can carry heavy equipment deliveries.
Airports and flight paths that can limit building and crane heights.
And nearby industry that could bring vibration or dust.
Then come the business factors.
Tax incentives, which can be worth millions over the life of the campus.
Latency, meaning how close the site is to the users it will serve.
And today, maybe the most underestimated factor of all.
Community acceptance.
More and more projects are delayed, or even stopped, because neighbors object to
noise, water use, and traffic.
Let's put all of this together with a real-world style case study.
A development team is comparing three sites.
Site A has the cheapest land and excellent fiber, but power won't be available for
six years.
Site B is mid-priced, with two utility feeds in eighteen months, but ten percent of
the land sits in a flood plain.
Site C has power in two years, but strong local opposition to the rezoning.
An experienced team chooses Site B.
Power is the hardest thing to get, and Site B has two feeds in eighteen months.
The flood plain is a known, manageable issue.
You simply don't build on that part of the land, and use it for stormwater ponds or
green space.
Site A's six-year power timeline makes it almost worthless for now.
And Site C's opposition puts the whole timeline at risk, because a delay in rezoning
can cost more than the land itself.
Choosing the site is only the beginning.
Next comes development, which turns a promising site into a buildable one.
It has three stages.
Stage one.
Due diligence.
A boundary and topographic survey.
A geotechnical investigation of the soil and rock.
A Phase One environmental site assessment.
Traffic studies, and a review of every easement on the property.
And due diligence has become much faster thanks to new technology.
Drones carrying LiDAR scanners can map an entire site in a single day, creating a
precise three D model of every slope and contour.
Geographic information systems, many now powered by A I, layer power lines, flood
zones, fiber routes, and zoning onto one map, so a team can compare hundreds of
sites before visiting a single one.
Ground-penetrating radar finds buried pipes and cables before anyone starts digging.
And many owners now create a digital twin of the campus, a living three D model that
follows the project from the master plan all the way into operations.
Stage two.
Entitlements and agreements.
Zoning and site plan approvals from the local authority, and at the same time, the
electric service agreement with the utility, along with water, sewer, and fiber
agreements.
Stage three.
The campus master plan.
Where each building goes, and where the substation, generator yards, water tanks,
parking, security fence, and future phases will be.
A good master plan lets the campus grow, building by building, without disturbing
the buildings already running.
Let's bring it together.
Start every site search with power, and get both the capacity and the timeline in
writing.
Make sure fiber arrives on separate routes, and check water and natural hazards
early.
When the grid can't keep up, on-site generation, battery storage, and nuclear are
changing what's possible.
And remember the three stages of development.
Due diligence, entitlements and agreements, and the master plan.
In the next video, we'll look at the resources every data center site must have, and
the design and technology that go inside the building.
Subscribe so you don't miss it.
See you there.

metadata.title: Powered land: The asset behind the data center | Reed Smith Data Centers series
metadata.author: Reed Smith LLP
metadata.shortDescription:
Data center developers are focused on securing power, and power now comes first, with real estate second. Reed Smith lawyer Joy Zumbro explains how to diligence powered land, starting with the fact that “powered land” is a marketing term. 

She covers the difference between a letter of intent, a utility load ramp, and a signed electrical services agreement, and why a gigawatt delivered in five years still carries timing risk. She also shows how off-ramps and termination rights protect developers acquiring or leasing a site from uncommitted power. 

This film is part of our series “Data Centers: Navigating Today and What Comes Next.”
https://reedsmith.law/DataCenters

#DataCenters #PoweredLand #EnergyLaw

I'm looking at having off ramps, power commitments flexibility to terminate a deal if the power is not contractually committed or cannot be contractually committed in the timeframes that our clients are looking to secure power. So if we have contracted to acquire or lease a particular site and a moratorium comes into place that no longer allows that data center to be built there, at least for some period of time, we need to give our clients the flexibility to say, "This transaction no longer works for us." That list has, has expanded. We're looking at power. We are looking at land use. We're also looking at environmental. metadata.title: How to Reach Business Owners Who Already Want to Sell (Deal Sourcing Outreach Sequence)
metadata.author: Wolf of Main Street
metadata.shortDescription:
Your job in deal sourcing isn't to convince a business owner to sell. Nobody is good enough at selling to talk someone into selling a company they've run for 30 years. The job is to find the owners who already want to sell, and make it easy for them to raise their hand.

This video walks through the outreach sequence we run on every buy-side deal sourcing campaign, touch by touch: email, a call that mentions the email, an email that mentions the call, social, another email, a handwritten letter, and a call a week after the letter lands. It covers what we say in each touch, how we set up the infrastructure so emails land in the inbox and calls don't get flagged as spam, the cold call openers our team uses, and how the sequence changes in a small market versus a large one.

If you're a search funder, independent sponsor, private equity firm, family office or anyone buying a small business and running outbound yourself, this is the playbook.

Chapters:
0:00 Your job isn't to convince owners to sell
1:18 Outreach finds sellers. It doesn't create them
2:00 Where this fits: data, infrastructure, people
2:26 The sequence, touch by touch
3:18 Every touch references the last one
3:53 Touch 1: the first email (under 60 words, plain text, one yes or no question)
6:10 Don't ask for a call. Ask if they want it
7:04 Send from a generic domain
9:07 The cold call opener: permission, not a pitch
10:29 Double dial like you're trying to reach family
11:13 Get your calls answered, not flagged as spam
13:30 Social: reach out where the owner actually is
14:15 Handwritten letters (written by a robot)
15:10 Market size changes the sequence
16:24 Why I won't quote you a response rate
17:37 Running this yourself? Start here
19:42 Want us to run this on your market?

Want us to run this sequence on your market? Book a call: https://axiagrowth.com

Previous video: how we build owner lists that Apollo and ZoomInfo miss: https://youtu.be/174DJf0_nt0
Next up: the people side, and how to staff your campaign.

Cold Calling for Off-Market Deals: Exact Script That Closed 6-7 Figure Real Estate Contracts

Cold Calling Scripts for Off-Market Real Estate Deals: My Exact Template
If you're still calling owners asking, “Are you looking to sell?”—you’re losing before the conversation even starts.

In this video, I reveal my exact cold calling framework built on credibility, clarity, and respect—the same script responsible for six and seven-figure off-market acquisitions.

This script helps you:
✅ Turn strangers into serious sellers
✅ Build trust within 60 seconds
✅ Avoid sounding like a broker or spam caller
✅ Get financials without pressure
✅ Convert “No” into “Not Yet”
✅ Stay unforgettable when the timing is right

🔥 What you’ll learn today:
➡✅  How to follow up after a certified letter
➡✅ The perfect opening line that gets sellers to listen
➡✅ What documents to request (without sounding pushy)
➡✅ How to disarm resistance immediately
➡✅ How to set next steps like a professional buyer

This is not a pushy call.
This is a controlled, strategic conversation that leads to deals.

👇 Comment below if you want the full script PDF.
👍 Like this video if you're ready to make real calls
🔔 Subscribe for off-market negotiation, acquisition & deal-closing strategies!

What does it actually look like to run a family office with $10M in cash—step by step—from first wire to buying real private companies?

In this POV-style walkthrough, we go inside the real mechanics of starting and operating a lean family office. No fluff, no theory—just the practical playbook wealthy operators use to move from “I have money” to “I own assets and companies that compound.”

You’ll learn:
- What to do in the first 30–90 days after you get $10M liquid  
- How to structure entities, trusts, and accounts for a true family office  
- Which key hires and advisors you actually need (and which are a waste)  
- How to design your investment mandate and allocation strategy  
- How to transition from public markets into private deals without getting burned  
- How real deal sourcing works: brokers, off-market deals, and networks  
- The biggest mistakes new family offices make when buying their first company  
- What happens after closing: governance, reporting, and not blowing up operations  

If you’re a founder with an exit, a high-income operator planning ahead, or just obsessed with capital allocation and private equity, this video will give you a clear, realistic roadmap for building your own family office and eventually owning businesses outright.

Subscribe to Frankie Finance for more deep-dive, no-BS finance explainers on wealth building, private deals, and the real-world side of money.

Sources:
• The Complete Family Office Handbook — Kirby Rosplock

• The Family Office Book: Investing Capital for the Ultra-Affluent — Richard C. Wilson

• HBR Guide to Buying a Small Business: Think Big, Buy Small, Own Your Own Company — Richard S. Ruback and Royce Yudkoff

• Buy Then Build: How Acquisition Entrepreneurs Outsmart the Startup Game — Walker Deibel

• The 2024 Search Fund Study — Stanford Graduate School of Business Center for Entrepreneurial Studies

• Private Equity at Work: When Wall Street Manages Main Street — Eileen Appelbaum and Rosemary Batt

How to raise capital from family offices and ultra-high-net-worth investors when you don't have a warm intro: where to find them, who to contact first, and what to send.

📊 Free Capital Raise Assessment: https://andrewlebaron.com/yt/assessment/LlJs_vz0sPs

📅 Book a call: https://andrewlebaron.com/yt/call/LlJs_vz0sPs
📰 The LeBaron Letter: https://andrewlebaron.com/yt/letter/LlJs_vz0sPs

Everyone says "go get a family office," but nobody tells you where the ultra-wealthy actually are, or how to get in the room without a warm intro.

If you've got a few exits under your belt and you've already tapped your existing investors, this one's for you. Family offices and ultra-high-net-worth investors are writing checks into deals like yours. You just need to know where they move money, and who's already sitting across the table from them.

In this video I break down 8 places I find them:
1. Business brokers and M&A attorneys
2. Family office analysts (not the principals)
3. CEO peer groups like YPO, EO and Vistage
4. Estate attorneys and trust officers
5. Corporate CPAs
6. RIAs (the long game)
7. Church (the right way)
8. Title companies and escrow officers

Plus how to turn these relationships into warm introductions, and how to nurture a new list without spamming high-profile contacts.

I help seasoned sponsors and fund managers build capital raising systems and investor relations teams, so they raise all year and not only when a deal is under contract.

This video is for educational purposes only and isn't investment, legal, or tax advice.

metadata.title: $250 Billion Family Office Founder on Wealth Preservation, Taxes, and Building Wealth
metadata.author: How I Invest Podcast
metadata.shortDescription:
What if the greatest threat to generational wealth isn’t bad investing—but the inability to think beyond the next liquidity event?

In this episode, I sit down with Eric Becker, Founder and Chairman of Cresset, to discuss why he built a modern multi-family office after decades as an entrepreneur and investor. Eric explains the structural conflicts inside traditional wealth management, why most ultra-high-net-worth families lack true family office infrastructure, and how long-term thinking changes the way businesses, portfolios, and families compound over generations. We also explore governance, tax-aware investing, succession planning, and lessons from companies that have endured for centuries.

Highlights:
- Why most wealth management firms fail entrepreneurs after liquidity events
- The hidden conflicts embedded inside traditional wirehouses
- Why family governance matters as much as investment performance
- The concept of “asset protection as compartments in a submarine”
- Why the next generation is often the greatest risk to family wealth
- How enduring companies survive across centuries and multiple crises
- Why building a business for the long term paradoxically accelerates growth
- The overlooked importance of stewardship in investing and leadership

Guest Bio: 
Eric Becker is the Founder and Chairman of Cresset, a multi-family office and wealth management platform overseeing more than $250 billion in assets under management and advisement. Prior to founding Cresset, Eric built and invested in multiple businesses as an entrepreneur, beginning with a healthcare technology company he launched while attending the University of Chicago. He is also the author of The Long Game, a book exploring the lessons behind companies and families that have endured for generations, drawing on interviews with some of the world’s longest-lasting organizations and business leaders.

Jamie Dimon likes to go around say we have one of the world's largest balance sheet. I believe it's over 4 trillion AUM. Why does that matter for them clients is they're able to borrow money and borrow against their assets at a lower rates. How does Crestwood compete with that? >> Sure. Um it really does not come into play. It's so interesting because lots of people say that what you just said, but we don't find it to be an issue and here are the reasons why. The first is at 235 billion of of AUM and and AUA, we're able to bring banks to the table for our clients needs and we're actually able to get the banks to compete. So like in my own personal circumstance, I was with a traditional wirehouse that also had a bank affiliate for 25 years and at one point I needed a mortgage. My advisor arranged for a mortgage with the bank affiliate. I didn't think twice about it. Later on I asked my advisor, were you compensated on my loan? I'm just curious. And after a fumbling and bumbling for a bit he said, yes, I was. Which at the end of the day made me think, okay, I mean, I did fine on the loan. I don't think I was paying credit card rates, but clearly it wasn't competitive and clearly I wasn't paying probably the lowest rate possible. Um so, it was actually a conflict more than uh than an advantage. I think that actually making banks compete for our clients' business is a much better model. And then let's talk about securities lending um and let's talk about custody. So, with custody, we use Fidelity, Family Office, Schwab Family Office, and Pershing, which is Bank of New York. So, we have, we think, three of the best custodians anywhere in the world and we'll put their balance sheets up against anyone. Um and their model, by the way, in these custody businesses, it's designed completely around safekeeping of these assets, from technology to not using leverage and all the things that I think are actually really inherently different in the third-party custody model. So, it's it's just a great question for you to ask, but it doesn't affect us really at all. It's great for JP Morgan. I think it's it's fantastic. And if JP Morgan is the right place for you, then then that's great. >> Let's say, as I'm sure you oftentimes have, you have somebody have a billion-dollar exit, a once-in-a-generation, once-in-three-generation exit. What would you advise in terms of their model portfolio? One of the things that family offices and their CIOs have stressed to me is that there's no such thing as a wealth preservation strategy in the long term. >> Mhm. >> Most family offices don't make it to the third generation. Even with great tax planning, you have the death tax, the estate tax that's constantly eating away. You have divorces, you have marriages, all these things. Do you think that this is a misnomer, this idea of a wealth preservation strategy? >> I think that you can have a wealth uh preservation strategy. And for me, I would start with two things. Tax efficiency and asset protection. So, I would start with the foundational most basic thing and that is making sure that what we're investing in, we're investing on a tax-aware basis. And we can talk a little bit more about that. And then in terms of of asset protection, I think sometimes people don't realize some of the liabilities or things, you know, you invest in a in a building and then there's litigation associated with that. Well, did you invest Did you have like a blocking company that you invested in that then made that investment? Did you do that on a tax-efficient basis? Are you protected if something bad happens at that asset? So, I think thinking of your wealth like a submarine and having these different compartments that you can seal off so that if you end up with either a bad investment that at least all you can lose is the equity that you invested in that or the capital that you put into it. So, I would start with that. And then within the portfolios themselves, I do believe that a well-constructed portfolio that's highly diversified include say global equities and exposure to private equity that we're just talking about and and um and a good portfolio of of of income-producing things like Treasury bills and municipal bonds, something that's really well diversified and has a global aspect to it. And you're investing for the long term and you have sufficient liquidity that in a drawdown, you don't panic and do panic selling, I think that you can actually compound your wealth over generations. But you have to also match that with the right planning around the psychology of money, and you have to match it with the right education of the next generation because the threat to the wealth isn't bad investments or bad asset protection or inefficient taxes. The greatest threat to the wealth would be the next generation or the generation after that changing the plan and losing the money through excessive spending or bad investments or fighting over it. And there just so many ways in which people can lose their capital and really ruin an incredible plan. So, I think you have to match a well-architected plan with the right family education and governance so that future generations can actually take that responsibility and be successful. >> I love that you went there. Structuring. Perhaps the only thing that's more boring is tax. Structure and tax are the two least sexy parts of asset management. >> But that's where the good >> And I would argue I I I would argue yes, that's where you begin, but also I would argue that they are really the some of the last points of alpha as an individual investor. >> Absolutely. >> For several reasons. One is so much of the capital markets is you are betting against somebody else. So, if you are day trading in your basement on the public markets, who is your counterparty? It is Baupost, it is Point72, it is Ken Griffin, the smartest people in the world with the smartest people working for them in the world with the smartest technologies. And oftentimes literally literal wires going into the New York Stock Exchange for for trade execution. >> That's your betting against. >> When you talk about tax alpha, tax-aware strategies, structuring, nobody's taking the opposite side of that bet. Nobody's saying don't put an LLC into your structure so that you have unlimited liabilities. The IRS might not love some of these strategies, but there are some regulatory ways to look at it and and legislative things that have been passed for better or for worse. So, these structural alpha and this tax alpha also, on top of it being not sexy, it's a difficult thing to sell. When you're a large bank trying to win business, structural alpha is not really the thing that you tout. >> Certainly in the traditional model, my own experience is that family office services were hard to find, um hard to pay for. You know, sometimes it's like, "Well, if you put more assets with us, then we'll provide this service." So, it was really not transparent in the pricing and, you know, you bring up a really good point in terms of, um are those services really available and will they make a difference? The whole trading explanation you gave, I think, is a great explanation and, you know, my view, if you're a young person and you want to be a day trader, go get a job in one of the places that you were mentioning. Go learn how to do it and make that your business. That never was my business. My alpha, before I even learned about great planning, was in starting and building companies. And that's how I created wealth for my family. Abby Stein, my co-founder, the same. My brother Doug, the same. We all were cut from the same cloth, business builders. And that is an opportunity to compound wealth over time on a tax efficient basis because you're not trading and you're not selling your business every day. So, it compounds on a tax deferred basis over a long time. >> That That's the riddle I used to ask people. If the taxes are so bad in California, why are there so many billionaires? >> [laughter] >> And the answer is, if you pay one-time tax, even if it's 38% versus 25% in in another jurisdiction, you have compounded that often times for decades and decades. >> Yes. >> Until now, I they're contemplating the wealth tax, of course, but absent of the wealth tax, you're compounding over and over again. You have these network effects. We were talking about if you want to be in venture capital, the value of being around San Francisco, and you keep on compounding. And then, once it's worth billions and billions and billions of dollars, you pay that one-time tax. It's obviously painful, and there's obviously structuring around that you could do if it's a public company and things like that. But that's the answer to the riddle, which is if the tax schema is so bad, why are there so many billionaires? And actually, the opposite of that is also true. It's a very state Some of these high-tax jurisdictions is very difficult states to build traditional businesses where you're paying taxes on a yearly basis and that don't have this kind of losses until they're 10 100 billion dollars. >> California is a beautiful place to visit. I mentioned to you earlier, I lived there for, you know, a few months over the summer to visit our kids, and it's a beautiful place to visit. It's most challenging for, you know, high-income earners and for small business people. Exactly what you said. But if you are If you have a a very large tech company, if you're in a whole different It's a whole different thing, and that's why that riddle exists. But it is challenging for small businesses especially and for high-income earners who don't have the assets that an entrepreneur would have in starting building successful tech company. >> I'm going to put you to a specific asset class or sub-asset class. What do you think is underrated today as an investment? >> a few things that I think are are interesting and underrated. And by the way, it is a fantastic question because so many things are so elevated in their valuation constructs that I think it's like not easy to find things that are truly out of favor. But I would say, first, I've been an investor for years now in multi-family real estate. The last few years in real estate were really challenging, but as a result of that, new construction slowed. There is a housing challenge in the US, an affordability challenge. And so, I do think that we're actually at the beginning of a an upward period for real estate which would include certain multi-family for sure where we'll see more upward pressure on rents which will be good for real estate investors. So I think that's an interesting asset class to look at and to understand better. The BDCs that we spoke about earlier, you know, the opportunity to buy portfolios of loans where if you go and look at where loans are traded on tradeable loans and you can actually see that a loan might be trading at a 5% discount, but then the portfolio in a BDC that that loan is in is trading at a 17% discount. Um and it's diversified. If you can get a hold of the loan portfolio, you can go to Edgar at the SEC and you can download these reports and you can really dig into it. And if you do your homework, a well-constructed BDC that's trading at a 17% discount is super interesting, especially if you can put together portfolio for four or five of them. Private credit as an asset class has been given a really good drubbing right now and it's probably overdone. And within private credit, I think tax-aware like equipment leasing because of the big beautiful bill, you can turn around and get nice tax deductions by investing in equipment leasing. And so it's not a permanent tax benefit, but you are deferring taxes and compounding your benefit on a tax advantage basis. So I would say those would be the areas right now that I see opportunity. >> The asset classes that regularly come up with single family office, one as you mentioned earlier, lower middle market PE at a previously Professor Steve Kaplan, I think friend of yours, he showed that private equity has roughly a one beta. So you're not getting more risk than being S&P 500, but there's still that that alpha and that alpha is mostly in the lower middle market. Large buyout is just getting so big that it's becoming more and more difficult to generate alpha. But in the lower middle market, if you know what you're doing, you have a team, and you have a smart way to access that. Second, perhaps extremely obvious, top quartile venture or top decile. >> Yes. >> Another Steve Kaplan research, 52% persistence for many decades, top quartile staying top quartile. >> Venture would be an access class, not an asset class. You have to get into those best funds. >> Absolutely. Also, as just a general principle of how to invest, one of the things I think is very misunderstood about asset classes is the supply and demand dynamics in the asset classes. If an asset class, no matter how overpriced it was, if it becomes unfavorable for a long enough time, the capital and the demand goes away from that asset class, and it reaches an equilibrium point where it now has become favorable. The example I like to use is early stage venture capital. Let's say people think that's overpriced at 50 million. If the capital keeps on leaving that asset class, and it keeps on going 40, 30, 20, at some valuation, maybe it's $5 million, it now becomes one of the best asset classes. >> That's right. >> But yet, people like to pretend like these asset classes are fixed fixed pricing. Like early stage venture must be at $50 million. Often times, some of the best asset classes are below the headline. I had the CIO of Texas Tech, Tim Barrett, and he was going after probably one of the most hated asset classes, office space, because the headline was so bad, nobody was investing. And he went one layer below that, and he looked at specific geography, specific structures, where the baby went out with the bathwater, and he saw these great returns because, not in spite of it and being unfavored, but because of the very fact that it was unfavored, there was the equivalent of free money on the floor where nobody was there to pick it up. >> Yeah, I agree with you. When I was in the ninth grade, I had a teacher, Mr. Reese, and he talked about the cycles of life and the cycles of business and boom and bust. And it's absolutely the same thing within asset classes. Asset classes cycle into favor, investors get excited, there's a lot of press that supports us, especially now with social media, there's so many outlets that can get behind something. And we get and particular areas just get overheated, um valuations soar, and then eventually it changes. Having an understanding of the fundamentals of investing and having the ability to pick and choose certain asset classes that you want to become an expert in. And if it's two or three, great. And then your ability to watch those and to have a sense as to when to get in and when to get out. I mean, let's take multifamily real estate as an example. There are many you're talking about family offices. There are many single family offices where the source of the family's wealth came from real estate. We're sitting in New York, New York City, some great families that made tremendous wealth over generations here in New York real estate. They know about what properties you want to hold forever, what properties you might want to sell under certain circumstances, when to finance, when to refinance, when to recap and pull money out. They have such a great understanding of their asset class and they're experts in it and that makes it hard for new people to come into it. But if you can do that in two or three things where you really understand them at a granular level, then you have a good sense as to when to double down and when to perhaps pull back and maintain more liquidity in your portfolio. >> And on that vein, you wrote the book The Long Game. Why did you decide to write a book? >> So 30 years ago, I mentioned I'm from Baltimore. From humble beginnings, my dad was the first one who went to college and he started a business in college to pay his way, where he hired his fraternity brothers to dress up like Santa Claus. He rented them to department stores like a temporary service agency. And this only could happen in America. Department stores became shopping centers, became malls. My dad did 400 malls in the US. That meant that for 53 years, if you took a child to have their photo taken with Santa, that everything around it, the set, the chair, the whole mall, that was our business. And it was a great family business, and my dad had that company for 53 years. But my brother Doug and I did not want to go into the business. We loved Dad, and we loved the business. It was fun to grow up in it. We didn't want to that to be our careers. So, my dad, unfortunately, didn't have a great succession plan, and eventually he was forced to sell the business into kind of an ESOP, not a super successful employee ownership model, and then eventually that was sold to a large, uh, kind of convention company that basically handles the the really big conventions. And after working there for a year, for the buyer, my dad called my brother and me and said, um, this company that he sold it to, he goes, "They're bad at Christmas. They're bad Santas, and I don't want to work here anymore." And he quit. And it became such a sad chapter in his life. So, the book, my very first inspiration for the book was my father. And how could I come up with some kind of a construct where his company could have continued beyond the 53 years that it stayed in our family, and so that it could have thrived for a longer time. And one day I was walking in downtown Baltimore, I picked up the Baltimore Business Journal, and there was the Book of Lists, and it was the oldest companies in the state of Maryland. And it was companies back then like Alex Brown, which was a great, great investment bank. They had lasted for 195 years. Johns Hopkins, a name everybody knows. And some defense companies, I think Lockheed Martin was maybe on it back then, and then I see this name, the Loan Brothers Tent Rental Company. And I look at Loan Brothers, and they were like 200 years old. And this is years ago. And like, oh my gosh, how does a small business, kind of like my dad's business, how do they last for like 200 years? That means that they lived through pandemics and like the Civil War and I mean, I'm just making a list of all the things in my mind. So, I went and I go look the company up, and I find out that uh Joseph Loan left England in like 1815. There'd been a volcanic eruption, and there was darkness kind of around the earth, so it was cold everywhere, so it was dark and cold in England, and he's like, I'm going to leave, and he picks Baltimore cuz it's a great port back then, and he makes his way to Baltimore, and he opens up the Joseph Loan Sail Company, making sails for the clipper ships that are going back and forth doing trade with probably Alexander Brown, and it becomes Alex Brown Company. And I'm like, wow, what an incredible origin of that company. How did they last for 200 years? So, I end up calling Brian Loan and interviewing him, learning his lessons, and that became a hobby of mine, where we would travel as a family, I'd bring my kids and my wife Jill. If we were in Italy, we're meeting with uh you know, the Frescobaldi family, 33rd generation. Think about that. That means that they bought land in the center of Florence in the year 1500. So, this is a family that's lasted for 33 generations. And so, we sat uh with Lamberto Frescobaldi, his two sons, and our two sons, and we had a great conversation about life, about succession, about family education, and family values. And I just did that over and over again, and then finally, about 2 years ago, I was talking to my co-founder Abby Stein about our hopes and dreams for Cresset. We want Cresset to be a 100-year business. And Abby said, you You Take those interviews, put them together in a book, let's put that out to our team. So, originally the book was going to be written for the team at Cresset. And then my daughter-in-law was talking to me about it and some other friends and they're like, this this could really be a book. Like you should put this out here. And the reason you should put it out there is because there's this amazing fascination that we have as a society around technology, innovation, disruption, you know, what's new? How fast can we get to the exit? All that's great, super cool, and we should celebrate it. But we put almost nothing into what are the lessons we can learn from companies and organizations that have stood the test of time. And it could be Hasbro or Whirlpool or it could be Ferragamo and Frescobaldi in Italy. These are companies that have stood the test of time, that have survived moments of truth where they if they had taken the wrong turn, we wouldn't even know their names anymore. But they were able to make the right decisions over the scale of 100 years. And that's probably 15 or 20 moments of truth where they were able to get through the pandemics and the wars and the recessions and depressions, um having a bad, you know, generation. I mean, 33 generations for the Frescobaldi family. You know, they said to us, "Not every one of us was so great over 33 generations. You know, there were a couple of not so good ones in there, but the business was resilient enough that it could even survive a bad generation." That's pretty cool. >> What was the most surprising lesson you learned from interviewing these organizations that have been around for 100 years? >> Sure. So, one that I absolutely love, especially spending time uh visiting Asheville, North Carolina, is the Biltmore, um which is the Vanderbilt family. So, the Cecil Pickering family, they're a six-generation family now in Asheville managing this American treasure, the Biltmore House, 8,000 acres, spectacular beauty, and they have been able to survive from George Vanderbilt who built this all the way now for six generations through great family planning, through a family culture of conservation and preservation, and of stewardship, where they view this amazing, again, American treasure of this this home that we have here in America that was George Vanderbilt's home, they treat this as something that's not even theirs for their generation, but something that they're taking care of future generations. And it's powerful. It's really powerful. And they've proven that they can do it. And they've been very successful. It's a great place to visit. I highly recommend it. >> Said another way, they bought into the vision. They bought into >> Multiple generations have bought into long-term vision. >> And each generation has taken the responsibility of helping the next generation to come up to speed on what all of that means. So, like G5, you know, they spent a lot of their youth on the property working the farm, working the house, working the hospitality. Um one uh you know, one gentleman uh his background, he worked at Disney and learned hospitality at Disney. He also was in Africa with Jane Goodall and learned about conservation. Um and so, he's running part of the business. And then another uh gentleman spent his time uh in investment banking and learned about capital markets and investing. And so, he's helping and working that part of the family. So, you've got operators and investors. You've got entrepreneurs. Uh there's a family member who started a jewelry business, uh which is fantastic, taking some of these inspiring uh pieces that uh that previous generations had, and then bringing her design ideas to make them contemporary and cool, and has really created a wonderful uh jewelry business. So, there's innovation, entrepreneurship, operators, investors, but they all share this passion for the property and this tremendous responsibility of stewardship and making sure that it's great for future generations of Sassos and Pickerings, but it's also great for those of us that want to come and visit this property and experience it. >> Do you think those lessons could have be applied to a company that's not family owned? >> Yes, I do think that that these ideas around stewardship, around thinking over the long term, you know, how you spoke about balance sheets earlier, how you manage your balance sheet, how much leverage you're going to put on to a business, how much you're going to invest in the future. All of these decisions, I think that whether it's a family owned business or whether it's a business that you were running for somebody else, that you can use these same principles to allow a business to be a whole lot stronger and and and very successful over a longer period of time. And what I find with a lot of short-term thinking is if you're a buyer of a business that's been built for the short term, you better do your diligence because you'll find in many cases corners that have been cut. And so, if we we use a real estate analogy, you know, you're walking around a property and it needs paint and it needs work and you can just tell that someone hasn't really been taking care of it. If it's an operating company, you can see that they're short-staffed. On the capital equipment side, things are falling apart. You can just tell when something has been well taken care of and someone has created a very powerful cash flow machine that is built to last. >> Before me and my business partner who's sitting here, Curtis, before we started Whiteboard Capital, we sat down and we used this framework that I learned from my mentor, Eric Anderson, who's now on his fourth unicorn. And he's learned through his experiences that he's only interested in building the business he wants to work in for the rest of his life. And it sounds trite or it sounds it sounds like a slogan or something, but if you truly embrace it when you're building the business, you fundamentally build a different business. And it's in the DNA, it's in the values, it's in how you hire, it's in how you incentivize. And I think there's something to this whole aspect, and maybe it's the asset management business in itself that's turned everything to these three, four-year cycles. In fact, we're so short-term focused as a society that the public markets are day-to-day. So, when you have a private equity fund holding for three to five years, you're like, "Holy crap, they're so long-term thinking." But if you take a step back and look at the original businesses, these family-owned businesses, there is something to holding these assets for 10, 20, 30 years. I had a guest on the show, Brent Beshore, uh who's in the Midwest and he has this 30-year fund. And you mentioned this concept of leverage. He oftentimes buys companies and waits for this once-in-a-decade opportunity where hits the fan and there's a buying opportunity. And by not having leverage, he's the only one that's not uh like a chicken running around with its head cut off. I think there's something to this compounding, and the the thought experiment is, if tomorrow you sell your company, what are you going to buy? >> Right. >> If you're just going to put it into a 60/40 portfolio, if you're going to buy the S&P 500, why? >> Yeah. >> Why not compound what you know, your asymmetric information, something that you control, in order to compound your wealth that way? People are just so incentivized to just get that mark, get that pat on the back that they over-index on that and under-index on what are they going to do the next day? >> Yeah. I think that's a a great concept. I totally agree. Um I have a saying which is uh you should run your business like you're going to own it forever because you just might. I mean, we have long periods of time sometimes where, for whatever reason, capital markets, you can't sell something at what you might think is a fair price. And I actually think that what is counterintuitive of say the long game of a 100-year business or in your example of owning a business for decades is that a lot of times people think that that means like never selling. And certainly that is a possibility. I mean looking at this fantastic Biltmore property, never been sold and probably never will be. But what it means is you're building a more valuable business, a more durable business and that makes it more desirable. And so when you were talking about your friend's concept, I think that what's so interesting about I'm going to run the business like I'm, you know, going to own it forever or or in his example, I guess it was run it for decades. This idea that um that you're thinking more over the long term and you were building a better business, a more durable business, a more valuable business and that is something then that ironically and interestingly acquirers will desire even more and at some point they're knocking on your door. >> The paradox. I've also found the paradox, the more long-term you think, the faster your growth. Yeah. The more short-term results you will have from the long-term thinking. It it's a good way >> We should collect these paradoxes. So I think of like having been a parent and now becoming a grandparent, you know, one of the great ironies is how independent are your children? And this is so ironic because the more you love your children, the more you would want to hold them so close and protect them from every little bump and bruise. But that's so ironic because if you want independent children, you have to allow them to fail, you have to allow them to do their own thing. But that is that's kind of a paradox. Uh you'd think that actually the people that love their children the most would actually be holding them so close, but that's exactly the opposite of the outcome you're looking for. You want independent children that are capable and can carry on their own lives without us. That's the highest thing that a parent can do. Um another great paradox and irony is the sale of a business, the exit of a business to be celebrated. Now you have a pile of capital, but the funny thing about is that capital will not manage itself. And so, someone thinks that hey, I worked so hard to build this business and take these risks, and now I'm going to diversify. But, the pile of capital sitting there, and they're not putting the same level of expertise and effort into managing that that they that they did in their business. You know, they had a board of directors, they had top leaders and executives in the company, they had talent and culture and all the things it takes to build an organization. Now, suddenly you get a pile of capital, and it's like one guy and a dog. And that's just an unbelievable and kind of funny paradox that people don't always put the same level of rigor into how they're going to manage the capital after they have that exit. And the last one that I think is a funny paradox is around great leaders, um CEO founders, or really leaders in any particular field. It could be a great professional athlete or entertainer. Anyone who's great at something, they're able to focus on it with an level of intensity. And as a result of that, everything else is is excluded through the focus. And then, if they're a family person and they want to stay married, they're going to have to be investing and putting time into their family. And if they're a good citizen, hopefully they're doing some good works in their community. Is there any time after that for like deep planning around estate tax and some of these other things that we talked about? And what I found, which I thought was just my secret, that I didn't put time into those things until eventually we created something like Cresset and I could become a client of it, it turns out that every high-performing CEO founder that I've met, they all have the same thing. And that is that they were focused on their main thing and their family and then hopefully the community. And they all actually had this drawer where they put everything in it, statements, plans, all this other stuff, and they've just closed the drawer, and once a year they'd send it all to their accountant. And so, that has been a very funny paradox. >> On that note, Eric, this has been an absolute masterclass. Thanks so much for stopping by. >> Thanks for having me. >> Thanks for watching. If you enjoyed this episode, please press subscribe above so that you don't miss future episodes with the world's top investors.

metadata.title: The Deposit and Escrow Instructions
metadata.author: Title's Not Borin' with Lauren
metadata.shortDescription:
The deposit is the buyer’s responsibility to deliver to escrow within 3 days of acceptance. The contract defaults to electronic funds transfer. Acceptable funds are wire transfer,  personal check, cashiers check or money order (check with the lender).

Buyer, seller and agent packages are furnished once the preliminary title report is completed. They contain escrow instructions, general provisions and forms to be completed. Escrow instructions are drawn directly from the purchase contract and restate what buyer and seller have instructed escrow to execute. 

It is important to provide later amendments to the contract within 3 days of acceptance. Escrow can only act upon mutually agreed to instruction provided to us in writing.

metadata.title: How to Wire Money for Closing
metadata.author: Hauseit
metadata.shortDescription:
How to wire money for closing? Overview by Chris at Hauseit® (https://www.hauseit.com).

Save money when buying, selling and renting real estate in New York and Florida with Hauseit. Available in NYC, Long Island, the Hudson Valley and South Florida. Established 2014.
.
Often times, wiring money for closing will be the biggest amount of money a person moves in their life. How can you safely complete this transaction given the prevalence of wire fraud these days?

It's important to double & triple check the account number and routing number, and the wire instructions before hitting send on that wire transfer.

Ideally, you should call the escrow agent (who is often either the seller's attorney or the closing attorney) to confirm by phone the wire transfer details that have been emailed to you.

That's because it's possible that someone has hacked the attorney's email and send you fraudulent account details. So make sure to be especially vigilant if you see different account details being sent to you, especially if you've already received another set of instructions.

Remember, as the buyer, the onus is on you to do your due diligence and know what you're getting into. If you become the victim of wire fraud, unfortunately it's very hard to retrieve the money. That's why there is the principle of "caveat emptor" in New York and California when it comes to real estate deals, meaning "buyer beware." Buyers are responsible for doing their own due diligence, hence the diligence period etc.

We explore this mystery and explain further in the following video.
.

Thinking about getting your Pennsylvania real estate broker license, but not sure it's worth it if you never plan to open a brokerage? Here's why knowing real estate law can keep you out of trouble AND help you close more deals.

🎓 BROKER IN A BOX — all 8 courses, all 240 hours of PA broker education, taught live by Janis Benstock
📅 Jan 4 – Apr 24, 2027 · Zoom orientation Nov 16
💻 Every class live on Zoom, weeknights + Saturdays
💲 $2,900 in full or 2 monthly payments of $1,550 (about $12 an hour)
👉 Reserve your seat: https://jbrea.net/registerbibpublic-465224

📖 Read the blog: The Benefits of a PA Broker License
👉 https://jbrea.net/post/benefits-of-pa-broker-license

You passed your licensing exam, but how much of pre-licensing class do you actually remember? Most agents learned RELRA, contract law, and agency before they ever wrote an offer, so none of it had context. Then you get busy building your business, and the regulations fade into the background… until they don't.

In this video, Janis Benstock — Philadelphia broker and instructor at Janis Benstock Real Estate Academy — shares:
✅ Why experienced agents often aren't fluent in PA real estate law
✅ How a well-known agent got hit with a $5,000 Real Estate Commission fine over a billboard
✅ Why 14 hours of CE every two years isn't enough to stay sharp
✅ How understanding options, seller financing, and title helps you save deals that seem undoable
✅ Why broker education is worth it even if you never open your own brokerage

Chairman of the Business Brokers of Florida 2021-2023, Joe Shemansky alerts the public that a license is required to sell and buy businesses in the State of Florida.

Joe Shemansky is the Broker-Owner of We Sell Construction Businesses. Dedicated to understanding the construction industry, from the hard-working individuals on the job site, the supply chain and related manufacturing and distribution companies, the firm sells construction businesses only - from small contractors to large corporations. 

When you're looking to sell one of your biggest investments ever, you want an experienced professional who understands you, your clients, your projects and your business - beyond the financials - to deliver the right message to the right buyer prospect. We Sell Construction Businesses is here to help you realize your goals. 

#WeSellConstructionBusinesses
#SellMyBusiness
#BusinessBroker
#BBF
#DBPR

segments.text: Hello, My name is Joe Shemansky.
I'm the Chairman of the Business Brokers of Florida.
I've come to you today, to share important information.
Whether you are buying or selling a business in Florida, under Florida Real Estate Law 475, anyone
who is transacting in the sale or purchase of a business on behalf of another is required to have
a valid real estate license with the Department of Business and Professional Regulation.
Or better known to those of us who hold valid licenses: The DBPR.
This is critical to protect the public, not only in dealing with moral or ethical
issues. But even more crucial in legal matters such as contracts and disclosure concerns.
The Business Brokers of Florida, encourages you to ask if the Business Broker that you're
working with is licensed to sell businesses in the state of Florida.If you're unsure
you can check the DBPR's website @ www.myfloridalicense.com and click on
the verify a license button to confirm that the individual who is offering to
help you sell or buy a business in Florida maintains a valid license with the state.
Just as you would only hire a licensed real estate agent or a licensed commercial real
estate agent to help you buy or sell residential or commercial property. You
should only hire a licensed Business Broker to ensure that you've hired
someone who understands the lawful steps of buying or selling a business in Florida.
When it comes to selling your business after all the years of hard work that you've put into
it or if you're on the other side, looking to make quite possibly the most significant
investment of your life, I urge you to hire a licensed, professional, business broker.
Please join the Business Brokers of Florida in protecting the buying and
selling public and report all unlicensed activity.
And may God bless you while keeping you and your family and friends safe and healthy. Thank you.

🏡 **Brokerage Operations Explained | Real Estate Exam Prep 2026–2027**

Who is responsible for supervising real estate agents? What happens when a broker improperly handles client money? And what's the difference between commingling and conversion?

In this episode of **REPA Explained**, we're breaking down BROKERAGE OPERATIONS—an essential topic for anyone preparing for the national real estate licensing exam!

Join Ben Eger, Principal Real Estate Broker and Real Estate Instructor, as we explore how real estate brokerages operate through engaging animations, real-world scenarios, and exam-style questions.

🎓 **WHAT YOU'LL LEARN:**

✅ What a real estate brokerage does  
✅ Broker vs. salesperson responsibilities  
✅ Brokerage supervision and compliance  
✅ Agency relationships and disclosures  
✅ How real estate commissions work  
✅ Trust accounts and earnest money deposits  
✅ Commingling vs. conversion explained  
✅ Transaction management and recordkeeping  
✅ Real estate advertising requirements  
✅ Fair housing and consumer protection  
✅ Common brokerage operations exam questions

💡 **REAL ESTATE EXAM TIP:**

Remember these three important concepts:

**COMMINGLING:** Improperly mixing client funds with personal or business funds.

**CONVERSION:** Wrongfully using or exercising control over another person's money or property.

**BROKER SUPERVISION:** The broker's responsibility to oversee licensed activities and ensure compliance with applicable laws.

Understanding these distinctions can help you avoid common mistakes on your real estate licensing exam!

📚 **PREPARING FOR YOUR REAL ESTATE EXAM?**

Our REPA Explained animated series makes complicated real estate concepts easier to understand, remember, and apply.

Whether you're preparing for the national real estate exam or studying for your state-specific licensing examination, we're here to help!

We create educational content for students in:

📍 Hawaii  
📍 California  
📍 Nevada  
📍 Utah  
📍 Florida  
📍 And across the United States!

🚀 **ABOUT REAL ESTATE PRO ACADEMY**

I'm Ben Eger, a Principal Real Estate Broker and Real Estate Instructor.

At Real Estate Pro Academy (REPA), our mission is to help aspiring real estate professionals develop the knowledge, confidence, and skills necessary to succeed.

**EDUCATE • EMPOWER • ELEVATE**

On this channel, you'll find:

🏡 Animated real estate exam lessons  
📚 Real estate practice questions and explanations  
🎧 Comprehensive audio lessons  
🧮 Real estate math tutorials  
📝 Real estate terminology and vocabulary  
🎓 National and state-specific real estate exam preparation  
💼 Real estate agent training and professional development

🔔 **SUBSCRIBE FOR MORE REAL ESTATE EXAM PREP!**

If this lesson helped you better understand brokerage operations, please LIKE this video, SUBSCRIBE to @BenEgerRealEstate, and share it with someone preparing for their real estate exam!

A. Conversion

Let's keep learning together!

Your shortcut to smarter exam prep starts at https://quizzprep.com/ .
. California Real Estate License 2026: Salesperson vs Broker Career Paths

The decision to pursue a California real estate salesperson license or a broker license in 2026 carries significant implications for your long-term earnings and professional autonomy. With the Department of Real Estate updating its standards, staying informed on the specific qualifications is essential for anyone entering the housing market or looking to elevate their current status. This breakdown analyzes the fundamental differences between these two roles to help you select the most profitable path.

A salesperson license is the foundational requirement for individuals entering the industry. To obtain this in 2026, the DRE requires the completion of three college-level courses: Real Estate Principles, Real Estate Practice, and an elective. After passing the state exam, a salesperson must affiliate with a licensed broker. This relationship is crucial as the broker assumes legal responsibility for the transactions conducted by the salesperson. This structure allows new agents to gain experience under the guidance of a seasoned professional while focusing on building a client base and closing deals.

Stepping up to a broker license represents a major milestone in a California real estate career. The eligibility requirements are more demanding, typically requiring two years of full-time experience as a licensed salesperson or a four-year university degree with a specialization in real estate. In 2026, the broker exam covers a broader range of complex topics including business law, advanced finance, and the management of a brokerage office. Successful candidates gain the legal right to work independently, open their own firm, and employ other agents.

The financial benefits of holding a broker license are a primary driver for many professionals. As a broker, you are no longer required to share a percentage of your commission with an employer. Additionally, you can generate passive income by collecting a portion of the commissions earned by the agents working under your license. While this increases potential revenue, it also brings greater responsibility for legal compliance, trust fund management, and office administration.

We provide specialized licensing services, exam preparation tools, and career development resources to help you succeed in the California market.

Recent shifts in California law have emphasized the importance of high-level certification. Brokers in 2026 are increasingly focused on navigating digital transaction platforms and evolving disclosure requirements. For those who enjoy the entrepreneurial aspect of running a business, the broker license is indispensable. For those who prefer the flexibility of sales without the administrative burden of running a company, maintaining a salesperson license while working for a top-tier brokerage remains a viable and lucrative strategy.

The California Department of Real Estate continues to refine the examination process to reflect the technological advancements of 2026. Applicants for the salesperson license should expect a heavy focus on fair housing laws, consumer protection, and the ethical use of artificial intelligence in marketing. These topics have become central to the modern agent's toolkit. Mastery of these subjects not only helps in passing the exam but also ensures a smoother transition into a professional environment where digital transparency is mandatory.

salesperson versus broker. Question one.
Broker Ian receives an earnest money
deposit of $8,000 from buyer Walter for
a property in Los Angeles. Under
California law, how many business days
does Ian have to deposit this money into
a trust account or neutral escrow? One
business day, two business days, three
business days, five business days.
California real estate law requires a
broker to deposit trust funds like
earnest money into a trust account
neutral escrow or hand them to the
principal within three business days of
receipt.
Question two. Ian is a newly licensed
real estate salesperson in California to
renew their license after the first
4-year term. How many hours of approved
continuing education must Ian complete?
15 hours? 30 hours? 45 hours? 50 hours.
All real estate lences in California
must complete 45 hours of approved
continuing education every four years to
renew their license.

seller, Walter. When must Ian provide

Before entering into the listing
agreement, before showing the property
to any buyers. Before closing escrow
within days days of signing the
contract,
the listing agent must deliver the
agency disclosure form to the seller
before entering into the listing
agreement.
Question four. Ian purchases a home in
Los Angeles for $265,000
under California's Proposition 13. What
is the maximum annual percentage
increase in the assessed value of the
property? assuming no change in
ownership or new construction. 1% 2% 3%
percent.
Proposition 13 limits the annual
increase of the assessed value of real
property to a maximum of 2% per year
unless there is a change in ownership or
new construction.
Question five. Broker Ian hires an
unlicensed assistant, Walter. Which of
the following tasks can Walter legally
perform? Show a vacant property to a
prospective buyer. Answer questions
regarding the terms of a residential
lease. Type up and file real estate
documents and coordinate days,
appointments. Negotiate the price with a
buyer's agent.
Unlicensed assistants can perform
clerical duties such as typing, filing,
and scheduling appointments, but cannot
perform acts that require a real estate
license like showing properties or
negotiating.
Question six. Ian wants to claim adverse
possession of a vacant lot in Los
Angeles owned by Walter. In California,
one of the requirements is that Ian must
occupy the land continuously and pay
property taxes for a minimum of how many
years? 3 years, 5 years, 7 years, 10
years.
In California, adverse possession
requires open, notorious, continuous,
and hostile possession under a claim of
right or color of title, plus payment of
property taxes for a period of 5 years.
Question seven. Contractor Ian completes
a remodeling job on Walter's home in Los
Angeles, but is not paid the $8,000
owed. If Ian wishes to file a mechanic's
lean, they must have served a
preliminary notice within how many days
of starting work? 10 days, 15 days, 20
days, 30 days.
A preliminary notice must be given
within 20 days of first furnishing
labor, materials, or equipment to
preserve the right to file a mechanic's
lean in California.
Question eight. Broker Ian takes an
exclusive right to sell listing from
Walter for a property in Los Angeles.
The property sells for $265,000.
Ian retains all records of this
transaction under the California
Business and Professions Code. How long
must Ian keep these records? One year,
three years, 5 years, 7 years.
Real estate brokers must retain all
records regarding real estate
transactions for a period of 3 years
from the date of the closing or the date
of the listing if the transaction is not
consummated.
Question nine. Which type of deed is
most commonly used in Los Angeles,
California to transfer title to real
property, which includes two implied
warranties from granter Ian? Quick claim
deed, warranty deed, grant deed, trust
deed.
The grant deed is the most common
instrument used to transfer title in
California. It carries two implied
warranties that the granter has not
already conveyed title to another and
that the estate is free from undisclosed
incumbrances made by the granter.
Question 10. Ian applies for a loan of
and is provided a loan estimate under
the Tila Respa integrated disclosure
TRID rule. How many business days after
receiving the application must the
lender provide this estimate? one
business day, three business days, five
business days, seven business days.
Under TRID, a lender must provide the
loan estimate to the borrower within
three business days of receiving the
loan application.
Question 11. Under the subdivided lands
law in California, a public report is
required when a property in Los Angeles
is divided into how many parcels for the
purpose of sale, lease, or financing?
Two or more? Three or more? Four or
more? Five or more.
The subdivided lands law applies to the
subdivision of land into five or more
parcels for sale, lease, or financing.
Question 12. Ian is a broker who mixes
their personal funds of $8,000 with
their clients trust funds. This illegal
practice is known as conversion,
commingling, steering, redlinining.
Comingling is the illegal act of mixing
a broker's personal or business funds
with the trust funds of a client.
Conversion is actually spending the
trust funds.
Question 13. Agent Ian focuses marketing
efforts in Los Angeles by telling
homeowners that a certain minority group
is moving into the neighborhood to
induce panic selling. This illegal
practice is known as blockbusting,
steering, redlinining, flipping.
Blockbusting, also known as panic
selling, is the illegal practice of
inducing homeowners to sell their
properties by suggesting that people of
a particular race, religion, or
background are moving into the
neighborhood.
Question 14. If Ian obtains an easement
by prescription over Walter's land in
Los Angeles, Ian must have used the
property hostily, openly, continuously,
and notoriously for a period of at least
1 year, 3 years, 5 years, 10 years.
In California, an easement by
prescription requires 5 years of open,
notorious, continuous, and hostile use
under a claim of right.
Question 15. Ian and Walter sign a
written contract for the sale of a
property for $265,000.
In California, the statute of
limitations to file a lawsuit for breach
of a written contract is 1 year, 2
years, 4 years, 5 years.
The statute of limitations for bringing
a lawsuit on a written contract in
California is 4 years.
Question 16. When calculating the
property tax on Ian's home in Los
Angeles, the county tax assessor uses
the properties market value, assessed
value, appraised value, replacement
cost.
Property taxes are based on the assessed
value of the property, not the current
market value or appraised value.
Question 17. To create a valid joint
teny between Ian and Walter for a
property in Los Angeles, which four
unities are required? Time, title,
interest, possession. Time, title,
consent, payment. Agreement,
consideration, title, possession,
interest, possession, funding,
signature.
The four unities required to create a
joint teny are time, title, interest,
and possession. often remembered by the
acronym TTIP.
Question 18. Broker Ian holds an open
listing on Walter's property in Los
Angeles. Ian will only earn a $8,000
commission if they are the first to show
the property, the procuring cause of the
sale, the listing broker of record on
the MLS, able to hold days open houses.
In an open listing, the broker only
earns a commission if they are the
procuring cause of the sale, the one who
brings the willing and able buyer.
Question 19. Ian executes a deed
conveying property to Walter. For the
deed to be valid in California, it must
contain all of the following except a
granting clause. The signature of the
granter, N1. The signature of the
grantee, N2. An adequate description of
the property.
A valid deed must be signed by the
granter, but the grantee is not required
to sign it.
Question 20. A lender offers Ian a loan
to purchase a commercial property in Los
Angeles. The lender requires the
property to be used as collateral while
Ian retains possession. This is known as
subordination, hypothecation,
alienation, amortization.
Hypothecation is the practice of
pledging property as security for a debt
while retaining possession and use of
the property.

metadata.title: Confidential Information Memorandum (CIM)
metadata.author: Jim Loeffler
metadata.shortDescription:
📄 What’s the one document that could make or break your business sale?
It’s called the Confidential Information Memorandum (CIM) — and if you’re a manufacturing business owner considering a future sale, you need to know what’s inside it.

I’m Jim Loeffler, CPA, CFE, MBA — founder of InTune Business Advisors. For over 20 years, we’ve helped manufacturing owners unlock financial freedom through expert M&A strategy, business valuations, and exit planning.

In this episode of InTune Insights, I’ll break down:
✅ What a CIM really is — and why it’s confidential
✅ The key sections: Financials, operations, risks, and more
✅ How it supports due diligence, protects your data, and boosts buyer confidence
✅ Why a well-crafted CIM can increase your valuation — before you go to market
✅ How to turn the CIM process into a roadmap for long-term business improvement

📊 If you're planning to sell in the next 3–5 years (or even in the next decade), don’t wait. Start preparing now.

🎯 Don’t just list your business. Prepare it like a pro.

👉 Book a free call with me today:
🔗 https://meet.getintune.com/discovery

📲 Let’s connect and grow together:
🔵 Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/profile.php?...
📸 Instagram: @getintune_now
💼 LinkedIn: Jim Loeffler
👥 Join our CEO group for manufacturing business owners: /1176495547

🔧 Know your numbers. Maximize your value. Sell with confidence.
Get the insight. Get the value. Get InTune.
