metadata.title: What is the Confidential Information Presentation - 8 Milestones of M&A - Transact Capital
metadata.author: Transact Capital
metadata.shortDescription:
Greetings, everyone, and thank you for joining our enlightening series on the Eight Milestones of Mergers and Acquisitions. I'm your host, Jacob, and in today's episode, we're diving deep into the world of the CIP, the Confidential Information Presentation. This document, often referred to as your executive summary, is the cornerstone of your M&A journey.

In simple terms, your CIP is a comprehensive document, sometimes exceeding 50 pages, that provides potential buyers with in-depth insights into your business. This invaluable resource is exclusively shared with interested buyers who have not only viewed the teaser but have also signed an NDA (Non-Disclosure Agreement).

Before we delve into a real-world example, let's explore the key aspects and insights surrounding the CIP.

We'll equip you with a robust set of marketing materials, and here's why it matters:

Speed: The more information we provide in your CIP, the more questions we answer for prospective buyers, saving precious time that can make or break deals.
Impression: Your buyers are human, and we're here to present your company in a highly professional manner, maximizing your impact as we navigate the market to find the best-suited buyers for your consideration.
The primary purpose of the CIP is to inform potential buyers and allow them to truly grasp your business. Each CIP is uniquely tailored to you and your company's needs. Some of the key areas we can cover include your executive summary, company history, sales process, manufacturing capabilities, and your stellar management team, just to name a few.

Beyond educating your buyers, our goal is to qualify them. We arm them with the most relevant information to optimize the M&A process and position ourselves for success in the future.

In the video, we'll showcase some example pages from a generic CIP we've created. Please note that this isn't a real company, but these slides offer a glimpse of the kind of document we aim to craft for you. Your CIP will be customized with your logo and company colors, ensuring it presents your business in the most professional and appealing manner.

Don't miss the rest of our eight-part series on the Milestones of M&A, brought to you by Transact Capital. Stay tuned for more valuable insights on your journey through the world of mergers and acquisitions.

#MergersAndAcquisitions #CIP #ExecutiveSummary #MandAInsights #BusinessMarketing #DealMaking #ConfidentialInformation #TransactCapitalSeries

metadata.title: What Buyers and Sellers Need to Know About the Buyer Broker Agreement in 2025
metadata.author: Think Real Estate
metadata.shortDescription:
It’s been a full year since the NAR Commission lawsuit changed the way agents and buyers work together — and the sky didn’t fall. In this video, Dave Robles, team leader at Think Real Estate, breaks down how buyer broker agreements are working in practice, why commissions haven’t vanished, and how buyers and sellers alike can navigate this new landscape with confidence.

Dave explains why most sellers are still paying buyer agent commissions (even without MLS offers), what today's average commission looks like, and how this shift is empowering buyers to choose smarter representation. You'll also hear Dave’s take on why these changes are a win — if you’ve got the right agent in your corner.

👥 Buying soon? Make sure you understand what you're signing — and how to get the best value from your agent.

📩 Questions about buyer broker agreements or how to negotiate commission as a seller? Let’s talk: dave@thinkrealestategroup.com or 213.712.4343.

🧠 Ready to work with a team that knows how to navigate the new real estate landscape? Reach out anytime.

⏱ Timestamps
00:00 Where we are one year after the NAR commission lawsuit
00:20 What the buyer broker agreement really means
00:40 Why the expected drop in commissions didn’t happen
01:10 What sellers are actually doing about buyer commissions
01:40 The current average buyer agent commission
02:00 Why Dave supports this change
02:20 The upside: better representation for buyers
02:40 Honest money conversations: why they matter
03:00 Negotiation opportunities for sellers in today’s market

❓FAQs
02:00 What is the average buyer agent commission in 2025?
→ It's currently 2.37%, down slightly from 2.45% the year prior.

02:10 Do sellers still pay buyer agent commissions?
→ Yes, over 90% of sellers still agree to pay if asked during negotiation.

02:20 Why is a buyer broker agreement required now?
→ It ensures buyers are formally represented and encourages smarter agent selection.

02:40 Does this change help or hurt buyers?
→ Done right, it helps. Buyers are better informed and get stronger representation.

segments.text: It's been about a year since real estate
agents have had to work with the new
rules and procedures that came as a
result of the N commission lawsuit
settlement. So, how's it going? Where
are we now with agent commissions? The
big changes from the lawsuit were that
buyers would have to hire their own
realtors by signing a buyer broker
agreement. That agreement states that if
the buyer wants to buy a home and the
seller will not pay a buyer broker
commission, then the buyer will have to
pay their own agents commission.
Proponents of this settlement believe
that if the seller didn't have to pay
agent commission, then they would be
willing to sell their house for two or
3% less than they normally would have.
Now, why would a seller do that? I'm not
really sure. It was also thought that if
buyers were paying their own realtor
that the amount of commissions paid
would drastically fall and this whole
thing could potentially tank the real
estate market. Well, that didn't happen.
But what has happened after a year of
this? What are we actually seeing in the
practice of selling homes in
commissions? It appears that most
sellers, and by most I mean well over
90% of homeowners, are still agreeing to
pay a buyer broker commission if they
are asked to in the offer from the
buyer. The seller is not allowed to make
an offer of compensation in the MLS the
way they used to, but agents are
communicating and the seller's
intentions are being shared. Most recent
data shows that the average buyer's
agent commission is 2.37%.
And that's down from the 2.45%
a year earlier before the new rules were
unveiled. Now, that equals to about an
$800 discount of buyer agent commissions
on a $1 million sale. So, what's my
opinion of all this? I like it. I
thought this was a very good idea a year
ago when it was proposed, and I still
do. Requiring buyers to sign a buyer
broker agreement and hire a realtor
gives them more incentive to vet their
realtor more thoroughly, resulting in
them getting better representation. And
it makes them have conversations with
their agent that they should have been
having all along. And I mean
conversations about money. People don't
like to talk about money, but in an
expensive purchase that requires
commissions to be paid potentially by
them, buyers and their agents absolutely
need to be talking about money. And from
the seller's perspective, commissions
are more negotiable than they've ever
been. And if you're working with the
right realtor who understands how to
negotiate these terms successfully,
maybe you can even save a little more
than that $800. And you know what they
say, a penny saved is a penny earned.

metadata.title: Tax Credit 101 with Andrew Dubinsky | Part 2: How Transferable Tax Credits Work (Section 6418)
metadata.author: Andrew Dubinsky
metadata.shortDescription:
In Part 2 of Andrew Dubinsky's Tax Credit 101 webinar series, Andrew breaks down how the Section 6418 transferable tax credit market works under the Inflation Reduction Act — including who can buy and sell credits, which credit types are still active after the One Big Beautiful Bill, and what the transfer process actually looks like from registration to claiming on Form 3800.
In this session, Andrew covers:

Transfer vs. Direct Pay — what's the difference?
Which credits were eliminated and which are still transferable (solar, 45X, clean fuel, hydrogen, nuclear & more)
The rules every buyer and seller must follow
What an IRS registration number actually means (and what it doesn't)
How risk and liability are allocated between buyers and sellers
Key deadlines and common misconceptions

Whether you're a tax professional, project developer, or corporate buyer exploring the credit transfer market, this is a practical overview of how these transactions work in the real world.

Building a Boutique Brokerage Firm: AI, Business Exits & Growth Tips | Christine McDannell---
Business Broker Growth.

**What if your easiest business deals are falling apart—not because of price or terms, but because you're overlooking the emotional side of selling a business?**

In this episode of the **Business Broker Growth Show**, Jason Cutter sits down with **Christine McDannell**, Founder of **The Magnolia Firm**, to explore what truly separates top-performing business brokers from everyone else.

From managing seller emotions and keeping deals alive to using AI strategically and building a boutique brokerage that closes deals faster, Christine shares the systems, mindset, and real-world strategies that have helped her consistently deliver successful business exits.

Whether you're a **Business Broker, M&A Advisor, Business Intermediary, or Business Owner preparing for an exit**, this episode is packed with practical insights you can apply immediately.

In This Episode You'll Learn:
✅ Why seller psychology is often more important than negotiation
✅ How emotional support can prevent deals from falling apart
✅ Why "Time Kills Deals" and how to keep transactions moving
✅ How AI is changing business brokerage and business valuations
✅ Common mistakes business owners make before selling their companies
✅ Why relentless follow-up creates more closed deals and referrals
✅ How boutique brokerages can outperform larger firms
✅ Proven business broker marketing and growth strategies
✅ How to qualify better clients and build a stronger buyer pipeline

Christine also shares lessons from real deals, explains how AI is reshaping business sales, discusses common valuation misconceptions, and reveals why understanding a seller's true motivation is essential for closing successful transactions.

If you're serious about growing your business brokerage, improving your deal flow, and becoming a trusted advisor instead of just another broker, this episode is for you.

📍 How to Choose Your First Real Estate Brokerage (What Actually Matters)
Your first brokerage can make or break your real estate career — but most new agents don’t know what to actually look for. In this video, we’re breaking down what really matters when choosing your first brokerage so you can make a confident, informed decision.

🎯 What you’ll learn:

 ✔️ Why your brokerage choice impacts your success more than you think
 ✔️ The 3 types of brokerages you’ll run into (and who they’re best for)
 ✔️ 5 smart questions to ask during interviews
 ✔️ Red flags to avoid at all costs
 ✔️ How to choose based on your learning style + goals

Whether you’re a brand new agent or just thinking about getting licensed, this video is your roadmap to choosing the right fit — not just the flashiest one.

THE 5 QUESTIONS YOU SHOULD ASK WHEN INTERVIEWING A BROKER:

1. What kind of training and mentorship do you offer new agents?
🔍 Why it matters: Fancy offices and signs don’t close deals — training does. Ask for specifics: Is it classroom-style, one-on-one coaching, or shadowing? How often? Who leads it?

2. How are leads generated, and who owns them?
🔍 Why it matters: Some brokerages offer leads — but take a big split or keep the relationship. Ask if you'll be working your own sphere or mostly company leads. Know who keeps the client long-term.

3. What are the monthly and annual fees, and what do they cover?
🔍 Why it matters: It's not just about your commission split. Some “high-split” brokerages charge tons of fees that add up fast — tech, desk, E&O insurance, marketing. Know your full cost to operate.

4. What support systems are in place when I need help with a deal or have questions?
🔍 Why it matters: Real estate is fast-paced, and having a broker who is MIA when you’re panicking over a contract clause is a nightmare. Ask how available support is — and who provides it.

5. What does a successful agent look like in this brokerage?
🔍 Why it matters: This reveals the culture and unspoken expectations. Are they all about volume? Nurturing community relationships? Part-time agents welcome? Make sure your values align.

metadata.author: Jesse Ebner
metadata.shortDescription:
Today Brie and I are discussing the differences you can find in boutique real estate brokerages vs. franchised real estate brokerage. Signature Properties Ebner & Associates is a boutique brokerage in Crested Butte, CO and we love it! Both of us have previous experience working for franchised brokerages so we are comparing the differences and pros of staying boutique in this podcast. The best part of it for us is that we are able to keep our clients money local and support local businesses and charities.

__________________________________________________________________________________
I am super passionate about real estate. I love my job! I love helping people and I would love to work with you! Give me a call today and let me know how I can help you whether your thinking about buying, selling, investing or just looking to start learning about the Crested Butte Real Estate Market.

Jesse Ebner - Real Estate in Crested Butte
Call or Text - 970-901-2922

But, as you kind of touched on, that leverage is kind of a an idea, not so much a reality because people are coming to you for everything. The profit margins aren't as lucrative as most people assume. There's obviously outliers, but across the general basis. So, what did that look like as you started to scale? Because from the outside looking in, a lot of people say four offices, 137 agents at 30 years old, holy I want to do that. Um but behind the scenes, it wasn't all sunshine and roses. No, no, it wasn't. Um and because we had to we we ended up going through a few iterations of our pricing structures as well because we were trying to find out what works well in the marketplace and you know, if you're trying to figure that out, it does take a lot of time and effort to come up with something that makes sense. Um Initially, we weren't charging nearly enough. We gave every agent of ours that joined a a 90/10 um and there was a monthly fee attached to it. Um and you know, they would they would cap at 10,000 No, $15,000 when we started. So, you'd cap at 15,000. We were giving them a 90/10. We had a $150 transaction fee. And the reality is is that's not enough to keep the doors open. It's just not. The only way that you can get support and and staff and office spaces is you need to charge more. And you know, we didn't understand that at first because we'd never ran a business, right? Um there's a drastic difference between over eight being an agent and running an actual business. And when we looked at the back-end margins of what actual profitability looked like at the end and this is at the very peak, right? We were getting somewhere around uh 10% profit margins. And so, when you think, "Oh, but I'm giving my broker $10,000, $20,000." Really, the profit margin to ownership is $1 to $2,000. And that doesn't account for any signs they gave you, cards they gave you, marketing they gave you, time they gave you. And so, when you start to extrapolate that at scale, it's definitely not not as good as it needs to be. And that that even comes to at the very end we finally dialed in what was necessary to make profitability really make sense. We were charging a 70/30 split, a $500 transaction fee where we actually did transaction management for them at the end. And we had a 2.25% servicing fee on the top of every single deal of every single agent at the brokerage regardless of whether they hit their cap. And that's what was needed to actually start scaling and actually start making profitability make sense. And so, if you're in a position that you can't charge that much, then frankly, you're going to have a very difficult, if not an impossible, task to try to scale it because brokerages are heavily commoditized now, and people just do not want to pay those types of fees because, let's face it, the big brokerages, they have better scale, they have cheaper systems because they have the scale, they have better staffing because they have the scale. Uh It's just all already there versus you have to build from nothing, so you need a little bit more margin. And unless you're giving the agent something drastically different than the marketplace, which, let's face it, if you're giving them the moon, that's the best you can do. And so, when you when it comes down to looking at all of the different options, uh it becomes very difficult to see why you would scale. Because if there's no money, why do you want to scale? Why do you want to talk to all of these agents? Why do you want to recruit them? And ultimately, that's where we hit our pain points. We said, "Why do we want to service these agents? Why do we even want more agents? They're not worth any money to us anyways." And we kept coming full circle back to that. And we said, "Okay, well, remember I said we did the math and we said, 'If we get to 1,000 agents, like no matter how we cut the math, we finally made it.'" But then we said, "How can we actively get to 1,000 agents?" Well, no matter how you slice it in an in in an independent model, people are expecting local touch. They're expecting boutique local people to help them at the local level. And so, the average brokerage, if we were lucky, and and if we were better than everybody else, would have needed to have 50 agents in each one of those locations, and we would have needed 20 locations to get there. We were at four, right? And so, we said, "Do we want to sit down and try to make this extra 16 locations over the course of probably 16 years, and hopefully keep that retention, and hopefully market dynamics don't shift on us that make things difficult. Or do we want to do something else? And ultimately, we were looking at other states because you can only take so much market share in a given state. So, we were looking at okay, what other states make sense that we could dominate quickly? And when we started delving into that, we realized it that half the states we would need a different managing license there. We had to get another license here, and you had to get a different brokerage license here, and you had to connect it to here. And the logistics alone for trying to attempt that scale was going to take at least 16 years to properly do. And then we would have a footprint in probably 15 states. So, if we were sitting at 15 states, the servicing of that would have been a full-time job. And the reality is is if you're just a high-producing agent, you're going to make more money than a brokerage owner. You just are. Unless that brokerage owner somehow has hundreds of agents in one location and charges you a lot. Um, but if that's not the case, stay doing production. The only times I've ever talked to brokerage and independent brokerages that feel like they have great margin is because they're running a glorified team. And that's a totally different subject, but the reality is if you're a broker owner now, and maybe you're running Zillow leads or you're running some sort of paper click or or or something like that, and you're disseminating those leads to your agents, and you're charging them maybe 50/50s on them, let's just say. And you look at your balance sheet, and you're saying, "We make a ton of money." Well, I needed you got to take a step back, cut out all of those leads that you're getting paid for, and just look at your brokerage splits and transactions because that's what your brokerage is making you. The leads can be done as a team. There's no reason to own a brokerage to run leads. You could have done the same thing while not having the liabilities, which is a completely separate issue. And I've dealt with that, too. Dealing with 137 agents, we ended up dealing with two lawsuits in 4 years because of the behavior of those agents. And the larger you scale, the larger that that liability becomes. And each one of those lawsuits resulted in a like combined, I think it was just south of $200,000 in legal bills to get both of them to be dropped because they were frivolous. But that did not allow us to get away from those legal bills because when you're a brokerage owner, you have to have an entity and and entities are not able to self-represent. So, if you even get in one of those, you're going to lose profitability for the average brokerage of 30 or less agents for a year or two just because of one frivolous lawsuit that you had to fight. And so for us, it became an equation of economics. What makes sense from here? Yeah, man, it's there's there's so many good points there because I've talked to so many broker owners as well and, you know, I I know a lot of really strong agents and the agents as solo producers are more profitable than brokerages of 50 to 100 people, but they don't have the liability, they don't have the headache, they're not the middle cog in the wheel for absolutely everything. And and it's it's one of those things, too, that as you started going through the franchise, you know, uh initiative and being able to spread into these different markets, you need somebody with the local licensing requirements in each of those places. metadata.shortDescription:
Choosing a real estate brokerage is the biggest decision for a new real estate agent. Learn how to evaluate your options.

After getting your real estate license, the path forward can feel overwhelming. Many agents struggle to determine which firm aligns with their long-term goals. This video breaks down my personal journey as a California real estate broker to help you navigate the industry landscape with clarity.

I share a transparent illustration of how I weighed my options, providing a framework so you can deduct your own reasoning and conclusions. Whether you are aiming for independent growth or a support-heavy environment, understanding the nuances of a real estate career is essential. This week’s guest is Tim Garrity, and he took a different route. Tim wanted to run things his way. Listen to the episode and discover: The strategy Tim used to build his client base and grow from 10 to 40 agents and $10M to $40M in volume, the 3 steps he takes to ensure agents can be productive and accountable, and the distinctive content strategy he’s been using since the beginning to generate leads. 

Be sure to check out our show notes at staypaidpodcast.com for more in-depth information and added details not included in the episode.

How do you choose a real estate brokerage after you get your license? 
🏅 Earn Your CRES Designation 
👉 https://www.usrealtytraining.com/certified-real-estate-specialist?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=youtube&utm_campaign=choosebrokerage&utm_id=youtube
📋 Free New Agent Checklist 
👉 https://www.usrealtytraining.com/new-agent-checklist-pdf?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=youtube&utm_campaign=choosebrokerage-checklist&utm_id=youtube

This video gives new agents four things to compare: the office culture ("the vibe"), the leadership, the formal training, and the commission split. It also explains the difference between national brand brokerages, local boutiques, and virtual brokerages so you can pick the right fit.

In this video, you'll learn:
✅ Why office culture matters when you pick a brokerage
✅ What to ask leadership before you sign
✅ Why formal training can matter more than your split
✅ How commission splits work and what to ask about
✅ National brand vs boutique vs virtual brokerages

QUICK ANSWERS

What should a new agent look for in a real estate brokerage?
The instructor recommends comparing four things: the office culture, how supportive the leadership is, whether there is formal training (contracts, prospecting, and business planning), and the commission split.

What is a commission split?
A commission split is how a commission is divided between you and your brokerage. For example, on a 70/30 split, you keep 70% and the brokerage keeps 30%. Ask what your split will be before you sign.

Is the commission split the most important factor?
In this video, the instructor argues it isn't. A high split doesn't help if you aren't closing deals, so training, leadership, and culture should weigh into your decision too.

What is the difference between national, boutique, and virtual brokerages?
National brand brokerages are large, well-known companies that often offer classes, events, and a big office community. Boutique brokerages are smaller local offices with a more personal feel. Virtual brokerages typically have no physical office, and agents work from home.

CHAPTERS
0:00 The vibe: office culture
0:54 Leadership
1:51 Formal training
2:44 Commission split
4:07 National vs boutique vs virtual brokerages
6:00 Why training is your foundation

🌐 https://www.usrealtytraining.com

Learn more about partnering with me at eXp Realty: https://www.kylehandy.com/partner/

You’re ready to get your broker’s license (or perhaps you already have one). It feels like the time is right to start a brokerage of your own. But if you don’t know how to start a real estate brokerage, it can seem like a daunting task.

How do you go about creating a real estate business from scratch?

If you’ve become a successful real estate agent, you already have the skills that you need. While running a brokerage is different, it’s hard work, preparedness, and networking that will continue to drive your success.

metadata.title: How to Manage Deals in HubSpot Sales Pipeline 2026 | Deal Stages, Pipeline & Sales Management
metadata.author: Hema Glory
metadata.shortDescription:
Learn how to manage deals in the HubSpot sales pipeline in this complete 2026 step-by-step tutorial. metadata.title: The Silent Deal Killer in Due Diligence and How to Avoid It - Mark Sims
metadata.author: Amped Success - Matt Uhler
metadata.shortDescription:
What does a business look like through the eyes of a big corporate buyer? Matt Uhler sits down with Mark Sims, managing principal of Consult MSG and former CIO and head of strategy and M&A at Scotts Miracle-Gro, to break down what really happens in due diligence. Mark explains why clean, trusted numbers drive valuation, how deal friction quietly kills transactions, the difference between strategic and private equity buyers, and his 5 C’s of Value Creation for owners preparing to sell in the next few years.

metadata.title: Before You Wire the Money: What Real Due Diligence Looks Like in Private Market Deals
metadata.author: Family Enterprise Perspectives
metadata.shortDescription:
Many bad deals start with a trusted referral, a polished track record, and a few assumptions nobody verified.

Family offices and passive investors are deploying capital into private markets where a pitch deck, a sponsor questionnaire, and a few reference calls often stand in for real due diligence. When something goes wrong, the warning signs were frequently there all along: a lawsuit in another state, an undisclosed affiliated company, or a portfolio the sponsor manages but barely owns.

Join me for a live conversation with Shane Pogue, founder of AEGIS Risk Solutions and Investigations, whose firm has conducted investigative due diligence on more than $800 million in assets, investments, and transaction exposure.

We will cover:
• How an investigation differs from a background check
• How to vet sponsors and verify track record and financial strength claims
• Lessons from recent fraud cases and the red flags investors missed
• Why risk extends beyond the deal itself, to the investors, partners, executives, and vendors around it

Bring your questions. This one is for anyone who wants to know exactly what they are saying yes to before capital is on the line.

Uh that's a very easy trap to fall into because you see the results but a lot of the times those results aren't even real. Uh they might be a car they might have bought that house with investor funds. So you have to be really careful when we look at social proof influencer celebrity that actually it doesn't have a very strong effect on our actual process and due diligence because we're going to verify what they're actually saying rather than what they're showing everyone that they have. So when they put out this image of success we're going to be like where's the money coming from? >> Mhm. >> Um which is actually verifying the underlying assets. For example if you have if you're like, hey, I'm a very successful real estate syndicator, you've only been in business for three years, and before that you were making less than 10 less than $100,000 a year, and then suddenly you buy a million dollar house, I'm going to want to know where that money came from. And sometimes it's like, oh, their spouse has money or their family has money, but you still need to verify that information. And when you do that, it kind of peels off the social proof layer where you're not looking at their image, you're looking at the actual actions and the actual assets of the person. >> Yeah. Yeah. No, definitely. And again, I'd emphasize the importance of not saying not not pay attention to it, but discount it heavily and treat it as again, put the proof aside or your friend's reference, which again is not an insignificant point, but reviewed from with a fresh set of eyes from your perspective, right, to see if it aligns. So the five pillars are basically how you should look at risk because a lot of people just look at the investment. They don't look at their vendors. We're all going to do due diligence on each other. segments.text: let's get into sde or sellers
discretionary earnings this is one of
the most common metrics used to measure
the cash flow of a small business it's
similar to eida which stands for
earnings before interest taxes
depreciation and amortization both of
the calculations of sde and eida involve
taking the net income and then adding
back certain expenses for both SD and
eida you're adding back interest taxes
appreciation amortization one-time
expenses and discretionary spending with
sde you're also adding back the owner's
salary the reason both of these numbers
are important is that by using sste or
iida over the net income of a business
you'll have a more realistic comparison
of two businesses and you'll have a more
realistic understanding of what the
financial picture of a business would be
like with you as the new owner for
example interest payment if you're
looking at a business to buy and there
is a loan on that business whether it's
an SBA loan an equipment loan or some
other type of debt you're going to see
interest payments listed as an expense
and lowering the net income but the
thing is when you buy a business you're
most of the time buying it debt free so
that specific interest payment wouldn't
apply to you you're going to have your
own debt payment on the business you're
going to have your own terms and your
own interest payment so you want to add
back that interest payment to the net
income as part of getting to your SD or
eida number so you have a more accurate
idea of the financials SD and ibida are
typically what a business's valuation is
based off a multiple of one of these
numbers usually between a 3 to 5x SD is
a more common metric used with smaller
size businesses so for example if you
see someone selling their business and
they have a 500K SD and they're valuing
it at a 4 X multiple then they're
selling their business for $2 million
what's really important to understand
when you're evaluating a business is how
did the seller or broker arrive at this
SD or eida number often times they'll
provide you with a spreadsheet that
shows all of the revenue all the
expenses the net income and then the
items that they added back to get to
their SD or eida number sometimes you'll
also see the phrases adjusted SD or
adjusted eida or adjusted cash flow you
usually mean the same thing the net
income plus some addb backs to get us to
a more useful metric for evaluating this
business now this is where I see a lot
of variance in the SBA world is what ADB
backs lenders will find acceptable for
example some lenders as part of an SD
calculation will add back the entirety
of an owner's salary some lenders won't
add that back some lenders will add part
of that back some lenders will add an
entire depreciation cost back some
lenders will only add back a percentage
so things can get a little complicated
here and if you're looking at a deal
that's heavy on ADB backs it's really
important to find a lender that can work
with those ADB backs this is a lot of
the work that I do with clients is
helping them understand how are we
arriving at this SD number is this
calculation that A lender can get behind
and which lender is going to be the best
fit based on how we're analyzing this
cash flow so if you've got a deal that
you're interested in if you've got a
business you're interested in buying
let's have a conversation about that and
see which lender is going to be the
right fit for your deal

metadata.title: SDE v EBITDA.  Essential for Accurate Business Valuation.
metadata.author: Peter Nola
metadata.shortDescription:
SDE v EBITDA.  Just 2 of the alphabet soup brokers and accountants use as a term for the profits of the business.  Understanding these two financial metrics is crucial for a successful business appraisal. In this video I talk about how to calculate EBITDA and SDE, their definitions, and provides examples to illustrate the differences.   If you are buying, selling or just curious about the value of a business, an understanding of the essential differences between SDE (Seller's Discretionary Earnings) and EBITDA (Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation, and Amortization) is the cornerstone of building an accurate business valuation.  SDE v EBITDA.  Essential Differences for Accurate Business Valuation.  

0:00  Intro
0:37  What is Seller's Discretionary Earnings (SDE)
1:36  What is Earnings Before Interest, Tax, Depreciation, and Amortization (EBITDA)
2:40  Key Differences:  SDE
2:53  Key Differences:  EBITDA
3:15  When to Use SDE or EBITDA
3:37  When to Use SDE
4:12  When to Use EBITDA
4:58  SDE or EBITDA
5:18  What is EBIPTDA?


Business Vlogs:  https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLawa4-Z6sbTiimn5Yj5x1qkxyGcN0p7H9

How to Buy a Business:  https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8ZGQ6kTyIuo&list=PLawa4-Z6sbTiyFzs5n31y08LQ_GlAEHT-

How to Sell a Business: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=S2pHvqzGn_s&list=PLawa4-Z6sbTgmF5zkO-bdSSila_Wypq-M

How to Start a Business in New Zealand:  https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pIw4nq0bHig&list=PLawa4-Z6sbTh-H3PwGYG0rTZlEbV99qRM

These videos are general in nature and not intended to be a substitute for detailed and specific advice.  It is important that you get the right professional advice and I strongly suggest you talk to legal or accounting professionals to help you structure for tax, budgeting, interpret contracts and leases and all the other specific details of your own situation.  They will help you to make sound decisions in the best interest of you and your business

Keep in touch:
LinkedIn:  https://www.linkedin.com/in/peternola
Website:  https://www.businessesforsale.co.nz/broker/peter-nola

Learn what SBA lenders will allow as add backs and how to calculate a debt coverage ratio and a ROI on your downpayment.

metadata.title: How to Value a Business: SDE, Multiples & Add-Backs
metadata.author: Ryan C. Winter, Business Broker
metadata.shortDescription:
How much is your business actually worth? In this video, business broker Ryan C. Winter breaks down the exact formula used to value small businesses, how Seller’s Discretionary Earnings (SDE) work, and how to increase your overall multiple. 

Whether you are planning to sell your company, looking for growth capital, or just curious about your market value, understanding SDE add-backs and key value drivers is essential.

CHAPTERS:
0:00 - How Small Businesses Are Valued
0:48 - The Valuation Formula (Earnings x Multiple)
1:42 - What is SDE (Seller's Discretionary Earnings)?
1:52 - Key Add-Backs That Increase Business Value
2:48 - What Determines Your Multiple?
3:00 - Top Value Drivers Buyers Look For
4:04 - Common Valuation Mistakes & Myths

KEY TAKEAWAYS:
• Buyers price most small businesses as a multiple of SDE, and that multiple rises or falls with risk.
• Every legitimate add-back raises your SDE, and the multiple applies to each added dollar.
• Businesses that operate without the owner's daily involvement command significantly higher multiples.

Connect with Ryan C. Winter:
💼 Website: ryancwinter.com
📩 Consultation: https://calendly.com/ryancwinter/one-to-one-with-ryan
📱 LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/ryancwinter/

Get a free estimate of what your business is worth: https://ryancwinter.com/business-valuation-calculator/

The full written guide to multiples and SDE: https://ryancwinter.com/what-multiple-of-earnings-sell-business/

Ryan C. Winter, licensed Florida business broker with Truforte Business Group | (904) 789-1276

And even if you're not in Northeast Florida, stick with me because these principles apply to any business owner thinking about selling their business. So, in the next 5 minutes, I'm going to show you how businesses like yours are really valued with no jargon, no guesswork. So, you can walk away with a grounded idea of your own number, that is how much your business is actually worth. So, here's the whole thing in one sentence. For most small businesses, value comes down to two numbers multiplied together. Your real earnings times a multiple. Perhaps you've heard those terms before, especially multiple. Sometimes it's confusing. So, let me break it down. Your earnings, what the business actually puts in the owner's pocket. And the multiple, how many years of those earnings a buyer will pay for up front. So, if your business earns $300,000, and businesses like yours sell for a multiple of three, you're in the neighborhood of about $900,000. It's a pretty simple idea. The whole skill is getting those two numbers exactly right. And this is where most owners get it wrong. Let me show you how. Number one, your earnings. Here's the mistake almost everyone makes. They look at the profit on their tax return. That is not your earnings. The number buyers actually care about is called seller's discretionary earnings, or SDE. And it's almost always higher than what your tax return shows. So, why is it higher? Because we add back the things a new owner won't be paying for. We add back your salary, a buyer replaces you. We add back interest, taxes, and depreciation. We add back one-time expenses, and we add back the personal stuff that runs through your business, which is very normal. Things like your vehicle or your phone or business travel. And this is genuinely what matters most, because every dollar we add back gets multiplied. A $10,000 add back at three times multiple is $30,000 of value. That's $30,000 in your pocket when you sell your business. That's why owners are so often surprised. Their business earns 40, 50% more than than the tax return ever showed. Okay, so number two, the multiple. If earnings tell a buyer how much you make, the multiple tells them how safe those earnings are once you're gone. Basically, how predictable is your business? So, let me give you the big ones. Number one, and this is the big one, owner dependence. If the business can't run without you, you're not selling a business, you're selling a job. And that pulls your value down hard. The next one is recurring revenue. Customers who come back for repeat business, who are on some sort of subscription plan, that's worth a lot of money. And then customer concentration. If one client is half of your revenue, a buyer sees that as a huge red flag. And your trend. Is your business steady or stagnant or is it growing? Does it look like your business is going to make more next year than it did this year? If it does, that's a good thing. Also, some of the basics, like having clean books, clean financials. Do we know how to figure out what your business is worth based on the numbers? And do you have a team that can run your business if you step away? Those are things that move you from a two to a four when it comes to your multiple. And that's a huge swing in your final number, what your business actually sells for. Business Valuation - Part 5 - How to Calculate Seller's Discretionary Earnings

👉Seller's Discretionary Earnings (SDE) is a critical number used to determine the value of a business that the multiple is applied to in order to calculate the business' value.

👉SDE represents the core profitability of a business and is calculated by starting with the gross sales and subtracting chargebacks, refunds, rebates, cost of goods sold, selling and administrative expenses, non-operating income, and non-typical income.

Expenses that are considered add backs, such as personal travel or meals and entertainment, can be added back to the calculation.

👉Depreciation, interest, and amortization expenses can also be added back, as well as one-time upgrades or expenses that the buyer wouldn't have to incur in the future.
SDE helps standardize a company's earnings, making it easier to compare to other businesses and determine its value.

- **Introduction to Seller's Discretionary Earnings (SDE)** (00:00): Nate Lind discusses the significance of calculating Seller's Discretionary Earnings, which is essential for evaluating business worth.
  
- **Understanding Business Valuation** (00:27): The value of a business is determined by multiplying its SDE by a standard multiple (e.g., a $1 million SDE at a 4x multiple equals a $4 million valuation).

- **Components of SDE** (00:53): SDE is defined as the business's core profitability, calculated by starting with gross sales and adjusting for various expenses and incomes.

- **Adjustments in Calculation** (01:21): To arrive at SDE, deduct chargebacks, refunds, cost of goods sold (COGS), selling and administrative expenses (SGA), and non-operating income.

- **Ad backs Explained** (02:56): Expenses that may be added back include personal travel, meals, entertainment, depreciation, interest, and one-time upgrades, which the new buyer typically wouldn't incur.

- **Evaluating Non-Typical Income** (02:25): Non-recurring incomes like loans and settlements should be excluded from the income calculation as they don't reflect ongoing business performance.

- **SBA Buyer Considerations** (03:30): Buyers using SBA funding may not scrutinize small personal expenses, affecting what can be added back to the financials.

- **Unique One-Time Expenses** (04:29): Expenses that arise from one-time activities or unusual market conditions can often be added back to the SDE calculation.

- **Upcoming Examples** (05:31): Nate suggests that he will provide practical examples in future videos to illustrate SDE calculations more clearly.

- **Final Encouragement** (05:58): Viewers are invited to engage with the content through likes and subscriptions, with a reminder of the importance of understanding their business's valuation and financials for successful deals.

metadata.title: What Is Seller’s Discretionary Earnings or SDE (and How to Calculate It)
metadata.author: Quiet Light Brokerage
metadata.shortDescription:
Seller’s Discretionary Earnings (SDE), also called Seller’s Discretionary Income (SDI) or Owner’s Discretionary Income (ODI), is a key business valuation metric for online businesses, e-commerce, SaaS, and Amazon FBA.

SDE isn’t just “profit” or “cash flow.” It’s the real number buyers care about when valuing your business - and the metric that can make or break a deal. In this video, Mark Daoust breaks down what SDE really is, how to calculate it accurately, and why even small errors can affect your business valuation long term. 

Learn the common pitfalls, the one-time expenses to account for, and practical tips for turning SDE into a tool for smarter business decisions.

Get a free, no-pressure business valuation ➡️ https://quietlight.com/sell
Meet our expert advisors ➡️ https://quietlight.com/team

#SDE #BusinessValuation #OnlineBusiness #EntrepreneurTips #ExitPlanning

00:01 Intro
00:31 Key metrics for sellers & buyers
00:53 What are Seller’s Discretionary Earnings
01:01 SDE technical definition
01:13 SDE breakdown
01:39 True one-time expenses
01:50 Purpose of calculating SDE

Subscribe for practical insights on buying, growing, and selling online businesses - from entrepreneurs who’ve actually done it.

segments.text: If you've ever had evaluation of your business done,
you've probably run across the term SDE or Seller's Discretionary Earnings
and you probably figured out that it's pretty important to the value of your business.
But what exactly is SDE and how is it different from a regular profitability?
Before we get into the details of what discretionary earnings are,
let's first take a look at why it's an important metric for you to understand.
If you're a seller you can maximize your evaluation by knowing which expenses impact your value.
You see, your business's value is based on a multiple of your earnings.
So the higher this number goes, the more valuable your business becomes.
If you're a buyer, discretionary earnings gives you a baseline level of profitability
so you can understand your potential return of investment for your particular scenario.
So what exactly are discretionary earnings?
Simply put the amount of earnings the seller has to spend on the discretion.
The technical definition is a bit more complex.
There are the pretax and pre-interest profits before non-cash expenses,
one owner's benefits, one-time investments,
and any non-related income or expenses.
That's a lot to process so let's break this down.
If you look at an income statement you'll often see a few expenses where you never actually spent cash
such as amortization or depreciation.
And the first step to calculate discretionary earnings,
we remove these non-cash expenses as well as taxes or interest earned or paid.
From there we remove expenses that are actually on our benefits
such as your salary or home or office.
We remove this because how much you pay yourself is entirely up to you.
We'll also look for true one-time expenses.
For example, if you built an app free business, this is usually just a one-time investment.
There are further adjustments which might be made depending on your situation.
The goal of the discretionary earnings calculation is to give buyers a baseline number to work with.
Of course buyers, sellers and brokers won't always agree on the adjustments we make to an income statement.
Now as I said, part of the calculation require some interpretation.
If you have any questions on this, or if you like us to do a discretionary earnings calculations for you,
you are always welcome to reach out to us directly.
Be sure to subscribe to this channel so you could see all of our videos

How do acquirers value a company, and if someone says "how much is company X worth?" How do you think they actually put a number on it?

metadata.title: How To Value a Business for Sale (Mergers and Acquisitions)
metadata.author: Brett Cenkus
metadata.shortDescription:
Both sellers and buyers often ask how to properly value a company for sale. Today we'll look at valuing a company in the lower-middle market, or a business worth up to $25 million. 

You'll often see discounted cash flow, comparable company analysis and EBITDA quoted as metrics by which to value a company, but those are really only practical for larger, publically traded companies.

Comparable transaction analysis is a much more reliable metric for businesses in the lower-middle market range. In order to equalize the companies being compared, we look at something called Seller Discretionary Earnings (SDE).

In this video, Brett dives into these metrics and how we utilize them to value the businesses he assists with in the sale and purchase of as a corporate attorney and business broker.

_____________________________________________


Have questions? Book a call, and talk to Brett today: 
https://rebrand.ly/clarity-brettcenkus117

_______________________________________________


You can reach Brett through:
 
https://www.linkedin.com/in/brettcenkus
https://twitter.com/BCenkus
https://cenkuslaw.com
https://braatenwoods.com
https://merger-resources.com


_______________________________________________



Brett A. Cenkus has 20+ years of experience in business law, finance, and entrepreneurship. Through Cenkus Law, PC, he provides advice and services for mergers & acquisitions (M&A), securities offerings, founders’ agreements, and other general business law issues.
 
Through Braaten Woods, LLC, Brett helps business owners in the lower middle market ($2MM - $25MM) position themselves for sale, find buyers, negotiate, and close M&A deals. 

Brett also maintains merger-resources.com, a site packed with free articles, videos, checklists, deal diagrams, template contracts, and other tools to help pass M&A knowledge to others. 

Brett regularly consults with entrepreneurs and invests his own capital as an angel investor. 

From 2010-2013, Brett served as Chief Legal Counsel of a publicly-traded international oilfield services company. From 2001 to 2006, he and a partner founded and built Paragon Residential Mortgage. Bridge Investments acquired Paragon in 2006. 

Brett holds a Juris Doctorate from Harvard Law School and a Bachelor of Arts degree in Economics from Messiah College in Grantham, Pennsylvania.

Brett lives in Austin with his wife, Cathryn, and two children. He enjoys reading, squash, classic movies, great food and wine, and the New England Patriots.

Subscribe for weekly high ticket sales strategy, B2B closing frameworks, and practical sales leadership systems.

metadata.title: How To Turn Low Ticket Buyers Into High Ticket Clients (My Follow-Up Sequences)
metadata.author: Hernan Vazquez
metadata.shortDescription:
You don't sell a cheap product just to sell a cheap product. You sell it so better buyers move up to your high ticket offer. But even a healthy low ticket offer only gets about 7 to 10 percent of buyers to book a call on their own. In this video I break down the follow-up sequences I use for the other 90 percent.

📌 In this video:
✅ Why the real point of a low ticket offer is getting better buyers for your higher priced offer
✅ The places you can ascend buyers: your front end offer, your upsells and your thank you page
✅ Why the thank you page matters so much, since it's when buyers are most excited
✅ The consumption sequence: 2 to 3 emails, once a day, so buyers use what they bought and get a win
✅ The next step sequence: 1 to 2 weeks of emails with testimonials, case studies and results that invite people to book a call
✅ How to add extra campaigns like webinars or a VSL after that
✅ The broadcast list, where every email links to your next step
✅ Why many people book after months or even years on your list

🔗 Resources:
📘 Low Ticket Profits, my book on Amazon: https://LowTicketBook.com
🚀 Rapid Scale Mastery, my high level community: https://RapidScaleMastery.com
👥 Ads for Low and High Ticket, my free community: https://www.skool.com/high-ticket-marketing

▶️ Watch next:
🎥 How To Position Your Low Ticket Offer To Attract High Ticket Clients: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Tu80aUUzpY0
🎥 How To Get Free High Ticket Buyers Using Low Ticket Offers: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3tuWcDFym6M

🎯 About this video:
This video is for coaches, consultants, agencies and service businesses that run low ticket offers with Meta ads and want more of those buyers to become high ticket clients. You'll learn how to set up a low ticket funnel follow-up with email sequences that move buyers to a sales call or a webinar. It covers the thank you page, the consumption sequence, the next step sequence and the broadcast list, so you can get more out of the buyers you already paid for.

metadata.title: M&A Investment Banking Interview Questions - Middle Market ($50-300MM)
metadata.author: iBankerU
metadata.shortDescription:
The fees are very strong in the Middle Market.  So is the competition.  Therefore, it is of paramount importance to select the absolute best people to execute these transactions.  There are two types of questions that quickly let me know which you are:
(1) The basic knowledge test (e.g. eliminators)
(2) Case Study Questions (e.g. "How does this candidate's thought process work?")
Know these going in, or "It was so great meeting you...we'll be in touch."

segments.text: Investment Banking interviews. There are two types. The first one is bulge bracket. Let's
call these firms that do at least $300 million deals, because despite what they tell you,
firms will come down market, because those are still very significant fees. So we'll call it
$300 million deals and up, all the way to the multi-billion dollar deals you see in
the Wall Street Journal and on CNBC. We're not talking about those interviews. You can
get those questions in a Vault Guide. They're easy enough (to find). Maybe I'll do another
video on those. But today, I want to talk about Middle Market Investment Banking interviews. I
think they're much more interesting. So, Middle Market Investment Banking. These are companies
that will do deals at the very low end let's call it $10 million. That's quite a small fee though,
so we'll talk about Enterprise Values which are 25 million and up; let's call it to 10 times that;
to about $250 million deals. Those are sizable deals you'll get good fees on all of those. All
of those should be seven figure fees and even eight figure fees as you get into the multiple
hundred million dollar transaction size. So, what types of questions should you expect? it depends
at what level. Let's assume you're coming in as an Analyst. What amazes me, is I'll
get really pedigreed interesting candidates. They have good applications. They have good
recommendations. So after making pleasantries the very first question I love to ask is:
"walk me through an income statement." Should be easy. Anybody knows that the basic headlines for
an income statement are Revenue less your Cost of Goods Sold equals your Gross Profit; minus your
Operating Expenses equals your Net Profit. And so anybody, basically a freshman in college, should
be able to walk you through that! The amount of times I've more or less decided right then and
there to end an interview because a candidate could not walk me through the basics of what an
income statement were, let alone how to model one, just was impossible to believe. So number one,
know what the elements of an income statement are. There are trick questions like show me
depreciation on a balance sheet things like that. Be ready for the trick questions, but that's just
basic accounting. Now one of my favorites is a case study interview. Here is a question I always
like to ask, and this one was asked of me when I was interviewing. "So tell me what an airplane
weighs." Of course, we really we don't care what an airplane weighs. The reason we're asking for
this is we want to see how you think can you break things up into assumptions that are defendable and
can you source those assumptions. Therefore, do you think like somebody, who, when going
through the rigors of due diligence would have a model that could stand up to that
test? The last thing the MD wants to do basically is to have to go through the work of the Analyst,
the Associate and the VP and tear apart their model. We do it anyway but we're hoping not to
spend a whole lot of time doing that. So an example of how to answer that question: what
kind of airplane is it? So let's say it's a 747. So I'll say it's a 747. All right. Do I get to
just look this up on Google, or do I have to give you elements? Obviously I can't (let you) look it
up on Google, it defeats the point but asking the question. (Asking me) is good because it
shows that you're trying to immediately get to the heart of what the answer is. So it's not a
yes or no it's more of a thought process exercise. So the way to go about this, and I'll just rather
than going back and forth just kind of walk you through. So first off, is this airplane just a
frame? Does it have an engine in it? Are there seats in the airplane? Are there passengers in
those seats? Do these passengers have luggage? Is there carry-on luggage? Is there check on luggage?
Do I have Cargo in addition to the luggage and the passengers. What assumptions do I make about
all that: what does a seat weigh? Where can I get the sourcing for that? How can I look that up? Do
I get to look at FAA manuals? Do I get to look at manufacturer specs? How many people are on board?
What's the average weight of a person? How many men how many women? What's the average weight of
those (man and) women? If it's a 50 lb carry-on bag how many of those can I assume per passenger?
How many check on bags can I assume per passenger? What kind of cargo can I assume? so on and so
forth. So the whole point of this exercise is that you can put together a set of assumptions and
numbers that back the assumptions, and therefore answer the question. There is a lot more to
Investment Banking interviewing, but those are a quick couple of tips to the right approach. If you
have any further questions or if you want detailed answers drop a comment below and I'll answer!
those

metadata.title: How Business Sales Get Financed (Cash, SBA Loans, Seller Notes, Earnouts & Rollovers)
metadata.author: Deal Street - Small to Lower Middle Market M&A
metadata.shortDescription:
Two buyers make offers on the same business: $2.2 million and $1.9 million. Most owners would take the bigger number. But in a lot of deals, the smaller offer puts more money in the seller's pocket, and puts it there sooner.

In this video, M&A advisor and business broker Shep Campbell breaks down the five pieces most small and lower middle market deals are built from: cash at closing, the SBA 7(a) loan, seller financing, the earnout and the equity rollover. You'll learn how the SBA's 10% down and 1.25x coverage rules affect your sale, the seller note trick of the trade, the full standby catch on SBA deals, how to protect yourself in an earnout, and what a "second bite of the apple" really means. Then we put it all together and compare the two offers side by side.

Thinking about selling your business? Deal Street partners with M&A Specialists to provide a full range of M&A services, from valuing and preparing your business to finding the right buyer and closing the deal. Start the conversation at https://dealstreetdigest.com

CHAPTERS
0:00 $2.2M vs. $1.9M: which offer would you take?
0:30 Sale price isn't your check
1:04 The five pieces of a deal
1:18 Piece 1: Cash at closing
2:08 Piece 2: The SBA loan
4:42 Piece 3: Seller financing
6:44 The SBA seller note catch (full standby)
8:44 Piece 4: The earnout
11:33 Piece 5: Equity rollover
13:15 Putting it together: the two offers compared
14:09 Four questions to ask about any offer
14:40 Recap
15:17 How to work with me

Subscribe to Deal Street for straight talk on buying and selling businesses.

Next video: Asset Sale vs. Stock Sale.

Disclaimer: This video is for general educational purposes and is not legal, tax or financial advice. SBA rules change; confirm current requirements with your lender. Shep Campbell is a business broker and M&A advisor, not a CPA or attorney.

metadata.shortDescription:
In this episode, host Iyad Amer sits down with Ali Merchant, CEO & Founder of Hala Yachts, to break down the yacht charter business and explain why it closely mirrors private aviation and aircraft brokerage.

Ali shares how yacht charter really works—from prospecting and client vetting to contracts, sourcing yachts globally, and delivering white-glove service. Iyad and Ali compare both industries, highlighting the realities of serving the 1%, operating 24/7 across time zones, and handling high-pressure situations where execution and recovery matter most.

This episode gives aircraft brokers and charter professionals insight into another luxury industry built on the same foundations: trust, expectations, transparency, and precision execution.

How do you avoid every broker's worst nightmare: being cut out of your own deal [00:00:00]? 

Welcome to Day 37 of the 100 Day Law School with Dr. Chad Michael Altieri [00:00:04]. In this lesson, we break down what a Non-Circumvention Clause is—a contractual promise not to bypass, exclude, or cut out an intermediary, broker, adviser, mandate holder, or strategic connector from a transaction or business opportunity they introduced [00:00:06]. 

Discover why non-circumvention protection is a creature of precise drafting [00:00:45]: learn how buyers and sellers attempt to close directly behind a broker's back [00:00:28], why access and introductions carry immense commercial value in cross-border and investment deals [00:00:53], and the exact questions to ask to prevent being cut out [00:01:14].

What is a non circumvention clause, non circumvention non disclosure agreement NCNDA, broker protection clause in commercial contracts, how to prevent deal bypassing, intermediary and mandate holder agreements, international trade and broker law by Dr. Chad Michael Altieri.

segments.text: How do you avoid every broker's worst
nightmare? Being cut out of your own
deal. Welcome to day 37 of the 100-Day
Law School. A non-circumvention clause
or agreement is a contractual promise
not to bypass, exclude, or cut out a
party from a transaction, relationship,
or opportunity introduced through that
party's efforts. It is commonly used
where intermediaries, brokers,
introducers, advisors, mandate holders,
or strategic connectors bring parties
together. The clause is meant to stop
one party from using the connection
while eliminating the connector. For
example, a broker introduces a buyer to
a seller, and then the buyer and seller
try to close directly without paying the
broker. An advisor introduces an
investor to a company, and the company
later raises capital from that investor
while denying the advisor's role. But
here's what you might not know.
Non-circumvention protection depends on
the drafting. Why does this matter to
you? Because introductions have value.
Access has value. Relationships have
value. And in many cross-border,
commission-based, advisory, financing,
commodity, and investment deals, the
real asset is not just the paper, it's
the access. But if the clause is vague,
too narrow, too broad, or missing key
parties, the protection may fail when it
matters most. So, never ask only, "Did
the deal happen without me?" Ask, "Who
originated the opportunity? Which
opportunities are covered? Who
introduced the parties? Who is
protected? Which parties are restricted?

metadata.shortDescription: How a broker-dealer registers, what makes an office an OSJ or a branch, every non-branch exclusion and its numbers, foreign broker-dealers under Rule 15a-6, Rule 1017 continuing membership filings and Form BDW, told through the Stanford Financial fraud that ran through a registered firm. Refresher first: Series 7 E35 — Complaints, Arbitration, and SIPC. Full audio episode: The Finance Lab, Series 24 E01, on Spotify. Part of a 39-episode Series 24 season that follows the FINRA content outline. Educational content, not investment or legal advice.

with an absolutely massive fraud. And
honestly, the structure of his whole
scheme is just the perfect cautionary
tale for us.

broker-dealer right in Houston, and he
used it to funnel his clients over to a
bank he controlled down in Antigua.

us, you need to know enough to ask the
really hard questions.

registering a firm starting from the
very foundation.

definitions. Under the Securities
Exchange Act of 1934, a broker acts as
an agent. They're affecting transactions
for the account of others, and for doing

on the other hand, acts as a principal.
They're buying and selling securities
for their own account, and they earn a
markup or a markdown.
Now, in the real world, most firms
actually do both, which is we constantly
use the term broker dealer.
So the absolutely crucial point here is
captured right in section 15 A of the
Act. The magic phrase to remember is
engaged in the business. Look, if you're
just sitting at home buying and selling
for your own personal portfolio, hey,
you're a trader, good for you.
But if you regularly match buyers and
sellers for compensation, well, now
you're in the business.
And section 15 A makes it strictly
unlawful to use interstate commerce to
effect securities transactions unless
you are officially registered with the
SEC.
Sure, there are a few tiny carve outs
for purely interstate business or
certain specific bank activities, but
for your exam prep, the default rule is
brilliantly simple. If you are in the
business, you must register.
Now let's look at a dividing line that
trips up a lot of people. The boundary
between a broker dealer and an
investment advisor.
The Investment Advisers Act of 1940
technically defines an advisor as anyone
who is in the business of advising
others about securities for
compensation. But to prevent this super
broad definition from just swallowing up
every single broker whoever made a stock

gives brokers an exclusion. Here's how
it works.
If your advice is solely incidental to
your brokerage business and you receive
no special compensation for it, you stay
firmly over in the broker only category.

separate distinct fee for advice, like

an investment advisor.

lesson for both the exam and the real
world.
Think about Bernie Madoff for a second.
For decades, his firm was known as a
registered broker dealer, heavily and

But his advisory business, the part
managing the actual money for clients

When a firm's day to day activities
don't match its official registrations,
that unregistered activity is exactly
where nobody is looking. As a principal,
you have to know exactly which hat your
firm is wearing at all times.
So, what happens when a foreign firm,

four very specific exemptions. First up,

But watch out for this sneaky exam trap.

Third is the chaperone rule.
A foreign firm actually can actively

Finally, the fourth exemption covers
specific listed counterparties.
Think of organizations like the World
Bank or registered US broker-dealers or

Okay, let's see how this all builds into
the actual firm registration timeline.
A broker-dealer starts its official
legal life by filing Form BD through the

Once that form is filed, the clock

But getting SEC registration isn't the

supervisory procedures, and your

If a firm's business is strictly limited
to just mutual funds and variable
annuities, they are totally excluded
from SIP membership.
Finally, the whole process finishes up
with state registration.
Federal registration doesn't just
automatically preempt the states. You

single state where you do business with
residents.
And remember, anytime your Form BD
information changes in the future, like
you get a new owner or have a
disciplinary event, you must amend that
form promptly.
Once the firm is fully registered, we
got to talk about physical real estate.
Where do the people actually sit?
FINRA Rule 3110 categorizes every single
location into one of four distinct
types.
The heaviest scrutiny, by far, falls on
the Office of Supervisory Jurisdiction,
or OSJ.
An office becomes an OSJ if it handles
critical high-risk functions, things
like order execution, market making,
structuring offerings, holding customer
funds, or, and pay attention cuz this is
a big one, final acceptance and approval
of new accounts.
If a local branch manager starts giving
final approval to new accounts, boom,
that location instantly becomes an OSJ.
And OSJs require mandatory annual
inspections.
Next on the ladder is the supervisory
branch, which is basically an office
that supervises other non-branch
locations.
These also require annual inspections.
Then we have the standard
non-supervisory branch. This is where
regular day-to-day securities business
is conducted, but nobody is actively
being supervised from there.
These branches register on Form BR and
are inspected every three years.
Finally, we have the non-branch
location, which is presumed to be on a
three-year inspection cycle. But to
qualify as a non-branch location in the
first place, you have to fit into a
very, very specific exclusion.
And this is where things get really
interesting,
and where the test makers absolutely
love to set number traps for you.
If an office wants to avoid registering
as a full-blown branch on Form BR, it
has to perfectly fit into one of these
exclusion buckets. For instance, let's
say a representative has a nice lake
house, a non-primary residence, and they
take some client calls from there on the
weekends.
That location avoids branch registration
only if it's used for securities
business for fewer than 30 business days
in a calendar year. Hit day 30 and
you're a branch.
What about a rep who primarily sells
insurance out of a storefront but does a
little bit of securities business on the

non-securities locations is that they

pivot, they get bought.
When a broker-dealer is about to

1017 kicks in and requires what's called
a continuing membership application.
Basically, FINRA approved you as one

something materially different, they
want to take a good look at it.
The magic number you need to burn into

If there's an acquisition or a transfer

change it is.

are we registered?

metadata.title: SEC Rule 15c3-3 Customer Reserve Calculation Explained | Broker-Dealer FINOP Training
metadata.author: FINOP Controller
metadata.shortDescription:
In this episode of the Broker-Dealer / Investment Advisor FinOp Controller Series, we provide an introductory overview of the SEA Rule 15c3-3 Exhibit A Customer Reserve Calculation.

This presentation is designed for new broker-dealer operations, finance, accounting, treasury, regulatory, internal audit, and external audit professionals who are learning how customer reserve requirements work at a carrying or clearing broker-dealer.

Topics covered include:

Purpose of the Customer Protection Rule
Customer credit and debit balances
Common transactions included in the reserve formula
Exhibit A credit and debit items
Customer Reserve and PAB Reserve calculations
Back-office systems used to track customer cash and securities
Stock record basics
Securities allocation reports
Potential controls over the reserve calculation process

The goal is to help new staff and auditors understand not only what goes into the reserve calculation, but also where the information comes from and why strong controls are important.

This video is for educational purposes only and is not legal, accounting, regulatory, or compliance advice. Broker-dealers should consult their legal, compliance, regulatory, and audit professionals when evaluating specific Rule 15c3-3 issues.

metadata.title: Broker-Dealer Supervision: WSPs and Office Inspections - Series 63 Exam Prep
metadata.author: CertFuel
metadata.shortDescription:
Broker-dealer supervision sits at the heart of the Series 63 regulations of broker-dealers unit and represents one of the most heavily tested topics in that section. In this 8-minute explainer we build a firm's supervisory system from the ground up, covering reasonably designed systems, written supervisory procedures (WSPs), the three office classifications, inspection timelines, and principal review of communications. You will leave knowing exactly which location gets which inspection cycle and who holds final responsibility when violations slip through.

By the end of this video you'll be able to confidently answer Series 63 questions about:

• Why a "reasonably designed" supervisory system does not require perfection, and why one missed violation does not automatically mean system failure
• What written supervisory procedures (WSPs) must specify: the responsible individual, the supervisory activities, the frequency, and the documentation manner
• Why WSPs must be updated promptly when business changes, and where copies must be kept
• The three office types (Office of Supervisory Jurisdiction (OSJ), branch office, non-branch location) and which activities bump a location into the OSJ tier
• How inspection timelines work: annual for OSJs, annual for any branch that supervises another location, and at least every three years for all other branches and non-branch locations
• Why a supervisor generally cannot supervise their own activities or report to someone they supervise, and the unavoidable-conflict documentation exception
• Why electronic complaints and internal communications are treated identically to paper for principal review purposes, and who retains final responsibility

0:00 Reasonably designed supervisory systems and the no-perfection rule
1:38 Written supervisory procedures: the four required elements
2:42 Supervisor credentials and the self-supervision trap
3:15 Classifying the three office types: OSJ, branch, and non-branch
4:41 Inspection timelines: annual, inherited annual, and three-year cycles
5:58 Principal review of complaints, email, and internal communications

metadata.title: Exclusive agency vs exclusive right to sell explained for the real estate exam.
metadata.author: Just Call Maggie

segments.text: Let me challenge you with something real
quick. Two listing agreements, both say
exclusive. Both hire one broker, but
only one of them guarantees the broker
gets paid. And this exact trick shows up
on the real estate exam all the time.
All right, here's a quick professor
challenge. A homeowner signs a listing
agreement with broker Maggie. A week
later, the seller finds their own buyer.
Maybe a friend, maybe a neighbor, maybe
somebody from church. The house sells.
Here's the question. Does the broker
still get paid? Think about it because
the answer depends on which listing
agreement was signed. Was it exclusive
agency or exclusive right to sell?
Here's where the exam tries to trick
people. Both of these agreements sound
almost identical. Exclusive agency,
exclusive right to sell. Students see
the word exclusive and they assume they
mean the same thing. They don't. In an
exclusive agency listing, the broker has
the exclusive right to represent the
seller. But, if the seller personally
finds the buyer, the seller does not owe
the broker a commission. That's the key
phrase. Seller finds the buyer, broker
might not get paid. Now, let's look at
the other one. Exclusive right to sell.
This is the most common listing
agreement in real estate and guarantees
the broker the most protection. And
here's the rule. If the property sells
during the listing period, the broker
gets paid. Doesn't matter who finds the
buyer, the broker, another broker, the
seller's cousin, the seller themselves,
commission is owed. That's why it
guarantees the broker the highest
protection. The exam shortcut is this.
Exclusive agency means seller might
avoid paying commission. Exclusive right
to sell, broker gets paid no matter
what. Here's how the exam loves to ask
it. A seller signs an exclusive agency
listing with a broker. Later, the seller
personally finds a buyer and sells the
property. Is the broker entitled to a
commission? A lot of students panic and
say yes because the agreement says
exclusive, but the correct answer is no
because the seller found the buyer. If
you want to pass the real estate exam,
you have to learn how the test tries to
trick you because the exam isn't testing
if you've memorized definitions, it's
testing if you can recognize
situations or traps just like this. And
that's exactly why I built PrepAgent
Call to show you how the exam actually
thinks. So, if you're studying for your
real estate license, go check it out and
remember, confusion is manufactured,
clarity is taught.

metadata.title: How to Build a B2B SaaS Website That Actually Explains Your Product (2027)
metadata.author: Launchcraft
metadata.shortDescription:
Most B2B SaaS websites make visitors work too hard to understand what the product does.

In this video, I'll show you how to build a SaaS website that explains your product clearly, earns trust, and gives the right visitor one obvious next step.

You'll learn:
• How to sharpen your SaaS positioning before touching the design
• How to rewrite your hero section so people understand the product quickly
• How to design pages for scanning instead of assuming visitors read everything
• Where to add customer proof, results, logos, testimonials, and trust signals
• How to actually show the product instead of hiding it behind vague marketing copy
• Why your website should have one clear trial CTA
• A realistic cost breakdown for building a strong B2B SaaS website
• A practical 60-90 day roadmap from positioning to launch
• 5 common mistakes that kill SaaS website conversions

CHAPTERS:
00:00 Your website has one job
00:25 Step 1 - Sharpen your positioning
01:30 Step 2 - Rewrite the hero section
02:30 Step 3 - Design for scanning
03:30 Step 4 - Add proof everywhere
04:30 Step 5 - Show the product
05:20 Step 6 - One clear trial CTA
07:50 Real 2027 cost breakdown
08:40 Your 60-90 day roadmap
09:20 5 mistakes that kill SaaS conversions
09:50 What are you building?

WHO THIS IS FOR:
This is for SaaS founders, early-stage teams, marketers, designers, and developers building or rebuilding a B2B SaaS website. It's especially useful if your product is good but your homepage still leaves people asking, "What does this actually do?"

Launchcraft publishes practical, step-by-step roadmaps for building things on the internet. No hype, no unrealistic income claims, and no pretending everything can be built in a weekend.

Subscribe to Launchcraft for more practical guides on SaaS, websites, online products, tools, costs, and realistic execution plans.

Freelancer resources mentioned in the video (so you can check real market costs):
