- Website copywriters: https://tinyurl.com/25m57dvo
- Product illustrators: https://tinyurl.com/24e765pe
- Demo video animators: https://tinyurl.com/23t3fo2v
- CRO experts: https://tinyurl.com/29dv5j6o
- SEO specialists: https://tinyurl.com/24xb5t2o

Disclosure: The links above are affiliate links. If you hire through them, I may earn a commission at no extra cost to you.

#SaaS #B2BSaaS #SaaSMarketing #WebsiteDesign #StartupMarketing

segments.text: Your product is great. Your website just
doesn't prove it. A B2B SaaS website has
exactly one job: make a visitor
understand what you do and start a trial
in under 60 seconds. Most SaaS founders
build something genuinely useful, then
lose the deal because their home page
reads like a riddle. If a visitor can't
explain your product to their boss after
one visit, they're gone. In the next 10
minutes, I'll give you the complete road
map for building a B2B SaaS website that
actually explains your product. Sharpen
your positioning, rewrite the hero
section, design for scanners, add proof
everywhere, show the product itself, and
build one clear trial CTA. Then real
2027 cost estimates, a 60-to-90-day
timeline, and the mistakes that silently
kill SaaS conversions. Clarity converts.
Let's build it.
Step one, sharpen your positioning.
Sharpen the positioning. If a visitor
can't say what you do in one sentence
after 5 seconds on your site, your
positioning is broken. Most SaaS home
pages lead with vague claims. The
all-in-one platform for modern teams.
That could be anything. Project
management, chat, HR software.
Positioning answers three questions
instantly. Who is this for? What painful
problem does it solve? And how is it
different from the alternatives? Weak.
Workflow automation for enterprises.
Strong. We help B2B sales teams book 30%
more meetings by automating their
follow-up emails. Name the buyer, the
pain, the mechanism. The brutal test:
show your home page to someone outside
your industry for 5 seconds, then ask
them what you sell. If they can't answer
clearly, rewrite it until they can. This
step costs $0. Just honesty, a
whiteboard, and five customer
conversations. Get positioning right and
every step downstream gets easier. Get
it wrong and no amount of beautiful
design will save you.
Step two, rewrite the hero section.
Rewrite the hero section. The hero, the
very top of your home page, does about
80% of the selling because most visitors
never scroll past it. It needs five
elements in this order. One, a headline
that states the outcome, not the
feature. Cut invoice processing time in
half. Beat AI-powered invoice management
every time. Two, a sub-headline that
names the buyer and the mechanism. For
finance teams at mid-size companies,
upload invoices, approve in one click.
Three, one primary CTA button. Start
free trial. Never learn more as the main
action.
Four, a product screenshot or short
visual. Show it, don't describe it.
Five, a trust line. Trusted by 2,000
finance teams or a row of customer
logos. And kill the stock photo of
smiling office people. It communicates
literally nothing about your product. As
a planning estimate, writing the copy
yourself costs zero, while hiring a SaaS
website copywriter typically runs $300
to $1,500 for hero plus page copy.
I've attached real freelancers for each
step in the description below. If you
want to take a look, you can see for
yourself what this kind of work actually
costs.
Step three, design for scanning.
Design for scanning. Nobody reads your
website. Everyone scans it.
Eye-tracking studies have shown this for
years. Visitors read in an F pattern,
catching headlines and the first words
of paragraphs, skipping the rest. So,
your design has one job, make the key
points impossible to miss. Short
paragraphs, two lines maximum. Clear
subheadings every few hundred pixels.
Bullet points for benefits instead of
walls of text. Generous white space so
each section can breathe. And a strict
visual hierarchy. The most important
thing on the page should be the biggest
thing on the page.
On mobile, this matters double. More
than half of your B2B visitors will
first see your site on a phone.
If your hero headline is smaller than
your footer text, something is deeply
wrong.
As a planning estimate, a clean premium
theme or template costs zero to $300,
while hiring a SaaS website designer
typically runs $1,000 to $5,000 for a
full site.
Remember, beautiful but confusing only
wins design awards. In business, clear
always beats pretty.
Step four, add proof everywhere.
Add proof everywhere. In B2B, nobody
buys on claims. They buy on evidence. A
stranger deciding whether to trust your
software with their company's workflow
needs reassurance at every scroll. So,
layer proof throughout the page.
Customer logos near the hero, so
visitors immediately think companies
like mine trust this.
Testimonials with real names, titles,
and companies. Sarah Chen, VP of sales
at Acme Corp, beats great product, five
stars, every time.
Case studies with real numbers. How Acme
cut their onboarding time by 40% in 90
days.
Review badges from G2 or Capterra with
your actual rating. Usage stats. 4.9 out
of five from 800 verified reviews.
The rule is simple. Every claim you make
should have proof within one scroll of
it. Claim the fastest setup in the
industry? Show average setup time, 11
minutes, measured across 500 customers.
New and don't have proof yet? Start with
beta customer quotes, pilot results, or
founder story credibility.
Borrowed credibility is completely fine
while you build your own.
Step five, show the product.
Show the product. The single biggest
mistake on SaaS websites, describing the
product in long paragraphs instead of
just showing it. A visitor should see
what they'll actually get within the
first two scrolls. Start with annotated
screenshots of the real current
interface, not mockups from three
redesigns ago.
Better, a 60- to 90-second demo video
that walks through the core workflow
from start to finish, narrated simply.
Best, an interactive product tour or
sandbox they can click through without
creating an account.
People don't buy software, they buy the
feeling of it working. If your product
is complex, a how it works section with
three steps and three screenshots will
outperform a 2,000 word features page
every time.
As a planning estimate, recording a
simple screen demo yourself costs zero,
while hiring a demo video animator
typically runs $500 to $2,500.
I've attached real freelancers for each
step in the description below. If you
want to take a look, you can see for
yourself what this kind of work actually
costs.
Step six, build one clear trial CTA.
Build one clear trial CTA. Your entire
website has exactly one conversion job.
Get the visitor to start a trial or book
a demo. Pick one primary action and
repeat it relentlessly in the hero,
mid-page, at the end of every section,
and as a sticky button in the header.
Start free trial for self-serve
products. Book a demo for sales-led
ones. Don't ask for both with equal
weight. One primary, one secondary,
always. Then remove every ounce of
friction. No credit card required for
the trial, one-click sign up with
Google, and a trial experience that
shows real value in the first session.
Every extra form field costs you
conversions. Name and work email is
enough to get started. The math is
brutally simple. Double your visitor to
trial rate, and you double your pipeline
without spending one more dollar on
traffic. That single button is the most
valuable piece of real estate on your
entire website. Treat it that way.
What a B2B SaaS website actually costs
in 2027. With a lean DIY path,
positioning and messaging cost your
time, a premium template or theme runs
zero to $300, hosting and basic tools 20
to $100 a month, and a self-recorded
demo costs zero. All in, roughly 300 to
$1,000 in the first year, plus your
effort. The assisted path, brand
identity $500 to $2,000, professional
SaaS copywriting $1,000 to $3,000,
custom design and development $3,000 to
$15,000, and a polished demo video $500
to $2,500. Realistically, $5,000 to
$20,000 one time to get everything built
professionally. These are 2027 planning
estimates for budgeting, not quotes, and
they'll vary with your market and scope.
Start lean, prove the message converts,
then invest in polish.
Your 60-to-90-day roadmap. Days 1 to 14,
sharpen your positioning. Interview five
real customers about how they describe
you, and rewrite the hero section. Days
15 to 30, redesign the page for
scanning. Add proof to every section,
and record your demo video. Days 31 to
60, rebuild the trial sign-up flow. Cut
every point of friction, and relaunch
the site. Then watch exactly where
visitors drop off. Days 61 to 90, AB
test your headline and CTA, publish your
first case studies from early wins, and
start SEO content around buyer problems.
This is an example timeline, not a
promise, but the order matters more than
the speed. Message before design, proof
before polish. Now, the five mistakes
that silently kill SaaS website
conversions.
Mistake one, talking about features, not
outcomes. Real-time sync, SOC 2
compliant, 99.99% uptime. Your buyer
doesn't wake up in the morning wanting
uptime. They want fewer missed
deadlines, no embarrassing outages, and
a quiet inbox. Translate every single
feature into the outcome it buys, or it
might as well not be on the page.
Mistake two, burying the pricing. Hiding
your pricing behind a contact sales wall
doesn't create mystique, it creates
suspicion. Buyers assume the worst when
they can't see a number. If you truly
can't publish exact pricing, at least
show pricing ranges or a plan start at
figure. Transparency converts, mystery
doesn't.
Mistake three, no proof above the fold.
If a visitor has to scroll three full
screens to find a single customer logo,
you've already lost them. Logos, hard
numbers, and your single best
testimonial belong in the very first
screen. Proof is the fastest trust
builder you have. Don't hide it at the
bottom.
Mistake four, asking for too much too
soon. A 12-field demo request form
before the visitor has even seen the
product is a conversion killer. Let them
experience value first, a trial, a tour,
or at minimum the demo video, and only
then ask for the meeting. Earn the ask.
Mistake five, designing for the founder,
not the buyer. Your homepage should
speak your buyers language, not your
internal jargon. If a new hire needs a
glossary to understand your own
homepage, your buyers never stood a
chance. Write it the way your best
customer would explain you at a dinner
party.
What are you building? Save this
roadmap, subscribe to Launch Craft for
more practical build guides, and comment
your SaaS product below. I read every
single one. I've attached real
freelancers for each step in the
description. Check what this work
actually costs, and watch the next video
to keep building.
Thank you for watching.

metadata.title: The State of SaaS in 2025: Multiples, Growth Strategies, Valuations, & Exit Planning
metadata.author: Quiet Light Brokerage
metadata.shortDescription:
In this  video, you’ll hear from SaaS M&A experts John Hainstock (Senior Advisor, Quiet Light) and Tom Buchok (SaaS Business Advisor). They dive deep into the SaaS market landscape, breaking down how valuations work, what buyers are looking for, and how to position your business for a successful exit. You’ll also hear personal anecdotes from both of their experiences as SaaS business owners.

Thinking about selling your SaaS business? Understanding market trends, valuation strategies, and the right timing for an exit can make all the difference in securing the best deal.

Here’s a glimpse of what you’ll learn: 
• [0:00] Intro – Meet John Hainstock & Tom Buchok
• [1:32] Why SaaS founders should start exit planning early

metadata.title: Axial’s Lessons From 10,000 Lower Middle Market Deals | Peter Lehrman of Axial
metadata.author: Minds Capital Podcast
metadata.shortDescription:
Peter Lehrman founded Axial in 2009, the leading deal origination platform for lower-middle-market M&A. Today, roughly 10,000 attempted transactions are launched on Axial each year, with approximately 25% closing, making it one of the most active M&A marketplaces in the U.S. lower middle market, and independent sponsors are the single most active buyer type by closed-deal volume. In this episode, Peter shares unmatched market intelligence and highly tactical insights on how independent sponsors source, win, and fund deals.

More on Peter Lehrman: https://www.linkedin.com/in/plehrman/
More on Axial: https://www.axial.net/

metadata.title: What Is The Difference Between A Business Broker And An M&A Advisor
metadata.author: Gill Agency
metadata.shortDescription:
It is important to know the clear distinction between a business broker and an M&A advisor.  Based on your company’s size and industry you will be able to choose the right professional when it comes to you exiting and selling your business.  

So when we talk about size of your company, what I mean is that business brokers work with entities that are usually main street businesses, generating $5MM in revenue or lower and an M&A Advisor works with entities that are generating $5MM to $50MM or even higher in revenue.  

Another clear distinction is that the business brokers are well versed in their niche as they have the resources and knowledge to bring a deal to completion based on their skill set in the main street businesses sphere.  

On the other side M&A advisors are accustomed to a lot of complexities that comes with the higher end entities.  They also have relationships with strategic buyers, private equity firms, family offices, and holding companies.  

Business broker will look for cash flow of the business or SDE, which stands for Seller’s Discretionary Earnings and M&A advisors will work with EBITDA, which stands for Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation and Amortization.  

Hiring the right team is extremely important in order to spend less time in the marketplace and get the maximum value for your business.  

To learn more on the key differences head on over to  https://gillagency.co where we have written an extensive article on other key differences

metadata.title: The Economics of Being a Luxury Yacht Broker
metadata.author: Wealth Pilot
metadata.shortDescription:
What does it really take to make money as a luxury yacht broker?

Selling multi-million-dollar yachts is a very different business from traditional real estate. Yacht brokers work with wealthy buyers and sellers, negotiate enormous transactions, arrange inspections and sea trials, coordinate paperwork, and compete for a relatively small pool of high-value clients.

In this video, we break down **The Economics of Being a Luxury Yacht Broker** — from commissions and brokerage fees to marketing expenses, client acquisition, yacht listings, negotiations, and the economics behind closing a multi-million-dollar sale.

We’ll explore:
• How luxury yacht brokers actually make money
• Yacht brokerage commissions and fee structures
• What happens during a multi-million-dollar yacht transaction
• Finding wealthy buyers and securing yacht listings
• Marketing, photography, boat shows, and client acquisition
• Surveys, sea trials, negotiations, and closing costs
• Why some yacht sales take months or even years
• The economics of selling new vs. pre-owned yachts
• Major risks and challenges in the industry
• What it takes to build a successful yacht brokerage business

A single yacht sale can generate a substantial commission, but the industry comes with high customer-acquisition costs, intense competition, unpredictable sales cycles, and a relatively small number of transactions.

If you enjoy deep dives into the economics of luxury industries, unusual careers, high-value businesses, and how wealthy people spend their money, **subscribe for more.**

#YachtBroker #LuxuryYachts #Yachting #LuxuryBusiness #Business #Economics #Entrepreneurship #Luxury

segments.text: Imagine walking onto the deck of a
300-ft super yacht complete with a
helipad, a glass-bottomed pool, and an
interior finished in rare marbles and
custom leathers. Now, imagine walking
away from that same yacht with a check
for several million dollars simply for
introducing the buyer to the seller.
This is the rarefied world of the luxury
yacht broker, a profession that operates
in the ultra-high-net-worth stratosphere
where nine-figure transactions are just
another day at the office. But behind
the shimmering champagne flutes and
sun-drenched marinas lies a cutthroat
high-stakes game of economics,
relentless networking, and psychological
endurance. Today, we are diving deep
into the fascinating financial engine
that drives one of the most exclusive
careers on Earth.
To understand how a yacht broker makes a
living, you first have to understand the
sheer scale of the asset. Unlike real
estate where a home sits firmly on the
ground, a luxury yacht is a
depreciating, mobile, floating mansion
that requires millions of dollars a year
just to maintain. When a vessel enters
the brokerage market, the price tag
often ranges anywhere from 10 million to
well over 300 million dollars. Brokers
do not earn a steady salary. Instead,
they operate on a commission-based model
typically taking a 10% cut of the sale
price. Now, before you start calculating
your retirement, that 10% does not go
straight into the broker's pocket. It is
split between the central agent
representing the seller and the broker
representing the buyer and then further
divided with their respective brokerage
houses.
Even after all those splits, a broker
walking away with a single percent of a
100 million dollar sale is looking at a
payday that most people will not earn in
a lifetime. However, the path to that
payday is paved with massive financial
risk and upfront capital. Being a luxury
yacht broker is essentially running your
own high-end business. Brokers often
spend thousands of dollars out of pocket
to attend international boat shows in
Monaco, Miami, and Fort Lauderdale,
renting exhibition space, hosting
private cocktail parties, and flying
across the globe at a moment's notice to
meet a prospective client. If a deal
falls through after 6 months of intense
negotiations, the broker makes $0 for
all those expenses and hours of labor.
It is a feast or famine economy. A
top-tier broker might go 18 months
without closing a single deal, only to
broker two megayacht sales in the same
month and make eight figures. Because of
this volatility, financial literacy and
cash flow management are just as
important as knowing the difference
between a displacement hull and a
planing hull. Beyond the initial sale,
the economics yacht brokerage thrive on
a brilliant ecosystem of recurring
revenue. Yachts are notoriously high
maintenance. They need fuel, crew
salaries, insurance, dockage fees, and
constant mechanical overhauls. This is
where yacht management and chartering
come into play. Many brokers do not just
sell the boat and walk away, they manage
it for the owner. By placing a yacht
into a charter fleet when the owner is
not using it, a broker can generate
hundreds of thousands of dollars a week
in rental fees, taking a management
commission on every single charter.
Furthermore, when the client inevitably
wants to upgrade to a bigger vessel 5
years later, the broker handles the
resale, creating a continuous loop of
commissions from the exact same client.
Breaking into this industry is famously
difficult because it is built entirely
on trust and access. Billionaires do not
buy yachts from strangers they met on
the internet. They buy them from people
who run in the same social circles, who
understand discretion, and who can
navigate complex international maritime
laws, flag registries, and tax
loopholes. A successful broker must be
part diplomat, part marine engineer, and
part financial advisor. They are dealing
with eccentric buyers who might change
their minds on a whim, and sellers who
have deeply emotional attachments to
their floating palaces.
Ultimately, the economics of being a
luxury yacht broker are a reflection of
global wealth concentration. As the
number of billionaires in the world
continues to grow, the demand for
superyachts has reached historic highs,
making top brokers some of the
highest-paid independent contractors on
the planet. It is an intoxicating mix of
high glamour and relentless hustle,
where fortunes are won and lost on the
roll of a nautical tide. If you have the
stomach for high financial risk, the
charm to mingle with the global elite,
and the patience to weather years of dry
spells for one glorious, life-changing
sale, it might just be the most
lucrative job you have never considered.
Thank you for watching. And if you
enjoyed peering into the hidden
economies of the ultra-wealthy, make
sure to subscribe for more deep dives
into fascinating careers.

A floating palace. A crew of dozens. A bill that can reach millions for a single week. But who actually profits?

In this video, we go behind the gold of the superyacht charter business: how the industry works, where the money goes, and why even the owners of the world's most luxurious yachts often charter them out just to offset the cost.

In this video:
• Weekly charter rates, from around €14,000 to €3 million
• The history of the industry, from Christina O to the founding of MYBA in 1984
• How owners, central agents and brokers split the business
• The hidden costs: the ~30% APA, broker commissions and the ~10% annual running-cost rule of thumb

0:10 What Is Superyacht Charter?
0:30 History and Business Model
1:10 The Surprising Economics
1:40 The Real Business

Note: Figures such as the APA, commission and annual running costs are industry rules of thumb and vary by yacht and contract.

In this video, Today I will be discussing the important topic of negotiating a 10% commission with your yacht broker. let's explore how To Negotiate the 10% Sales Commission with Your Yacht Broker on Yacht Hunter. 02:50 Outro

In this video, I will provide you with some tips and strategies that you can use to successfully negotiate a 10% commission rate with your yacht broker. I will cover topics such as:

1) What Price will you list the vessel at: This is where I’m critical of both brokers and owners; many owners have an infatuation and emotional attachment to their yachts, and therefore want top dollar. A broker stands to make a lot of money from obtaining a listing so they’ll agree to listing at a price that’s too high to actually sell to appease the owner, but then, brokers receive calls and take those clients to more realistic options or they schedule fake buyers to make it seem like there’s interest. Time goes on, your operating and maintenance costs continue to mount, and you end up getting pissed off at your broker, and they then suggest a price cut to what it should have been initially. Not good.

2) How is it presented: Browse through yachtworld and look at the quality of photos on some boats selling for a million, 5 million, 10 million. You as an owner should have photos 
professionally taken and allow you broker to use these images, which they will compensate you for after they sell the vessel. The reason why an owner should have these photos taken, is because if you have to hire another broker after firing one, well you have these done already.

3) Boat Shows (Your Cost or Brokerages) – Boat shows are great opportunities to get your vessel in front of qualified and interested buyers, but its costly and can be inefficient. You should know if you’re going to cover these costs or if the brokerage is. You should know how many shows your broker plans to put it in, and you should know if your broker will be the one onboard to show the boat or if they’ll have a friend, a model or a captain showing it. I can’t tell you how often you go to a boat show and the listing broker isn’t there to answer questions as their with other clients or off getting drunk and socializing which obviously lets a perfect sale opp slip through the cracks.

4) Dockage – More and more brokers are starting to pick up the cost of your dockage during a listing agreement which is really good, why? This is a big expense and your broker is more likely to be honest in what it will sell at as they now have skin in the game. 
So time to sell her, make sure that you have an open line of communication with your broker and make sure you hire a broker that tells you what you need to hear instead of what you want to hear. Big, big important thing. 

So even if you hate the idea of paying 10%, I’m still going to request that you give this video alike and subscribe for other yacht purchasing content. If you enjoyed with me, Please Don't Forget to Subscribe to My Channel for more tips and tricks on how to find the perfect luxury yacht.

metadata.title: The 4 Clauses That Save Deals (And Why Most People Skip Them)
metadata.author: Santiago Cueto | Miami Business Litigation Lawyer
metadata.shortDescription:
Speak to a Miami Business Attorney: https://cuetolawgroup.com/business-litigation-miami/
📞 Call Us Now - 305-615-6340

A strong non-circumvention agreement is vital to protect your business deals. Learn how to draft ironclad terms that hold up.

Business negotiation is high-stakes, and failing to secure your interests can lead to significant losses. This video breaks down the specific language you need to include in every non-disclosure agreement to ensure your trade secrets and partnerships remain protected. We focus on the practical application of these legal safeguards rather than abstract theory.

We explain how to define confidential information clearly and why establishing concrete penalties, such as liquidated damages, is essential for enforcement. Whether you are entering a new partnership or formalizing an existing one, these four clauses provide the necessary framework to prevent unauthorized use of your proprietary data.

Subscribe for more legal breakdowns on Florida business law, contracts, and litigation strategies.

segments.text: When engaging in sensitive business negotiations,
a well-drafted non-circumvention and non-disclosure agreement (NCNDA) is
critical to protect your interests. Here are the four essential clauses to include:
First, be sure to include a n iron-clad Non-Circumvention Clause
This clause ensures that the receiving party cannot bypass you to engage directly with
your partners, clients, or suppliers for their own benefit. It’s crucial to specify the relationships
protected, such as both existing and potential business contacts, along with the duration of
the restriction. This safeguards your business connections from being exploited unfairly.
Second, include a Confidentiality Clause The confidentiality clause defines and
protects the sensitive information disclosed during discussions, such as trade secrets,
financials, or business plans. It should specify what constitutes “confidential information” and
how the receiving party can use or disclose it—typically restricting use to the intended
business purpose only. This ensures that your competitive advantage remains secure.
Third, be sure to include a Liquidated Damages Clause
To discourage breaches, a liquidated damages clause sets a pre-agreed financial penalty
for violations, such as circumventing business contacts or disclosing confidential information.
This clause provides predictability by outlining compensation upfront, making it easier to enforce
and minimizing the need for costly litigation. Finaly, a solid agreement also includes
a Duration and Remedies Clause It’s essential to specify how long
the non-circumvention and non-disclosure obligations will last. Additionally,
the remedies available in case of a breach—such as injunctive relief or actual damages—should be
clearly outlined, ensuring the agreement remains enforceable and effective.
Together, these clauses provide a solid framework to protect business relationships,
sensitive information, and offer legal recourse to mitigate risks.

segments.text: Sometimes in our business and personal
lives, we just need other people to keep
secrets. We want to share information
with others, but we don't want them
spreading that information or publishing
it. When we make legal promises with
others to keep secrets, we call these
promises non-disclosure agreements. But
some promises to keep secrets are just
bad ideas. They're bad for business or
they're unenforceable or they may even
be illegal. In this video, I'm going to
talk about what are non-disclosure
agreements, what do they typically
contain, and how can you spot a
non-disclosure agreement that you or
your business should never sign.
Hi, my name is John Ferrell. I'm a
Silicon Valley patent attorney.
Welcome back to my channel. Okay, so
what is a non-disclosure agreement?
Sometimes we refer to this as an NDA. A
non-disclosure agreement is a legally
binding contract between two people who
promise not to share information with a
third party. There are five terms or
components that are typical of most
non-disclosure agreements. And we're
going to go through those quickly and
then we'll practice with a hypothetical
explaining each of the components in a
bit more detail. The first and probably
most important term in the typical
non-disclosure agreement is a definition
of the confidential information.
What information is agreed to be
confidential? It could be a trade secret
or a business plan or pricing
information. The agreement doesn't need
to specifically disclose the
confidential information, but it needs
to describe what comprises the
information. Maybe it's a trade secret
or a business plan. It could be pricing
information or employment terms, but
it's important to draw a distinct
boundaries about what information is
confidential and what's not. The second
term identifies the obligation of the
receiving party.
What can the receiving party use the
information for? A third common term in
most non-disclosure agreements are
something that we call the exclusions.
And there are typically at least three
exclusions. These three exclusions
include information that's already known
by the receiving party,
information that is independently
developed by the receiving party,
and information that's rightfully
obtained from others by the receiving
party without restriction. There may be
other exclusions listed, but most
non-disclosure agreements include at
least these three. A fourth term of most
non-disclosure agreements is the length
of the agreement. How long will the
agreement last? Is it 6 months, a year,
3 years, or longer? Most non-disclosure
agreements include a specific period of
time in which the agreement is
enforceable. And the fifth term of most
non-disclosure agreements is what are
the consequences of breach? What happens
if the secret gets out? These
consequences for the breach of the
agreement may include money damages, or
they may include injunctive relief,
which is an order from the court to stop
the breach of the agreement. Okay, let's
try a really simple hypothetical to
exercise some of the terms of this
non-disclosure agreement. Let's say
you're a famous rapper and you get lost
one night at around 2:00 a.m. and you
drive your Lamborghini over my mailbox,
through my yard, and through my front
door. I wake up from all the commotion
and stumble to my living room and see
you sitting there in your Lamborghini,
one of my favorite rappers. We're both a
little dazed, me from just having woken
up and you from having taken a wild ride
through my front yard. And as soon as
the pleasantries are out of the way, you
explain to me that it's important to you
that we keep this encounter on the down
low. That you don't want your public to
find out that you've been driving
through people's front yards and front
doors. And you tell me that if I keep
this whole incident a secret, you'll
have your crew come over tomorrow and
fix my mailbox and front door, replant
my front yard, and even throw in some
fresh flower plants along my driveway.
Now, I think about this for a minute,
and then I tell you, "Okay, if you'll
throw in a selfie with me, you've got a
deal." But since I'm a lawyer, I feel
like I have to remind you that if you
walk out what used to be my front door
into what's left of my front yard, and
the yard is full of paparazzi, that
publish this to the press tomorrow, I
can't be held responsible. And likewise,
if the tow truck driver or your gardener
spills the beans, we still have a deal.
These are exclusions that don't
constitute a breach of our agreement.
And you're no slouch of a negotiator
either. And you say, "Okay, John, you've
got a deal. But if you breach this
contract within the next 3 months,
you have to erase the selfie." And after
contemplating the dire consequences of
the breach, we shake hands and we have
an agreement. The non-disclosure
agreement is binding. And normally, it's
preferable to have our non-disclosure
agreements in writing. Non-disclosure
agreements can last a long time, and it
can be difficult to remember exactly
what the terms of the agreement were.
So, when the agreements are important,
write them down, store them away. Now,
there are some circumstances where
non-disclosure agreements can be very
helpful. When discussing business deals
with potential partners or disclosing
business secrets to contractors or
consultants, evaluating new employees,
or contemplating a sale or acquisition.
Developing a new technology, maybe you
think contemplating or thinking about a
new startup, and handling intellectual
property matters. These are all
circumstances
where a written non-disclosure agreement
would be appropriate. Now, while
non-disclosure agreements can be super
helpful, there are certain situations
where it just doesn't make sense, or it
might be counterproductive
to use a non-disclosure agreement. For
example, if a non-disclosure agreement
is overly broad, or encompasses too much
material, it's probably not a good idea
to sign the non-disclosure agreement.
And the reasons for this is these broad
agreements tend to discourage
collaboration. They're counterproductive
to the sharing of information. They can
create confusion, and they can
ultimately lead to legal disputes over
what was originally agreed to and
included in the non-disclosure
agreement. A second situation in which a
non-disclosure agreement is probably
counterproductive
is with respect to normal business
interactions. If you're continually
asking for non-disclosure agreements, it
can lead to distrust, and it can be very
off-putting to customers and those
people that you do business with.
Unnecessary non-disclosure agreements
increase business friction, and make it
more difficult for successful business
to ensue. Insisting on non-disclosure
agreements for readily available public
information, it reduces the credibility
of the insisting party. These types of
non-disclosure agreements just don't
make sense, and they increase the hassle
factor of doing business. You need to be
especially careful when requiring
employees to sign non-disclosure
agreements, especially with respect to
reporting illegal activities or
harassment or discrimination. In
addition to being unenforceable, these
types of non-disclosure agreements could
be illegal. Be wary of signing
non-disclosure agreements with long
durations. Contracts that last a long
time are hard to enforce. They get lost.
People change positions. And it's very
difficult to maintain
contractual integrity over a long period
of time. It's probably reasonable to
have a non-disclosure agreement for some
period of months or a year or perhaps 3
years. But longer non-disclosure
agreements should really be evaluated.
